attendance,  and  with  excellent  results ;  450  teachers  are  paid  an  average  of  $2  per  lesson  ; 
21  weeks  per  year  is  the  average  duration  of  classes ;  1  2-3  average  class  sessions  a  week. 
Of  the  20,526  different  men  in  the  classes,  about  12,000,  or  60  per  cent.,  study  commercial  and 
language  subjects;  5,000,  or  25  per  cent.,  study  industrial  subjects,  as  drawing,  manual 
training,  etc.;  3,000,  or  15  per  cent.,  other  subjects,  as  music,  etc.

ANNUAL  REPORTS  OF  THE  AGENTS  OF  THE 
INTERNATIONAL  COMMITTEE, 

To  FEBBUARY  1,  1893. 


REPORT  OF  RICHARD  C.  MOKSE, 

General  Secretary. 
I.  — In  direct  relation  to  the  Committee  and  its  administration  of  the  work. 

As  indicated  in  his  last  report,  the  General  Secretary,  at  the  beginning 
(April,  1892),  of  the  period  covered  by  this  report,  was  absent  by  direction 
of  the  Committee,  for  the  benefit  of  his  health,  returning  to  his  official 
duties  May  25.  In  July  following,  the  resignation  of  Mr.  Brainerd  as 
Chairman  of  the  Committee  was  accepted  and  made  necessary  a  further 
distribution  of  the  work  of  administration  to  a  larger  number  of  sub- 
committees. This  change  has  necessarily  increased  the  correspondence 
and  conferences  connected  with  the  administration  of  the  work. 

1.  The  General  Secretary  has  attended,  as  usual,  the  monthly  meetings 
of  the  Committee  and  its  sub-committees,  and  has  conducted  much  of  the 
correspondence  necessitated  by  these  meetings  and  incident  to  his  office. 

2.  The  Committee's  annual  dinner  was  held  in  New  York,  November  30, 
being  preceded  by  two  days  of  conference  of  the  Committee  with  its  .sec- 
retaries.    The  dinner  was  confined  to  the  members  and  secretaries  of  the 
Committee,  and  was  followed  the  next  day,  December  1,  by  a  dinner  given 
by  friends  in  Brooklyn,  and  attended  not  only  by  members  and  secre- 
taries of  the  Committee,  but  by  many  friends  and  supporters  of  the  work. 

//.  — In  relation  to  the  secretaries  and  agents  of  the  Committee. 

1.  Correspondence  has  been  maintained  with  each  secretary  and  agent 
in  pursuance  of  the  instructions  of  the  Committee  and  its  sub-com- 
mittees.    Owing  to  special  contributions  by  generous  friends  the  Com- 
mittee was  able  to  add  to  its  force  in  October,  1892,  a  secretary  for  the 
Educational  Department,  George  B.  Hodge.     His  work  has  involved  care- 
ful study  of  what  the  Associations  have  already  accomplished  in  this  de- 
partment,  and  of  methods  and   improvements  which  might  be  wisely 
employed  by  them.     L.  H.  Roots  was  added  to  the  force  of  the  Com- 
mittee in  September,  1892,  with  special  reference  to  work  in  the  College 
Department. 

2.  In  response  to  the  request  of  State  Committees,  arrangements  were 
made  for  the   representation    of  the    Committee  at  the   36   State  and 
Provincial  Conventions  held  during  the  year  closing  March  1,  1893.     Be- 
sides its  secretaries,  five  members  of  the  Committee  co-operated  in  this 
representation  and  in  aiding  the  State  and  Provincial  Conventions.     Their 
names  are  given  in  the  list  of  such  conventions. 

3.  The  Committee  has  been  obliged,  as  in  former  years,  to  employ  the 
services  of  special  agents,  in  order  to  respond  favorably  to  requests  for 


10 

help  which  it  was  out  of  the  power  of  the  regular  force  to  meet.     The 
following  gentlemen  rendered  satisfactory  service  in  this  capacity  : 

C.  H.  Moorman  was  engaged  through  the  year  in  special  work  in  the 
Railroad  Department,  his  chief  service  being  rendered  in  connection  with 
the  organization  and  development  of  new  Railroad  Associations  on  the  line 
of  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railroad.  W.  M.  Lewis  aided  the  state  work 
in  Georgia  and  South  Carolina,  and  has  since  become  State  Secretary  in 
these  two  states.  G.  A.  Beaver,  L.  L.  Doggett,  F.  H.  Burt,  O.  F.  Cook, 
J.  C.  White,  and  F.  A.  Keller  undertook  special  errands  relating  to  the 
College  Department  at  the  request  of  the  Committee. 

Ill— Conference  at  the  office  of  the  Committee: 

1.  Personal  calls  at  the  office  for  consultation  by  officers  and  friends  of 
the  Association  from  all  parts  of  the  country  have  multiplied.  Among 
the  problems  and  emergencies  discussed  may  be  mentioned :  Securing  a 
qualified  local  or  State  Secretary;  planning  a  building  fund  canvass  or  a 
building  itself,  involving  criticism  of  architects'  plans  in  the  light  of  the 
best  Association  experience;  new  phases  in  the  metropolitan  organization 
and  the  relation  of  some  department  of  the  local  work  to  the  others;  new 
phases  and  improvements  in  the  Educational  Department;  some  critical 
emergency  in  the  state  work  in  its  relation  to  local  organizations;  and 
such  treatment  in  state  and  local  meetings  of  new  themes  relating  to  the 
development  of  various  departments  as  would  make  a  positive  contribu- 
tion to  Association  literature. 

IV. — Correspon  dence. 

1.  In  connection  with  the  change  in  the  chairmanship  of  the  Committee 
the  correspondence  and  some  of  the  cares  of  administration  devolving  on 
the  General  Secretary  have  been  temporarily  increased.     In  connection 
with  the  re-distribution  of  the  work  to  a  larger  number  of  sub-committees 
— which  has  been  wisely  carried  out — the  General  Secretary  has  been 
needed  at  an  increasing  number  of  conferences  with  these  sub-committees. 

2.  The  usual  call  for  the  week  of  prayer  in  November  was  issued,  fol- 
lowed by  an  extended  correspondence  regarding  its  observance.     En- 
couraging reports  have  been  received  from  the  great  majority  of  the  Asso- 
ciations which  followed  the  Committee's  suggestions,  and  511  Associations 
responded  favorably  to  the  International  Convention's  recommendation 
for  a  collection  in  aid  of  the  international  work. 

•  m  >]><>ndence  with  the  contributing  friends  of  the  work  was  car- 
ried on  as  usual,  but  the  additional  duties  of  administration  assigned  to 
the  Gen*  •  tary  have  made  necessary  a  distribution  to  his  associates 

of  more  financial  solicitation  and  responsibility  than  in  previous 
years.  JJv  tin-  blessing  of  God  on  the  efforts  thus  put  forth,  the  Commit- 
tee was  enabl'-<l  to  provide  for  the  increased  expenditures  necessitated 
by  the  enlargement  of  the  work. 

Similar  ••onwjMMiilriicr  has  been  held  with  the  Associations  and  friends 
contributing  to  the  support  of  the  foreign  work  of  the  Committee.  In  this 
important  matter,  the  burden  of  which  was  overtasking  the  General  Sec- 
retary, the  co-operation  of  L.  D.  Wishard  was  happily  secured  upon  his 
return  from  his  foreign  mission  tour  in  May,  1892. 


li 

4.  Correspondence  with  the  World's  Committee  at  Geneva,  Switzerland, 
lias  been  maintained,  with  a  special  reference  to  the  proposed  meeting  in 
London  of  the  thirteenth  World's  Conference  at  a  period  in  the  year  1894, 
which  shall  include  the  date  of  the  semi-centennial  celebration  of  the 
founding  of  the  parent  English-speaking  Association  in  London  on  June 
6,  1844.  The  date  of  the  Conference  has  therefore  been  fixed  for  the  week 
in  which  that  anniversary  occurs. 

V  — Personal  Visitation . 

The  General  Secretary  has  attended  (1)  the  General  Secretaries'  Con- 
ference at  Providence;  (2)  the  Student  Summer  School  at  Northfield;  (3) 
the  Pennsylvania  State  Convention;  (4)  the  sessions  of  the  special  com- 
mittee to  prepare  the  "Topics  for  Young  Men's  Meetings  and  Bible 
Classes"  for  1893,  at  Orange,  N.  J. 

In  addition  consultations  were  held  with  Association  officers  in  a  num- 
ber of  cities,  and  several  anniversary  and  other  addresses  have  been 
delivered. 

He  has  also  continued  to  serve  upon  the  Graduate  Committee  of  the 
Yale  University  Association  ;  and  as  a  trustee  of  the  Association  Training 
Schools  at  Springfield  and  Chicago ;  and  has  co-operated  with  the 
National  Council  of  Great  Britain,  as  its  corresponding  member  for 
America,  and  with  the  International  Central  Committee  as  its  Ameri- 
can honorary  secretary. 


REPORT  OF  ERSKINE  UHL, 

Office  Secretary. 

The  office  force  is  the  same  as  last  year,  consisting  of  Messrs.  Wieting, 
Thorpe,  Glover,  Leonard,  and  Ninde,  each  of  whom  takes  part  in  the 
correspondence,  preparation  of  matter  for  publication,  and  general  office 
work,  while  Mr.  Glover  has  special  charge  of  the  secretarial  work,  and 
Mr.  Leonard  of  the  college  work.  Considerable  other  office  help  is 
necessary. 

The  following  statement  of  the  secretarial  work  covers  the  efforts  of  all 
the  International  Secretaries,  so  far  as  reported  to  the  office  : 

Since  April  1,  1892,  64  men  have  found  positions  as  general  secretaries 
and  physical  directors  through  our  aid. 

At  the  office,  personal  intercourse  or  correspondence,  sometimes  very 
extended,  was  held  during  the  year  with  118  others  that  were  not  pre- 
pared to  undertake  the  work,  or  that  found  places  in  it  through  their  own 
efforts.  The  visiting  secretaries  of  the  Committee  frequently  confer  on 
the  same  subject  with  young  men  that  do  not  come  into  any  communica- 
tion with  the  office. 

On  April  1,  1892,  13  vacancies  were  on  record  as  needing  our  help  ;  102 
applications  have  been  added  to  these,  making  115  altogether,  for  state 
secretaries  and  their  assistants,  for  general  secretaries  and  their  assist-, 
ants,  and  for  physical  directors.  Of  the  102  vacancies,  we  assisted  in 
filling  64  ;  30  were  filled  through  the  action  of  others  ;  3  were  postponed  ; 
and  18  now  stand  on  our  books. 


12 

Of  the  vacancies  just  mentioned  1  was  in  Canada  ;  6  in  New  England ;  22 
in  New  York,  New  Jersey  and  Pennsylvania  ;  16  in  states  west  of  these  ; 
and  19  at  the  south.  In  addition  to  the  vacancies  already  referred  to,  ad- 
vice has  been  sought  from  the  secretaries  of  the  Commitee  regarding  at 
least  double  the  number  mentioned  above,  but  not  so  definitely  as  to 
warrant  their  entrance  upon  our  register.  As  secretarial  positions  steadily 
grow  in  number  and  importance,  an  increasing  proportion  of  secretarial 
work  in  the  aggregate  is  done  by  the  State  Committees  and  their  secre- 
taries, independently  of  the  International  Committee. 

Besides  attending  to  correspondence  and  many  callers,  a  number  of 
plans  of  Association  building,  have  been  examined  and  considerable 
material  has  been  prepared  for  publication.  After  much  effort  prolonged 
through  several  years,  the  "  Hand  Book  "  was  issued  in  November  last. 


REPORT  OF  ROBERT  WEIDENSALL, 

Secretary. 

During  the  ten  months  covered  by  this  report  I  have  traveled  nearly 
19,000  miles  in  twenty -one  states,  spent  more  or  less  time  in  157  cities  and 
towns,  and  visited  32  Associations,  some  of  them  several  times,  affording 
them  special  assistance. 

I  attended  the  International  Secretaries'  Conference  at  Providence, 
R.  I.,  and  read  a  paper  on  "The  Evangelical  Basis  ;".  the  Massachusetts 
State  Convention  at  Pittsfield,  reading  a  paper  on  "Volunteer  Work;" 
the  Inter-Seminary  Alliance,  at  Auburn,  N.  Y.,  giving  a  paper  on 
"Home  Missions;"  the  Young  Women's  Christian  Association  Summer 
School  at  Lake  Gen<  ling  a  paper  on  the  evangelical  basis  of 

the  society.     By  request   I  was  present  and  delivered  Association  ad- 
dresses at  the  Rock  River  Assembly,  Dixon,  111.  ;  at  the  dedication  of  the 
Association  building,  Ottumwa,  la.;  at  the  anniversaries  of  the  Associa- 
in  Stockton,  Cal.,  and  Council  Bluffs  and  Des  Moines,  la.     In  ad- 
dition to  the  above  meetings  I  was  present  all  or  a  part  of  the  time  at  the 
nt   Summer  School  and  the  Western  Secretarial  Institute  at  Lake 
Geneva.     The    Chicago   and  Springfield  Training  Schools    were    both 
•;d. 

uvitation  I  !  t  \vo  papers  for  the  Kentucky  State  Convention, 

one  paper  and  an  address  for  that  of  Tennessee,  and  one  paper  each  for 
the  Georgia  and  South  Carolina  Conventions.  Conferences  were  held 
with  tin?  State  Committees  of  California  and  Nebraska,  with  a  number  of 
State  Secretaries  and  within..:  rectors,  particularly  at  Omaha  and 

Lincoln,  Neb.,  in  connection  with  local  finances,  some  assistance  being 
rendered  in  a  canvass  at  the  latter  place.  Conference  and  correspond- 
ence have  also  been  hud  with  international,  state  and  local  officers  re- 
garding finances,  secretarial  changes  and  other  difficult  problems  in  the 
work.  'laces  were  visited  in  connection  with  financial  solicitation 

mnal  work.     I  re-organized  an  Association  in  the  Western 
Normal  School  at  Lincoln,  Neb. 

Much  correspondence  has  been  had  concerning  the  county  work.  The 
reports  of  t  from  the  field  and  its  endorsement  by  state  and  inter- 

national officers  who  have  come  into  contact  with  it  are  convincing  proofs 


13 

that  it  is  not  only  feasible  but  when  properly  organized  and  officered 
proves  successful. 

In  addition  to  being  present  and  participating  in  the  Lake  Geneva 
gathering  of  the  Young  Women's  Christian  Association,  I  have  given  that 
organization  aid  by  writing  for  its  official  organ,  by  conference  with 
its  workers  at  Chicago  and  elsewhere,  by  assisting  in  inaugurating  its 
state  work  in  Massachusetts,  and  by  advising  with  the  State  Secretary  of 
Nebraska  and  Missouri  regarding  difficult  problems  in  her  work. 

Owing  to  partially  broken  health  my  work  has  been  more  or  less  scat- 
tered and  irregular.  I  trust  the  Lord  will  make  it  accomplish  what  in 
His  sight  will  be  for  the  best  in  extending  His  Kingdom  among  young 
men. 

EEPOET  OF  THOMAS  K.  CBEE, 

Secretary. 

Most  of  the  past  year  has  been  given  to  work  in  the  New  York  office, 
largely  in  the  direction  of  financial  correspondence.  Considerable  time 
has  been  given  to  assisting  local  Associations  in  different  parts  of  the 
country  in  arranging  the  finances  in  connection  with  building  movements, 
such  as  securing  loans  and  placing  buildings  in  the  hands  of  trustees,  and 
inaugurating  a  more  systematic  business  management. 

I  visited  Chicago  in  connection  with  the  proposed  exhibit  of  the 
Associations  at  the  Columbian  Exposition.  Eight  hundred  and  seventy- 
five  square  feet  have  been  secured  in  a  good  location  in  the  building 
devoted  to  education  and  the  liberal  arts,  and  arrangements  are  now  in 
progress  that  will  secure  a  creditable  exhibit  of  pictures  of  Association 
buildings,  documents,  and  statistics  relating  to  the  various  departments. 
It  has  also  been  arranged  in  connection  with  the  exposition  to  hold  a 
congress  in  the  interest  of  Association  work  in  all  parts  of  the  world.  A 
committee  has  been  secured  representing  the  various  countries  interested 
in  Association  work. 

In  the  spring  I  visited  a  number  of  Associations  in  New  England,  hold- 
ing conferences,  and  addressing  public  meetings  ;  the  Training  School  at 
Springfield  was  also  visited.  I  attended  the  Secretaries'  Conference  at 
Providence.  During  the  year  I  visited  a  number  of  Associations  in  New 
York  aod  Pennsylvania,  and  in  the  fall  I  visited  the  northwest,  aiding  a 
number  of  Associations  financially  and  otherwise,  and  conferring  with 
local  and  State  Committees. 

The  close  of  the  year  finds  me  in  the  south  where  seventeen  years  ago 
George  A.  Hall  and  myself,  as  representatives  of  the  International 
Committee,  aided  in  reorganizing  Association  work. 

I  have  kept  in  constant  communication  with  Associations  abroad,  more 
particularly  with  those  in  France,  with  which  I  have  been  specially 
identified.  The  new  French  Association  building  in  Rue  Trevise,  in 
Paris,  costing  $200,000,  is  now  completed  and  will  be  formally  opened 
with  appropriate  ceremonies,  April  25.  Some  of  the  most  prominent 
French  gentlemen  have  exhibited  their  substantial  interest  in  this  build- 
ing enterprise.  James  Stokes,  for  twenty-five  years  an  honored  mem- 
ber of  the  International  Committee,  and  his  family  gave  the  generous  sum 
of  $80,000  to  this  building  ;  all  the  rest  of  the  money  needed  was  secured 


14 

from  French  people.  The  resignation  of  F.  A.  Gaylord,  as  secretary 
of  the  Paris  Association,  is  deeply  regretted.  During  the  three  years  in 
which  he  has  been  officially  connected  with  it,  the  membership,  in  rented 
rooms,  has  increased  from  80  to  650,  and  with  the  new  building,  we  con- 
fidently expect  that  the  membership  will  soon  reach  2,000.  Paul  Theis, 
a  graduate  of  the  Springfield  Training  School,  will  succeed  Mr.  Gaylord 
as  secretary.  This  work  is  conducted  entirely  by  French  young  men  and 
is  in  the  interest  of  the  same  class  exclusively. 


KEPOKT  OF  LUTHER  D.  WISHAED, 

Secretary. 

During  the  last  four  of  my  eleven  years  work  (1877-1888)  as  College 
Secretary  of  the  International  Committee  among  American  students,  the 
conviction  steadily  grew  upon  me  that  the  Student  Young  Men's  Chris- 
tian Association  is  capable  of  adaptation  to  students  in  Europe,  and  also 
to  those  in  the  government  and  missionary  colleges  of  Asia,  Africa,  and 
South  America ;  and  that  a  Christian  movement  of  students  in  these 
countries  will  prove  to  be  the  van-guard  in  a  mighty  evangelistic  move- 
ment which  will  reach  all  classes  of  young  men  throughout  the  world,  and 
enlist  them  in  the  speedy  proclamation  of  the  gospel  to  every  creature. 
One  of  the  strongest  evidences  that  the  time  was  ripe  for  such  a  move- 
ment appeared  in  the  spontaneous  organization  of  student  associations  in 
Germany,  Africa,  and  several  countries  in  Asia.  This  evidence  was  sup- 
ported by  a  call  from  the  missionaries  of  Madras  for  a  man  to  devote  his 
life  to  the  organization  of  this  work  in  India.  Notwithstanding  these  in- 
<li<-;itions,  I  did  not  feel  justified  in  urging  this  foreign  movement  upon 
the  American  Associations  without  making  a  careful  study  of  the  wide 
t'u-lil.  Accordingly,  obtaining  leave  of  absence  from  the  service  of  the 
Committee,  and,  of  course,  without  expense  to  it,  I  left  America  in  March, 
1888,  for  a  five  months'  study  of  the  situation  in  the  European  univer- 
and,  later,  after  three  months  and  a  half  spent  in  this  country 
during  the  autumn  of  that  year,  I  sailed  for  Japan  in  December,  under 
the  instructions  of  the  Central  International  Committee  at  Geneva, 
rland,  and  after  spending  nearly  three  years  in  Asia,  a  month  in 
Egypt,  and  six  months  in  Europe,  returned  to  America  in  April,  1892. 

is  not  the  place  to  report  this  foreign  tour.     But  after  visiting 
nearly  two  hundred  mission  stations,  and  nearly  all  of  the  leading  educa- 
tional centers  of  Asia,  I  am  persuaded  that  the  American  Associations 
national  Committee  have  never  been  confronted  by  a  more 
respoi  nity — by  a  work  more  difficult  of  execution,  yet  more 

1  with  promise — than  this  movement,  whose  purpose  is  the  enlist- 
men  in  non-Christian  lands  to  seek  the  salva- 
t\\n  hundred  million  young  men  of  these  lands.    Never  has 
the  C<-  her  mark  of  confidence  than  is  expressed  in 

the  calls  from  hundreds  o  88,  representing  at  least  a  score  of 

denominations  in  Japan,  China,  India,  Ceylon,  the  Turkish  Empire  and 

uent. 

At  the  call  of  the  Committee  I  resumed  active  connection  with  it  on  the 
twentieth  of  last  April,  and  have  been  asked  to  assume  a  special  relation 


15 

to  the  Foreign  Department.  In  submitting  a  report  for  the  last  nine 
months,  the  fact  should  be  noted  that  although  associated  with  the  Com- 
mittee for  fifteen  years,  I  am  for  the  second  time  engaged  in  a  pioneer 
movement,  and  cannot  be  expected  to  report  very  much  progress  in  so 
short  a  period. 

The  time  has  been  occupied,  first,  in  helping  to  secure  support  for  the 
work  already  inaugurated  under  the  leadership  of  the  Committee's  Secre- 
taries in  Japan,  India  and  Brazil,  and,  second,  in  paving  the  way  for 
beginning  work  in  China,  and  at  one  other  point,  at  least,  in  India. 

First. — In  aid  of  the  work  already  begun,  the  time  has  been  divided 
among  Associations,  churches  and  individuals. 

1. — Work  in  Associations,  including  local,  state  and  international 
organizations.  In  public  addresses  the  members  of  the  Associations 
have  been  informed  of  the  condition  of  young  men  in  foreign  lands, 
and  the  beginnings  which  our  Associations  have  made  in  many  of 
those  lands.  They  have  been  incited  to  discharge  the  heavy  obligation 
which  the  awful  condition  of  young  men  in  non-Christian  lands  imposes 
on  us.  The  interest  thus  awakened  has  been  followed  up  by  planning  for 
the  immediate  formation  of  extension  committees,  and  the  appointment  of 
regular  meetings  to  study  the  fields  and  the  questions  relating  to  the 
extension  of  our  work  at  home  and  abroad.  It  has  been  invariably 
recommended  that  in  each  Association  one  committee  be  charged  with 
the  supervision  of  the  entire  extension  work,  state,  international,  foreign 
and  educational.  I  have  organized  the  extension  movement  in  several 
Associations,  strengthened  it  where  it  had  already  been  inaugurated,  and 
have  in  a  few  instances  made  special  appeals  in  behalf  of  the  support  of 
the  foreign  secretaries  of  the  Committee.  Eleven  conventions  and  twenty- 
eight  Associations  have  been  visited,  where  $3,475  were  pledged  toward 
the  extension  work  at  home  and  abroad. 

2. — Work  in  churches.  Every  convenient  opportunity  has  been  im- 
proved to  address  churches  on  the  home  and  foreign  work  of  the  Com- 
mittee, that  in  this  way  there  may  be  insured  a  deeper  and  wider 
spirit  of  prayer  for  this  movement.  The  Committee's  work  among 
students  is  so  direct  an  outgrowth  of  the  day  of  prayer  for  colleges  that  a 
wide  report  of  the  work  will  greatly  promote  the  observance  of  that  day, 
and  also  lead  a  multitude  of  Christians  to  continue  instant  in  prayer  for 
this  work.  I  have  addressed  twenty -five  prominent  churches. 

3. — Work  with  individuals.  Considerable  time  has  been  devoted  to  the 
work  of  selecting  a  number  of  men  as  contributors  of  twenty-five  dollars 
and  upwards  in  aid  of  the  foreign  work.  The  pledges  of  eighteen  such 
persons  amount  to  $5,884,  almost  all  of  which  it  is  hoped  will  be  per- 
manently renewed. 

Second. — The  occupation  of  new  fields.  Mr.  J.  Campbell  White,  a 
graduate  in  the  class  of  1890  of  Wooster  University,  having  had  experi- 
ence in  our  work  as  a  College  Secretary  of  the  Committee  and  also  as 
traveling  secretary  of  the  Student  Volunteer  Movement,  has  accepted  the 
appointment  of  the  Committee  to  become  one  of  its  secretaries  on  the 
foreign  field.  Mr.  White's  salary  and  a  large  part  of  his  expenses  have 
already  been  guaranteed  by  members  of  the  Montreal  Association. 

Frank  H.  Wood,   at  the  Committee's  call,  accepted  last  October   an 


16 

appointment  to  the  work  in  India.  After  four  months'  service  he  decided 
that  he  lacked  certain  indispensable  qualifications  for  the  work  and  has 
returned  to  this  country.  Effort  is  being  made  to  secure  a  substitute  for 
him. 

To  summarize.  Eighty -four  visits  have  been  made  to  14  conventions, 
28  city  and  13  College  Associations  and  25  churches.  Pledges  have  been 
secured  from  Associations  and  individuals  amounting  to  $9,359.  I  have 
traveled  27,000  miles.  My  time  during  the  nine  months  has  been  dis- 
tributed as  follows :  Visits,  four  months ;  travel,  two  months ;  office 
work,  two  months ;  vacation,  one  month. 

The  responses  made  to  appeals  in  behalf  of  the  foreign  work  have  been 
so  uniformly  hearty  that  I  believe  that  the  Committee  will  be  in  a  position 
at  an  early  day  to  answer  some  of  the  more  urgent  of  the  calls  which 
have  come  and  will  continue  to  come,  until  the  Gospel  shall  be  preached 
to  all  young  men. 


BEPOET  OF  HENEY  E.  BEOWN, 

Secretary. 

The  past  year  has  been  given  chiefly  to  Manitoba,  the  Dakotas,  Minne- 
sota and  Kansas ;  it  may  be  broadly  summarized  in  the  following  ten 
groups : 

1. — State  and  Provincial  Committees  have  been  conferred  with  at  five 
places  regarding  a  large  variety  of  questions.  More  and  more  the  travel- 
ing secretary  is  able  to  gather  facts  and  plans  of  work  in  one  section  to 
report  to  another,  together  with  any  suggestions  which  his  general  study 
makes  possible.  Volumes  of  printed  advice  can  never  take  the  place  of 
a  personal  statement  that  one  has  seen  a  plan  succeed  or  fail  in  an  ad- 
jacent field. 

2. — Local  Boards.  One  to  four  regular  meetings  have  been  held  with 
such  boards  in  seven  cities.  These,  together  with  many  informal  meet- 
ings with  chairmen  and  committees,  have  given  frequent  opportunities 
for  the  study  of  local  fields  and  for  advising  modifications  in  their 
methods  and  work.  Visiting  an  Association  when  called  on  account  of 
some  serious  trouble  evidently  is  useful,  but  also  an  unannounced  visit  of 
kindly  sympathy  and  cooperation,  in  the  hope  of  anticipating  serious 
differences  by  timely  remedies  has  been  found  to  be  equally  needed. 
Two  Associations  were  re-organized.  Lots  were  selected  at  two  points, 
Plans  for  buildings  were  considered  for  two  places.  One  canvass  for 
annual  expenses  was  begun.  Several  days  were  spent  at  one  point  aiding 
the  board  in  a  search  for  suitable  rooms. 

3. — ^  ^'cretaries.    A  constant  watch  for  suitable  men,  together 

with  some  Miiily  of  various  places  that  have  needed  men,  has  usually 
•  1  in  turning  the  whole  matter  over  to  a  State  Secretary  or  to  a 
local  boar.!.  I«T  such  action  as  shall  finally  seem  best.  In  one  case, 
after  interviews.  l«tt<  is,  telegrams  and  disappointments,  it  became 
necessary  to  commend  ami  secun;  the  employment  of  a  secretary  by  wire. 
Many  thanks  have  been  received  for  the  man  of  God  that  was  is  this- 
case  Bectu 


17 

4.— Conferences  have  included  Iowa  City  deputation,  St.  Paul  college, 
Providence  general  secretaries,  and  Faribault  county.  Each  became  an 
important  means  of  education  and  furnished  opportunities  for  promoting 
our  definite  work.  The  most  helpful  of  these  gatherings  was  the  college 
deputation  conference.  More  real  work  was  done  in  the  three  days  of  this 
conference,  under  the  direction  and  instruction  of  the  College  Secretaries 
of  the  International  Committee,  than  I  had  ever  before  seen  compressed 
into  so  small  a  compass. 

5. — Bible  Study.  Meetings  or  classes  for  promoting  special  forms  of 
Bible  study  have  been  held  in  four  cities,  three  colleges,  one  normal 
school,  and  three  summer  institutes.  Most  of  this  time  has  been  given 
to  the  study  of  books,  resulting  in  an  outline  of  each  book,  with  key- 
words by  which  to  recall  each  chapter,  prepared,  revised  and  committed 
to  memory  by  each  pupil.  Sample  outlines  have  been  prepared  and 
printed  of  the  whole  New  Testament  for  the  reference  use  of  students  and 
classes  as  they  continue  this  study  through  the  year. 

The  study  of  passages  for  inquirers  has  'also  occupied  considerable 
time.  Two  pamphlets,  formerly  prepared  as  aids  to  this  work,  have  been 
revised  and  printed  with  alternate  blank  pages  on  which  each  student 
records  the  results  of  his  own  thinking  regarding  each  class  of  inquirers, 
their  excuses,  real  condition,  the  kinds  of  truth  they  need,  the  passages 
needed  and  how  used.  In  both  lines  of  study  the  student  is  urged  to 
careful  original  work  and  frequent  comparison  with  the  printed  page  pro- 
vided. 

6. — Conferences  with  Pastors  have  been  held  in  five  cities,  regarding 
various  interests  of  the  young  men.  Such  meetings  always  result  in  a 
closer  relation  between  the  local  secretary  and  the  pastors,  to  the  decided 
advantage  of  the  churches  and  Association.  Such  meetings  are  found  to 
furnish  an  excellent  opportunity  for  correcting  erroneous  impressions  re- 
garding true  Association  work,  and  for  learning  how  the  general  secretary 
can  better  serve  the  churches  in  their  efforts  to  save  young  men. 

7. — Anniversaries  and  Other  Public  Addresses.  The  former  at  five  points 
and  the  latter  at  nearly  all  places  in  any  field  where  a  Sabbath  was  spent. 
It  is  not  easy  to  report  the  results  of  such  meetings,  though  many 
indications  have  been  noted  of  an  increase  through  them  of  public 
interest  in  the  local  Associations. 

8. — Business  Men's  Meetings  have  been  held  in  six  cities  for  increasing 
interest  in  local  or  general  work.  Remarkable  among  such  meetings 
was  one  at  which  the  business  men  assured  the  Association  board  that 
the  price  asked  for  a  proposed  lot  was  too  high,  and  they  could  (and 
afterwards  did)  get  it  materially  reduced.  At  another  such  meeting,  in  a 
Kansas  city,  leading  men,  after  many  questions,  expressed  themselves 
as  thoroughly  satisfied  with  the  present  plan  of  Association  work  in 
Kansas,  and  promised  renewed  help. 

9. — Colleges.  Eleven  colleges  and  one  normal  school  were  visited,  also 
the  officers  of  three  other  colleges ;  one  vacation  college  band  was 
conducted.  Meetings  with  college  boys,  whether  for  Bible  study  or  for 
considering  their  various  forms  of  work,  seemed  always  fruitful  of 
increased  interest  and  more  definite  work  by  and  for  students.  Classes  in 


18 

systematic  Bible  study  were  organized  in  about  half  of  the  colleges 
visited. 

10.  Conferences  with  State  and  local  Secretaries.  Some  such  are  arranged 
for  in  advance  for  special  purposes;  others  are  unexpected.  They  last 
from  a  few  moments  while  the  train  stops,  to  hours  or  days  spent  in  the 
Association  rooms,  or  at  the  home  of  the  secretary,  planning,  working, 
and  praying  together.  It  is  good  to  know  these  noble  men  in  these  ways. 
The  hardships  of  travel  are  forgotten  during  such  visits,  and  courage 
comes  for  future  difficulties. 

The  work  of  the  year  has  been  much  varied.  Plenty  of  difficulties  to 
keep  one  awake,  enough  failures  to  make  him  humble,  and  abundant 
blessings  from  above  to  give  hope  for  larger  harvests  in  the  year  to  come. 


REPOBT  OF  CLAUS  OLANDT,  JK., 

Secretary  of  the  German  Department. 

Of  the  .past  ten  months  nine  have  been  given  to  work  among  German- 
speaking  young  men.  Two  months,  during  a  number  of  visits,  were 
spent  in  Buffalo,  assisting  in  planning  for  the  new  building  and  in  helping 
to  increase  the  fund  from  $12,000  to  $17,000.  A  visit  to  Quincy,  111., 
resulted  in  starting  a  building  fund.  At  Chicago  I  assisted  in  enlarging 
the  building  fund  during  two  short  visits.  At  Brooklyn  help  was  given 
n  securing  funds  to  employ  a  general  secretary,  to  organize  a  German 
branch,  and  to  obtain  $6,000  toward  a  building  fund.  At  New  York  some 
Assistance  was  rendered  in  securing  the  funds  to  pay  the  mortgage  on  the 
branch  building.  At  Philadelphia  I  assisted  in  augmenting  the  building 
fund  and  in  securing  a  little  money  for  current  expenses,  and  was  also 
present  at  the  dedication  of  the  gymnasium  building.  One  week  was 
spent  at  St.  Louis,  and  a  short  visit  was  made  to  Baltimore.  Considerable 
time  was  given  to  office  work. 

Two  German  conferences  have  been  held  ;  at  Quincy,  111. ,  in  July, 
attended  by  forty  men,  and  at  New  York,  in  November,  at  which  thirty 
were  present.  I  was  present  and  participated  in  both.  One  month  was 
given  to  financial  solicitation  for  the  International  Committee,  and  I  also 
secured  some  money  for  the  work  in  India. 

As  in  previous  years  time  and  attention  have  been  devoted  to  securing 
men  as  general  secretaries,  assistants  and  physical  directors,  and  in  aiding 
them  to  obtain  a  preparation.  Several  are  now  in  training  at  the  Spring- 
field School,  and  two  have  for  several  months  held  the  position  of  assistant 
secretary.  The  secretarial  force  now  numbers  seventeen,  besides  several 
who  are  giving  part  of  their  time  as  physical  directors. 

At  Milwaukee,  where  there  is  a  large  field  for  work  among  German- 
•  men,  the  German  branch  has  been  changed  in  name  to 
branch. 

The  debt  on  the  New  York  German  branch  building,  amounting  to 
$20,000,  was  paid  December  31.  Toward  this  one  German  friend  gave 
$5,000,  the  largest  sum  ever  given  by  a  German  to  our  work.  The 
;">,000  for  necessary  alterations  and  better  equip- 
ment. The  building  debt  of  the  North  Side  German  branch,  St.  Louis, 


19 

lias  also  been  reduced  $1,100.  The  boards  of  trustees  rin  six  cities  now 
hold  property  for  German  work  aggregating  over  $160,000.  Aside  from 
this  San  Francisco  has  a  building  fund  of  $760,  and  Chicago  one  of  $1,100; 
•Quincy,  111.,  has  $10,000  pledged,  a  corner  lot  43x189  has  been  purchased 
and  plans  for  a  building  accepted,  while  the  organization  is  not  yet  two 
years  old.  Buffalo  has  $17,000  pledged,  has  secured  a  corner  lot  50x150, 
and  plans  have  been  passed  upon  and  bids  received.  At  Brooklyn  an 
option  of  sixty  days  has  been  obtained  on  a  corner  lot  50x100,  in  the  heart 
of  a  German  quarter,  to  cost  $26,000,  and  $6,000  have  been  secured 
toward  this  amount.  Three  hundred  young  men  have  also  pledged  for 
membership. 

In  many  other  respects  the  German  work  has  made  good  progress  and 
Ihe  outlook  is  hopeful. 

In  the  resignation  of  James  Stokes,  from  the  International  Committee, 
•the  German  friends  feel  that  they  have  sustained  a  great  loss. 


REPORT  OF  C.  K.  OBER, 

Secretary. 

The  time  covered  by  this  report,  from  May  16,  1892,  to  February  1, 
1893,  has  been  given  chiefly  to  the  general  work  in  the  south  and  south- 
west. The  last  part  of  May  and  the  whole  of  June  were  spent  at  Atlanta, 
•Ga. ,  and  at  Knoxville,  Tenn. ,  perfecting  the  preliminary  arrangements  for 
the  joint  session  at  Knoxville  of  the  Southern  Student  Summer  School 
and  the  Southern  Secretarial  Institute.  This  gathering,  attended  by 
170  college  students  from  50  southern  colleges,  and  by  over  30  represen- 
tatives of  the  state  and  local  Associations  in  the  south,  was  in  the  highest 
degree  successful  and  marked  a  new  era  in  the  development  of  Associa- 
tion work  in  the  southern  states. 

Directly  after  the  Knoxville  gathering  I  attended  the  session  of  the 
"World's  Student  Conference  at  Northfield,  Mass. ,  closing  July  14.  The 
last  half  of  July  and  the  month  of  August  were  given  to  rest,  office  and 
financial  work,  correspondence  and  preparation  for  the  fall  and  winter's 
work.  The  first  week  of  September  was  spent  with  College  Secretary 
Mott  in  Bible  study  and  in  revising  our  pamphlet  on  "  Personal  Work, " 
for  the  use  of  Bible  training  classes.  The  second  week  in  September  was 
spent  in  New  York  city,  in  office  work  and  conference  with  members  and 
secretaries  of  the  Committee.  From  September  15  to  30,  in  company 
with  State  Secretary  H.  O.  Williams,  I  visited  the  Associations  at  Newport 
News,  Hampton,  Norfolk,  Portsmouth,  Lynchburg,  Staunton  and  Roan- 
oke,  Ya. ,  and  also  attended  the  quarterly  meeting  of  the  Virginia  State 
•Committee  at  Richmond  and  a  district  conference  at  Harrisonburg,  Va. 

October  1  to  4,  in  Atlanta,  Ga. ,  I  attended  a  meeting  of  the  Georgia 
State  Committee,  at  which  the  plan  of  a  joint  state  work  of  Georgia  with 
South  Carolina  was  approved  and  adopted,  and  a  call  was  extended  to  W. 
M.  Lewis,  of  Waco,  Texas,  to  become  their  State  Secretary.  In  Atlanta, 
also,  I  held  conference  with  International  Secretary  Andersen,  then  act- 
ing State  Secretary  of  Georgia,  relative  to  the  work  in  Georgia  and  other 
southern  states ;  also  with  F.  L.  Willis,  State  Secretary  of  Alabama,  con- 
cerning the  work  in  that  state.  October  5  to  10  was  spent  in  Nashville 


20 

and  Clarksville,  Term.,  in  attendance  at  the  convention  and  in  conference^ 
with  the  officers  and  members  of  the  State  Committee.  From  this  time 
until  December  7,  I  gave  attention  to  a  line  of  systematic  correspondence, 
etc. ,  centering  at  the  New  York  office. 

On  December  10,  I  took  up,  at  St.  Louis,  Mo. ,  a  closer  relation  to  the 
general  work  in  the  southwest.  In  December  I  attended  a  quarterly 
meeting  of  the  Missouri  State  Committee,  and  with  State  Secretary  Child 
visited  the  St.  Joseph  and  Kansas  City  Associations.  I  also  had  a  con- 
ference at  Nashville  with  the  chairman  of  the  State  Committee  of  Ten- 
nessee, and  at  Knoxville  met  the  southern  State  Secretaries  and  Inter- 
national Secretary  Andersen  in  conference  concerning  the  general  work  in 
the  south.  I  also  visited  the  New  Orleans  Association  in  the  interests  of 
plans  for  a  larger  work  and  a  possible  building  canvass. 

During  January,  with  State  Secretary  Herr,  I  visited  the  Associations 
at  Pine  Bluff,  Little  Hock  and  Texarkana,  in  Arkansas,  and  attended  a 
meeting  of  the  State  Committee  in  Little  Bock.  At  this  meeting  the 
committee  approved  the  plan  contemplating  a  future  working  relation 
between  Arkansas  and  Louisiana,  by  which  one  State  Secretary  would 
superintend  the  work  in  both  states.  I  also  visited,  with  State  Secretary 
Wayte,  the  Associations  of  Waco,  Corsicana,  San  Antonio,  Houston, 
Galveston,  Dallas,  Denison  and  Fort  Worth,  in  Texas,  and  attended  a 
meeting  of  the  State  Committee  at  Dallas.  My  work  in  Texas  had 
reference  chiefly  to  the  strengthening  of  the  state  work  and  to  its  enlarge- 
ment by  the  placing  of  a  second  man  in  the  field,  and  substantial  progress 
was  made  in  this  direction.  Assistance  has  also  been  given  Mr.  Andersen 
in  arranging  for  a  state  work  in  Mississippi,  in  cooperation  with  the  State 
Committee  of  Alabama.  I  visited  the  Colored  Associations  at  Norfolk 
and  Lynchburg,  Va.,  and  have  conferred  with  International  Secretary 
Hunton,  concerning  the  plans  for  this  special  work  among  colored  young 
men  in  other  cities  and  in  educational  institutions.  Some  attention  has 
also  been  given  to  the  work  among  railroad  men  in  the  south,  chiefly  at 
Atlanta,  Ga. ;  and,  in  conference  with  Secretaries  Mott  and  Brockman,  I 
have  aided  in  the  extension  and  development  of  Association  work  among 
college  students,  particularly  in  the  south  and  southwest.  Some  atten- 
tion has  also  been  given  to  the  finances  of  the  International  Committee, 
especially  with  reference  to  the  enlargement  of  work  in  the  south,  and  in 
connection  with  work  among  college  students. 


REPORT  OF    P.    AUGUSTUS  WIETING, 

Secr< 

The  work  of  the  past  year  at  the  central  office,  where  my  time  has  been 

entiivly  spent,  with  the  exception  of  a  few  months  that  I  was  obliged  ta 

be  absent  on  account  of  the  ill  health  referred  to  in  my  last  report, 

has  been  fully  up  to  former  years,  and  in  some  respects,  more  taxing  than 

•i  -fore.     The  correspondence,  which  forms  so  important  an  item  in 

flk-e  work,  has  been  very  extend 

The  growth  in  the  publication  department  has  been  very  marked,  and 
has  required  more  careful  attention  than  in  any  previous  year.  The  usual 
annual  publications  of  the  Committee — the  Year  Book  and  the  Topics- 


21 

ior  Young  Men's  Meetings  and  Bible  Classes,  were  issued  in  May  and 
November,  respectively.  The  most  important  publication  of  the  year,  and 
indeed  of  any  year  since  the  Committee  undertook  this  line  of  work,  was 
the  "Hand  Book  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations,"  a  cloth 
bound  volume  of  over  500  pages.  This  valuable  book  was  the  result  of 
the  long  and  careful  efforts  of  several  competent  men,  and  the  reception 
that  has  been  accorded  to  it  has  fully  justified  its  publication. 

In  addition  to  the  above,  the  following  books,  pamphlets,  and  blanks 
have  been  published  by  the  Committee  since  my  last  report:  "Studies  in 
the  Gospel  of  Luke  "  (Robert  E.  Speer) ;  "  Studies  in  the  Book  of  Acts  " 
(Robert  E.  Speer);  "Christ  Among  Men"  (James  McConaughy);  "Per- 
sonal Work,"  revised  edition  (C.  K.  Ober  and  J.  R.  Mott);  "First  steps 
toward  Organizing  an  Association"  (W.  A.  Hunton);  "The  Railroad  De- 
partment a  Railroad  Specialty"  (C.  L.  Gates);  "The  Railroad  Depart- 
ment" with  testimonials;  "Railroad  Association  Buildings"  (C.  J. 
Hicks);  "Manual  for  Physical  Measurements"  (Dr.  Luther  Gulick); 
Memorandum  of  Payments  to  Treasurer;  Treasurer's  Report  Blanks; 
Treasurer's  Comparative  Report  Blanks;  Daily  Record  of  Work  and 
Statistics;  Monthly  Record  of  Statistics;  Comparative  Statistical  Report 
Blanks;  Applications  for  Membership;  Membership  Cards;  Railroad  As- 
sociation Financial  and  Statistical  Report  Blanks ;  Pentathlon  Certificates 
(small  and  large  sizes);  Penthathlon  Badges;  Commercial  Traveler's 
Report  Form.  Also  the  following  pamphlets  reprinted  from  the  Hand 
Book:  "State  and  Provincial  Work,"  "State  and  Provincial  Conven- 
tions," " District  Work, "  "  The  International  Work,"  "Suggestions  re- 
garding an  Association  Building,"  "  The  Membership  of  an  Association," 
"  The  Financial  Management  of  an  Association,"  "The  Work  of  Infor- 
mation and  Relief,"  "The  Relation  of  Women  to  our  Work,"  "The 
Records  of  an  Association  and  the  Public  Presentation  of  the  Work," 
"The  Bible  in  Association  Work,"  "Our  Religious  Meetings,"  "Our 
Educational  Work,"  "The  Social  Work  of  an  Association,"  "The  Phy- 
sical Work  of  an  Association,"  "  Work  for  Boys." 

The  sale. of  the  Committee's  publications  during  the  past  year  has  been 
larger  than  ever  before. 

The  Associations  have  been  asked  as  usual  for  annual  statistical  reports 
of  their  local  work.  These  reports  have  been  carefully  collated,  and  the 
results  are  given  in  the  statistical  tables  in  this  book.  Further  reports  of 
the  office  work  are  given  in  the  annual  statements  of  other  secretaries. 


REPORT  OF  JOHN  R,  MOTT, 

College  Sewetary. 

During  the  past  ten  months  my  work  has  taken  me  into  every  section  of 
the  United  States  (save  the  far  west),  as  well  as  into  Ontario  and  the 
Maritime  Provinces,  and  has  required  over  25,000  miles  of  travel. 

I.  VISITATION.— Three  months  were  spent  in  visiting  colleges,  thirty- 
four  institutions  being  reached.  In  a  few  cases  more  than  one  visit  was 
made.  A  majority  of  the  institutions  touched  were  among  the  most 
prominent  universities  of  the  United  States  and  Canada,  and  the  work 
done  in  them  had  more  than  a  local  significance  owing  to  their  strategic 


22 

position.  Owing  to  the  extent  of  the  international  college  field,  to  the 
increase  of  executive  work,  and  to  the  multiplication  of  conventions,  my 
-visitation  becomes  more  and  more  restricted  to  Associations  having 
peculiarly  pressing  problems,  or  which  sustain  a  marked  pivotal  relation 
to  other  Associations.  I  have  promoted  the  metropolitan  student  work  at 
several  centers,  and  have  also  assisted  a  few  general  Associations. 

n.  ORGANIZATION. — The  most  important  addition  to  the  intercollegiate 
movement  during  the  year  has  been  the  Association  formed  in  the  Univer- 
sity of  Chicago.  This  necessitated  five  visits.  The  Association  already 
takes  rank  among  the  foremost  organizations  on  the  continent.  Owing  to 
the  location,  rank,  wealth  and  possibilities  of  the  university,  and  also  to 
the  fact  that  so  many  of  the  students  have  been  identified  with  the  work 
elsewhere,  it  is  believed  that  this  new  Association  is  destined  to  exert  a 
marked  influence  in  the  intercollegiate  movement. 

III.  CONVENTIONS. — Over  four  months  have  been  devoted  to  work  at 
eighteen  conventions.  This  number  includes  three  summer  student  con- 
ferences, three  intercollegiate  deputation  conferences,  two  regular  college 
conferences,  four  state  and  provincial  conventions,  two  secretarial  con- 
ferences, one  district  conference  and  one  missionary  conference.  At  these 
conferences  fully  two  thousand  carefully  selected  student  delegates  have 
been  met,  representing  over  three  hundred  College  Associations,  and 
through  them  the  policy  of  the  entire  intercollegiate  movement  has  been 
happily  influenced. 

IV.— MATTERS  RECEIVING  SPECIAL  ATTENTION.  At  least  two  months 
have  been  given  to  purely  executive  and  office  work.  Among  other  things 
which  have  received  special  thought  in  this  connection  may  be  indicated: 

1.  Publication  Work. — Together  with  Mr.  Ober  several  days  were  spent 
revising  the  pamphlet  on  "Personal  Work"  and  in  preparing  a  new 
series  of  Bible  studies  to  be  used  with  it.     The  pamphlet  on  "How  Can 
a  College  Association  Secure  a  Building?  "  has  also  been  revised.     "  The 
History  of   the  Student  Volunteer  Movement. "  has  been  re- written.     An 
extended  report,  giving  the  "Progress  of  the  Intercollegiate  Movement" 
during  the  college  year  1891-'92,  was  prepared,  printed  and  given  a  wide 
circulation.    Five  articles  were  also  written  for  the   Young  Men's  Era, 
showing  the  religious  condition  of  the  colleges  of  the  Pacific  coast. 

2.  Student  Training  Conferences. — More  time  than  ever  has  been  spent 
in  the  development  of  the  training  conference  idea,  and  in  applying  it  to 
promote   the   solution  of   the  problems  of   the    College    Associations. 
Another  year's  experience  has  demonstrated  with  renewed  force  that  each 
of  the  following  conferences  is  essential  to  the  highest  advancement  of 
these    Associations :    (1)    The     Intercollegiate    Deputation    Conference 
for  the  training  of  leaders  of  the  college  work  in  the  state  or  section. 
Three  of  these  conferences  were  conducted,  and  one  hundred  and  three 
men  from  thirty-one  states  and  provinces  were  by  them  better  prepared 
for  leadership  in  the  work  of  their  respective  sections.     This  is  a  much 
larger  number  than  have  attended  these  conferences  in  any  previous  year. 
(2)  The  Presidential  Conference  for  training  the  leaders  of  the  Associa- 
tions of  a  given  state.    I  assisted  in  the  conduct  of  two  of  the  three  con- 
ferences of  this  character  held  during  the  year.    Fully  sixty  presidents 


23 

were  in  attendance.  Moreover,  at  two  of  the  Summer  Student  Confer- 
ences a  short  series  of  special  meetings  were  held  for  the  same  purpose, 
and  nearly  one  hundred  other  presidents  were  instructed  in  the  peculiar 
duties  and  responsibilities  of  their  office.  (3)  Summer  Student  Confer- 
ences for  the  training  of  the  leaders  of  the  various  departments  of  the 
College  Association  and  the  rank  and  file  of  its  membership.  Such  con- 
ferences were  held  at  Northfield,  Lake  Geneva  and  Knoxville.  They 
were  attended  by  nine  hundred  students  from  at  least  two  hundred  and 
fifty  colleges  of  the  United  States,  Canada  and  Europe.  Much  time  and 
thought  have  been  given  to  working  up  and  helping  to  conduct  these 
eight  training  conferences.  A  new  set  of  lectures  was  prepared  for  the 
deputation  conferences  and  a  partial  series  for  the  conferences  of  presi- 
dents. 

3.  Building  Enterprises. — I  assisted  in  the  inauguration  of  the  building 
movements     at    Otterbein    University,    the  University    of  Illinois,   the 
University  of  Ohio,  Denison  University,  and  the  University  of  Pennsyl- 
vania.    Aid  was  also  rendered  in  furthering  similar  movements  already 
started  at  several  other  institutions.     In  some  respects  the  most  remark- 
able canvass  conducted  was  at  the  University  of  Illinois,  where,  within 
twenty-four  hours,  one  hundred  and  fifty -two  students  pledged  $10,180. 
There  are  now  fourteen  College  Association  buildings  completed. 

4.  Student  Volunteer  Movement. — As  the  representative  of  the  Associations 
on  the  executive  committee  of  this  movement,  I  have  given  its  interests 
regular  attention.     Chief  stress  has  been  laid  upon  the  internal  develop- 
ment of  the  movement.     The  office  methods  have  been  reorganized  and 
made  much  more  effective.     Three  new  pamphlets  have  been  issued.     A 
monthly  organ — The  Student  Volunteer — has  been  started  and  already  has 
a  large  circulation  among  the  volunteers  and  Association  missionary  com- 
mittees.    It  will  do  much  to  build  up  the  missionary  department  of  our 
Associations.     At  the  summer  conferences  missionary  institutes  were  held 
for  training  leaders  of  the  many  volunteer  bands  of  the  Associations. 
The  tour  of  F.  A.  Keller,  the  traveling  secretary  of  the  movement,  has 
been  mapped  out  and  directed.     He  has  not  only  created  and  organized 
missionary  interest  in  many  Associations,  but  has  also  stimulated  in  a 
very  helpful  manner  other  departments  of  the  work. 

5.  Spiritual  Awakenings  in  the  Colleges. — For  another  year  I  have  had 
the  privilege  of  facilitating  Mr.   Sayford's  work  among  students.    His 
most  telling  work  continues  to  be  among  the  inconsistent  Christians.     He 
has  during  the  year  led  nearly  3,000  men  to  enter  into  the  higher  ground 
covenant.     There  have  been  at  least  300  conversions  in  connection  with  his 
student  work.     I  have  also  helped  in  the  promotion  of  the  notable  spirit- 
ual movements  at  Princeton  and  at  Northwestern  University,  and  in  pav- 
ing the  way  for  similar  work  at  several  other  colleges.     In  my  report  last 
year  I  stated  that  in  no  preceding  year  had  I  been  so  deeply  impressed 
with  the  presence  of  the  revival  spirit  in  the  Associations.     If  observa- 
tion and  reports  may  be  trusted,  the  year  now  closing  has  been  even  more 
remarkable  in  this  preeminently  important  respect.     I  question  seriously 
whether  there  has  ever  been  a  year  when  the  Holy  Spirit  has  wrought 
greater  things  among  college  men  on  this  continent  than  during  the  past 
year. 


24 

REPOET  OF  JOHN  E.  HAGUE, 

Secretary. 

The  ten  months  covered  by  this  report  have  been  spent  between  Maine 
;and  the  Missouri  Eiver.  Emergency  work,  that  is,  aiding  Associations 
which  requested  special  assistance  on  building  finances  or  plans,  or  cur- 
rent expense  debts,  occupied  nearly  five  months.  In  some  cases  the 
entire  property  was  in  danger  of  being  lost  or  the  work  abandoned 
through  mistakes  of  the  past. 

Sioux  City  has  been  aided  in  completing  its  admirable  building  and 
raising  a  portion  of  the  debt;  Eichmond,  Ind.,  and  Keene,  N.  H.,  in  in- 
creasing their  building  funds,  and  re-arranging  plans;  Grand  Forks, 
N.  D. ,  Dover,  N.  J. ,  Concord,  N.  H. ,  and  several  Eailroad  Associations  in 
plans  for  buildings  and  for  building  canvasses,  or  addresses  on  Associa- 
tion buildings,  accompanied  by  lantern  views  of  exteriors  and  interiors. 
Over  two  months  was  spent  in  assisting  St.  Paul,  Minn. ,  in  re-organiza- 
tion, securing  a  new  secretary,  raising  current  expense  debt,  etc. 

Forty-five  Associations  in  15  states,  and  several  State  Secretaries  and 
Committees  have  been  visited  and  counsel  given,  or  help  in  securing  funds 
or  men.  21  committee  and  19  board  meetings  were  attended,  5  parlor 
conferences  conducted,  and  over  500  personal  interviews  held.  27  men's 
and  one  boys'  meetings  have  been  addressed,  and  3  Bible  classes  con- 
ducted in  Associations;  15  gospel  talks  made  in  churches  or  halls;  16 
-ses  on  Association  work  delivered;  and  an  incomplete  record  shows 
55  persons  led  to  a  profession  of  Christ  through  personal  work  or  in  meet- 
ings conducted,  aside  from  several  score  who  have  made  profession  in  meet- 
^  here  only  assistance  was  rendered.  9  conventions  and  conferences 
have  been  attended  and  participated  in,  viz. :  the  State  Conventions  of 
New  Hampshire,  Vermont  and  Massachusetts,  district  conventions  in 
Massachusetts  and  New  Jersey,  secretaries'  conferences  in  Connecticut 
and  Vermont.  Two  days  were  also  spent  in  attendance  on  the  conven- 
tion of  Christian  Workers  at  Boston. 

Nearly  a  month  was  given  to  the  development  of  the  Educational  De- 
partment of  the  Association,  in  visits  to  Chicago,  Dayton,  New  York, 
Boston,  Brooklyn  and  other  places,  and  to  the  search  for  and  securing  of 
a  secretary  for  this  department.  Several  addresses  on  educational  work 
At  conventions,  at  the  anniversary  of  the  Bridgeport  Association  and  else- 
where, have  been  made,  and  aid  has  been  rendered  the  Indianapolis  Asso- 
ciation in  preparing  for  the  International  Convention.  Time  has  been  in- 
cidentally given  in  various  states  to  solicitation  of  funds  for  the  support 
of  the  International  work . 

Though  a  period  of  great  difficulties  and  trying  experiences,  it  has  been 
one  of  the  most  marked  in  God's  spiritual  blessing,  both  as  regards  re- 
ceiving and  imparting  to  others. 


EEPOET  OF  S.  A.  TAGGAET, 

,  Secretary. 

The  ten  months  covered  by  this  report  have  been  chiefly  given  to  general 
visitation  and  co-operation,  the  extension  work  being  made  in  most  part 
incidental  to  important  work  that  required  immediate  attention.
