I  have  represented  the  Committee  at  the  State  Conventions  of  Maine, 
Massachusetts,  Missouri,  Pennsylvania,  and  the  Maritime  Provinces;  at- 
tended general  secretaries'  conferences  at  Providence,  B.  I. ,  Newark,  N. 
J.,  and  Chester,  Pa.,  and  district  conferences  at  Sidney,  N.  Y.,  and  King- 
ston, Pa.  presenting  the  extension  work  and  otherwise  assisting.  My  general 
visitation  and  assistance  has  included  the  following  places :  St.  John  and 
Moncton,  N.  B.,  Halifax,  New  Glasgow  and  Pictou,  N.  S. ;  Charlottetown, 
P.  E.  I.;  Brattleboro,  Vt.;  Providence,  B.  I.;  Albany,  Binghamton, 
Brooklyn,  Buffalo,  Cohoes,  New  York  city,  Norwich  and  Troy,  N.  Y.; 
-Chester,  Erie,  Franklin,  Harrisburg,  McKeesport,  New  Brighton,  New 
Castle,  Philadelphia,  Scranton,  Sharpsburg,  Titusville,  and  West  Phila- 
delphia, Pa. ;  Ashtabula,  Cincinnati,  Cleveland,  Columbus,  Youngstown, 
and  Xenia,  Ohio;  Indianapolis,  and  New  Albany,  Ind.;  Louisville,  Ky.; 
Wheeling,  W.  Va.,  and  Washington,  D.  C.  In  the  distinct  interest  of 
extension  work  I  have  visited  Boston,  Mass. ;  St.  Louis,  Mo. ;  Montclair, 
Railway  and  Wanamassa  Camp,  N.  J. ;  Binghamton  B.  B. ,  and  Ithaca, 
N.  Y. ;  Cincinnati  and  Dayton,  Ohio;  Carlisle,  Chester,  Lancaster, 
Philadelphia,  Scranton  B.  B.,  West  Philadelphia,  and  Wilkes  Barre, 
Pa. ;  Lynchburg,  Norfolk,  Portsmouth,  Bichmond,  Bichmond  College, 
iind  Boanoke,  Va.  In  addition  to  special  service  at  these  points  meet- 
ings to  present  the  work  have  been  arranged  at  various  other  places. 
A  larger  correspondence  has  also  been  conducted  than  in  previous  years, 
embracing  165  points  in  all  sections  of  the  country. 

There  are  now  seventy -five  Associations  actively  enlisted  in  the  special 
extension  work.  A  few  of  them  have  made  decided  advance  in  their 
efforts  to  educate  young  men  in  systematic  giving  as  well  as  in  the  amount 
of  their  contributions.  On  the  whole  there  seems  to  be  a  steady  growth 
of  interest,  although  there  has  been  a  seeming  decline  in  quite  a  number 
of  places.  Nearly  two  hundred  Associations  have  reported  their  interest 
in  the  work  as  well  as  their  intention  to  take  it  up  as  soon  as  circumstances 
admit.  In  most  of  these  places  the  erection  of  buildings,  or  the  raising 
of  money  outside  of  ordinary  current  expenses  have  been  the  ostensible 
hindrances.  In  contrast  with  this,  the  most  successful  extension  work 
has  been  done  by  Associations  engaged  at  the  same  time  in  raising  money 
for  buildings,  or  to  meet  extra  obligations.  The  greatest  difficulty  has 
been  to  get  those  who  are  in  the  management  to  see  that  such  local 
enterprises  ought  not  to  hinder  the  giving  of  at  least  some  attention  to 
the  extension  work. 

During  the  year  closing  December  31,  1892,  $4,200  were  contributed  to 
the  home  and  foreign  field  under  the  supervision  of  the  International 
Committee  through  the  special  extension  fund.  It  is  estimated  that  fully 
as  much  more  was  given  through  the  same  channel  to  the  local,  state  and 
educational  work.  If  this  estimate  be  correct  there  was  contributed 
altogether  at  least  the  sum  of  $8,400. 

All  that  is  needed  to  make  this  department  fruitful  and  wide-reaching 
in  its  results  is  for  a  few  men  in  every  Association  to  determine  that  they 
will  personally  interest  themselves  in  its  earnest  and  vigorous  prosecution. 


BEPOBT  OF  CECIL  L.  GATES, 

Secretary    of  the    Railroad   Department. 
Territory  lying  west  of  the  Missouri  river,  which  may  be  aptly  termed 


26 

the  "western  field,  "has  demanded  a  large  proportion  of  the  time  specified 
in  this  report.  The  variety  of  service  demanded  has  been  very  great,  and 
the  work  performed  has  been  accomplished,  of  necessity,  with  little  refer- 
ence to  precedents,  and  without  the  easy  adaptation  of  established 
methods,  so  helpful  in  other  sections. 

The  work  reviewed  in  my  last  report  has  prospered,  and  has  rendered 
necessary  a  certain  amount  of  extension  and  largely  increased  the  demands- 
for  supervision. 

In  Colorado  the  task  of  developing  a  work  for  young  men  that  should 
be  definite  and  permanent  has  been  continued.  Assistance  was  given  at 
Trinidad  in  the  work  of  securing  financial  support  and  in  reorganization, 
and  that  city  now  has  a  successful  Association  in  charge  of  a  competent 
secretary.  Kailroad,  mining,  stock  and  town  men  are  included  in  the 
membership  and  are  rapidly  extending  the  use  of  the  very  attractive 
rooms  and  privileges. 

Canon  City  is  now  well  established  in  Association  work  with  excellent 
quarters  and  an  experienced  secretary.  At  Durango,  near  the  New 
Mexico  line,  sufficient  funds  for  the  work  of  the  first  year  were  secured, 
the  organization  perfected,  a  general  secretary  recommended,  and  active 
work  will  soon  be  commenced.  The  Associations  at  Aspen  and  Leadviller 
reorganized  in  1891-92,  have  had  special  attention,  and  are  both  doing 
good  service.  The  present  aspect  of  the  silver  question,  as  viewed  from 
these  great  camps,  has  in  it  something  of  menace  to  the  prosperity  of 
these  Associations,  but  it  is  believed  that  the  careful  management  and  the 
general  interest  that  has  characterized  their  work  will  save  them  from 
serious  disturbance.  , 

Pueblo,  Colorado  Springs,  and  the  Kailroad  Association  at  West  Denver, 
have  each  received  counsel  and  assistance,  and  are  maintaining  their 
usefulness.  The  Colorado  Associations  are  united  and  aggressive  and  are 
exerting  a  positive  influence  for  good  among  the  young  men  of  the  state. 

Aid  has  been  given  the  Association  at  Salt  Lake  City  toward  increasing 
its  financial  support  and  in  securing  a  general  secretary.  Perhaps  no 
Association  in  this  country  presents  a  more  interesting  situation,  or  con- 
tends with  a  greater  number  of  perplexing  conditions.  Its  success  has  a 
great  significance  in  the  pioneer  field  of  which  it  is  the  center. 

In  two  trips  to  the  northwest  visits  were  made  to  Pocatelio,  Idaho  y 
Butte  and  Helena,  Montana;  Walla  Walla  and  Spokane,  Washington; 
and  Albany,  Oregon.  Butte,  Helena,  Walla  Walla  and  Spokane  are  wisely 
awaiting  a  favorable  change  of  conditions  before  attempting  the  extensive 
and  costly  work  that  each  point  requires. 

In  connection  with  the  probable  extension  of  railroad  work  in  the  west- 
ern field,  visits  have  been  made  to  officials  of  the  Northern  Pacific,  South- 
ern Pacific,  Union  Pacific,  and  Denver  &  Rio  Grande  Eailroads.  Definite 
action  has  been  taken  in  some  instances,  and,  in  others,  awaits  a  more 
favorable  opportunity.  An  encouraging  interest  has  been  evinced  by 
every  official  approached,  and  requests  for  the  establishment  of  railroad 
departments  are  frequently  received  from  employees  of  these  lines. 

In  April  visits  were  made  to  several  points  in  •  Texas  with  reference  to 
the  establishment  of  railroad  work.  After  an  examination  of  the  situa- 
tion, it  was  thought  best  to  defer  any  attempt  at  organization  until  work 
upon  an  entire  system  could  be  assured.  While  in  the  state  the  Associa- 


27 

tion  at  Fort  Worth  was  visited  in  company  with  Mr.  Wilkie,  of  Corpus 
Christi.  The  work  of  the  Association  was  publicly  presented  and  a  plan 
for  that  work  involving  some  changes  was  recommended  and  accepted. 

Returning  from  Texas  a  visit  was  made  to  the  Railroad  Associations  and 
departments  located  in  Massachusetts,  Vermont  and  New  York.  Twenty- 
five  of  the  New  York  departments  were  included,  and  conferences  were 
had  very  generally  with  secretaries  and  officers  and  members  of  the- 
boards  and  committees  of  management.  In  concurrence  with  the  State 
Secretary  such  recommendations  were  made  as  seemed  desirable  at- 
certain  points  and  were  cordially  received  and  acted  upon.  Special 
attention  was  given  to  the  work  at  West  Albany,  where  an  entire  readjust- 
ment has  been  worked  out  to  a  successful  result. 

I  have  attended  the  State  Conventions  of  Texas,  Colorado,  California 
and  the  Pacific  Northwest.  I  was  present  at  the  International  Secretaries' 
Conference  at  Providence  and  also  the  secretarial  conferences  at  San 
Francisco,  Seattle  and  Colorado  Springs. 

During  the  time  covered  by  this  report  special  conferences  have  been 
had  with  one  hundred  and  twelve  railroad  officials,  general  secretaries 
and  officers  of  Associations,  eleven  meetings  of  boards  of  directors  and 
eleven  committee  meetings  have  been  attended,  and  thirty-one  addresses 
upon  Association  and  religious  topics  have  been  delivered.  One  hundred 
and  three  visits  have  been  made  to  fifty -three  towns  in  fourteen  states 
and  territories.  Assistance  has  been  rendered  in  procuring  general 
secretaries  for  nine  Associations,  and  much  work  has  been  done  in  estab- 
lishing sound  foundations  and  in  planning  details  of  organization  and 
service.  In  all  the  work  undertaken  the  aim  has  been  to  secure  thorough- 
ness and  permanence  rather  than  mere  extension. 

REPORT  OF  CLARENCE  J.  HICKS, 

Secretary  of  the  Railroad  Department. 

My  time  during  the  past  year  has  been  given  chiefly  to  work  in  the 
Railroad  Department,  although  I  have  endeavored  to  keep  in  mind  the 
interests  of  the  whole  work,  and  have  taken  many  opportunities  of  render- 
ing aid  in  other  departments.  More  time  has  been  given  to  office  work 
and  less  to  travel,  but  it  has  been  possible  to  accomplish,  through  corres- 
pondence, much  work  that  formerly  required  many  miles  of  travel. 

Work  at  the  office  has,  in  addition  to  a  very  general  and  continuous  cor- 
respondence with  the  railroad  and  State  Secretaries,  as  well  as  with  many 
railroad  officials,  included : 

1.  The  securing  from  the  Railroad  Associations  of  quarterly  statistical 
and  financial  reports  on  blanks  issued  by  the  Committee.     The  Associa- 
tions are  urged  to  send  these  reports  not  only  to  the  international  and 
state  offices,  but  also  to  interested  officials  of  contributing  roads.     The 
committees  of  supervision  are  thus  kept  informed  as  to  the  exact  condition 
of  the  railroad  work  at  each  point,  business  like  habits  are  cultivated  in 
the  Associations,  and  the  railroad  officials  are  shown  that  the  appropria- 
tions granted  are  producing  actual,  tangible  results.     The  Associations 
are  heartily  co-operating  in  this  plan,  and  the  reports  on  file  in  the  inter- 
national office  will  furnish  a  continuous  history  of  the  railroad  work  from 
year  to  year. 

2.  Much  correspondence  has  been  required  with  Associations  and  indi- 
viduals with  reference  to  secretarial  vacancies  and  changes. 


28 

3.  Considerable  time  has  been  given  to  the  preparation  of  plans,  and  to 
advising  with  architects  and  building  committees  with  reference  to 
buildings.  In  the  line  of  this  work  a  pamphlet  on  Railroad  Association 
buildings  has  been  prepared.  The  one  on  the  Eailroad  Department  has 
also  been  revised. 

Some  of  the  more  interesting  developments  of  the  year,  with  each  of 
which  I  have  been  more  or  less  intimately  connected,  may  be  briefly  out- 
lined as  follows:  The  generous  support  of  the  management  of  the  Chesa- 
peake &  Ohio  Bailway  has  made  possible  a  very  encouraging  growth  along 
this  line.  At  Handley,  W.  Va.,  a  beautiful  building  has  been  erected  and 
furnished,  entirely  at  the  expense  of  the  railroad  company,  and  a  secre- 
tary, assistant  and  cook  placed  on  the  pay  roll.  The  absence  of  material 
for  a  local  committee  of  management  has  thus  far  made  it  necessary  for 
the  International  Committee  to  take  direct  supervision  of  this  work.  At 
Clifton  Forge,  Va.,  $3,400  has  been  secured  in  subscriptions,  and  the  rail- 
road company  has  undertaken  the  erection  of  a  $10,000  building.  At 
Gladstone,  Va.,  a  building  similar  to  the  one  at  Handley  has  been  ordered 
erected.  An  examination  of  the  condition  and  results  of  the  work  along 
the  line  of  this  road  is  commended,  as  showing  what  can  be  accomplished 
on  a  single  system  with  the  hearty  support  of  the  officials. 

A  Pennsylvania  Railroad  department  has  been  opened  at  Trenton,  N.  J., 
and  considerable  preliminary  work  done  at  both  Camden  and  Jersey  City, 
where  the  support  of  the  railroad  company  is  already  assured.  At 
Columbus,  Indiana,  a  railroad  men's  club  has,  by  a  unanimous  vote 
of  its  members,  been  turned  into  a  Railroad  Association.  At  Mat- 
toon,  111.,  and  Atlanta,  Ga.,  the  Associations  have  been  thoroughly  re- 
organized, and  are  now  in  better  condition  for  effective  work  than  ever 
before.  At  Indianapolis  a  large  pledged  membership  has  been  secured, 
and  we  are  now  waiting  for  possession  of  quarters  that  have  been  promised 
free  of  rent  for  the  use  of  a  railroad  department.  At  a  large  number  of 
other  division  points,  an  investigation  has  been  made,  and  plans  laid, 
looking  to  the  organization  of  Railroad  Associations  in  the  near  future. 

The  Port  Jervis  Association  has  taken  possession  of  its  new  building 
during  the  year.  At  Crewe,  Va. ,  a  new  building  is  nearly  completed.  At 
St.  Louis  a  site  connected  with  the  new  union  depot  property  has  been 
secured,  and  plans  are  under  consideration  for  securing  a  building  at  this 
important  railroad  center.  Several  other  Associations  have,  during  the 
year,  added  materially  to  building  funds. 

Two  Associations  have  been  taken  from  the  list  during  the  year:  One 
at  Waycross,  Ga. ,  where  the  Association  never  received  sufficient  financial 
aid  from  the  corporation  to  insure  its  success;  and  the  other  at  San  Fran- 
cisco, where  the  former  street  railway  department  is  now  conducted  as 
city  Association  work. 

C.  H.  Moorman  has  rendered  valuable  service  throughout  the  year  as 
an  assistant  in  the  Railroad  Department.  A  large  portion  of  his  time  has 
been  given  to  work  on  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio,  and  to  work  in  several 
fields  in  Indiana.  In  January  he  accepted  a  call  to  a  local  field. 

During  the  year  I  have  attended  the  State  Conventions  of  Illinois,  In- 
diana, Delaware  and  New  Jersey  ;  also  the  General  Secretaries'  Conference 
at  Providence,  and  a  state  railroad  conference  at  Roanoke,  Va. 


29 

KEPOET  OF  W.  A.  HUNTON, 

Secretary. 

Of  the  period  covered  by  this  report,  only  five  days  were  spent  in  the 
visitation  of  three  of  our  twenty-six  College  Associations. 

I  attended  the  International  Secretaries'  Conference  at  Providence, 
and  the  Student  Summer  School  at  Northfield.  I  also  made,  in  connec- 
tion with  our  local  Association  work  among  colored  men,  forty-three 
visits  to  nineteen  points,  including  3  visits  at  Louisville,  Ky. ;  7  at  Norfolk, 
Va. ;  4  at  Washington,  D.  C.;  1  at  St.  Louis,  Mo.;  4  at  Eichmond,  Va., 
and  24  other  visits  of  from  one  to  nine  day's  duration  at  points  in  several 
of  the  eastern,  middle  and  South  Atlantic  states. 

During  the  five  years  since  the  organization  of  the  first  local  Associa- 
tion among  colored  men,  at  Norfolk,  Va.,  and  the  employment  of  the 
first  colored  man  as  a  general  secretary,  ten  other  local  Associations  have 
been  organized,  while  six  colored  men  now  devote  their  entire  time  to 
Association  work.  Four  of  these  Associations  referred  to  have  bought 
and  paid  for  real  estate  aggregating  in  actual  cost  over  {$12,000. 

In  addition  to  the  marked  advance  made  in  the  character  of  the  work 
done  by  the  Associations  already  organized  among  colored  men,  an 
advance  which  has  been  largely  due  to  the  supervision  of  the  Inter- 
national Committee,  three  new  Associations  were  organized  during  the 
past  year,  one  local  Association  at  Louisville,  Ky.,  and  two  College 
Associations. 

We  greatly  need  more  general  secretaries  and  money  for  their  support. 
The  former  can  be  obtained  more  easily  than  the  latter.  In  several  of  the 
southern  states  there  are  small  organizations  of  colored  men  who  are 
trying  hard  to  help  each  other  and  their  fellows  to  lead  better  lives,  but 
who  are  wholly  unacquainted  with  the  principles  and  methods  of  Associa- 
tion work.  They  have  repeatedly  called  upon  the  Committee  for  help, 
but  it  has  been  impossible  to  render  them  assistance  except  through 
correspondence. 

This  field — the  work  among  colored  young  men — is  extensive.  The 
urgent  necessity  of  the  work  is  evident.  The  demands  upon  my  time  and 
strength  are  often  overwhelming.  The  colored  men  in  the  south  look 
entirely  to  the  International  Committee  for  help  in  the  extension  and 
direction  of  their  work.  One  man  cannot,  therefore,  do  more  than  try  to 
meet  the  cases  of  emergency. 


EEPOET  OF  F.   S.   BEOCKMAN, 

Secretary. 

Since  my  last  report  to  the  Committee,  ten  months  ago,  my  time  has 
been  given  to  college  work  in  the  south  and  southwest.  Eighty-eight 
visits  were  made  to  seventy-seven  institutions  in  fourteen  different  states. 
These  colleges  report  an  attendance  of  over  fifteen  thousand  young  men. 
Eight  are  state  universities,  others  are  state  normal,  agricultural  and 
mechanical  colleges,  boys'  fitting  schools  and  denominational  institutions. 

The  plan  outlined  in  my  last  year's  report  for  the  development  of  the 
college  work  in  the  south  was  followed  in  these  visits.  Close  attention 
was  directed  to  the  better  organization  of  the  committee  system  and 


30 

careful  instruction  given  in  Association  methods.  The  history  of  the 
college  work  proves  that  isolation  is  death  to  the  individual  Association, 
consequently  every  attempt  has  been  made  to  secure  closer  intercollegiate 
relations.  The  unorganized  condition  of  the  state  work  in  many  instances, 
the  already  over- worked  force  in  the  other  states,  and  the  fact  that  south- 
ern colleges  have  but  recently  established  intercollegiate  relations  even 
in  oratory  and  athletics  have  rendered  this  difficult. 

The  efforts  just  described  and  those  of  the  State  Secretaries  have  been 
supplemented  by  twenty -five  well  trained  deputation  men,  so  that  almost 
every  Association  has  been  touched  during  the  ten  months  and  some  of 
them  more  than  once.  This  is  the  first  time  the  field  has  been  so 
thoroughly  covered  during  one  year.  The  increased  interest,  better 
organization,  improved  methods,  and  friendly  rivalry  in  good  works  are  a 
splendid  commentary  on  the  advantages  of  this  careful  supervision. 

Comparatively  few  colleges  have  been  visited  with  a  view  to  organizing 
new  Associations.  It  was  deemed  best  to  devote  most  of  my  time  to 
conserving  the  results  of  last  year,  which  marked  an  era  of  extension.  Six 
Associations,  however,  have  been  organized — two  of  them  in  prominent 
state  universities  which  had  previously  no  organized  religious  effort. 

One  month  was  spent  in  attendance  upon  the  Student  Conferences  at 
Knoxville,  Lake  Geneva  and  Northfield,  the  Secretaries  Conference,  and 
the  State  Conventions  of  Arkansas  and  Kansas. 

The  most  significant  feature  in  the  development  of  the  College  Associa- 
tion in  this  section  has  been  the  inauguration  of  a  summer  gathering  at 
the  University  of  Tennessee,  after  the  plan  of  the  Northfield  meeting. 
Jt  was  attended  by  one  hundred  and  seventy-five  students  from  at  least 
sixty  institutions  in  the  southern  states.  There  are  indications  on  every 
hand  that  it  has  exerted  a  marked  influence  upon  the  college  life  of  the 
south. 


BEPOBT  OF  H.  P.  ANDEKSEN, 

Secretary. 

My  time  has  been  given  to  the  South  Atlantic  and  Gulf  states. 
By  special  arrangement,  two-thirds  of  it  was  spent,  without  expense 
to  the  Committee,  as  acting  State  Secretary  of  Georgia.  Sixty-two 

have  been  made  to  21  points,  special  attention  being  devoted 
to  perfecting  local  organization,  finances,  and  Bible  study,  and  to  the 

thening  of  the  state  work.  I  assisted  in  raising  $2,900  for  local 
work  at  Borne,  Athens,  Macon  and  Brunswick,  aided  Athens  and 
Savannah  in  securing  general  secretaries,  and  Atlanta  in  finding  a 

•al  director.  I  co-operated  with  Secretary  Hicks  in  helping  to 
reorganize  the  railroad  department  of  the  Atlanta  Association  and 
in  securing  W.  A.  Waggoner  as  secretary.  Also  arranged  for  the  State 
Convention  at  Athens,  and  co-operated  with  Secretary  Ober  in  effecting  an 
arrangement  by  which  Georgia  and  South  Carolina  unite  in  the  employ- 
ment of  a  State  Secretary,  W.  M.  Lewis  being  secured  for  that  position. 

I  represented  the  Committee  at  the  State  Conventions  of  Alabama, 
North  Carolina  and  South  Carolina,  attended  the  convention  of  Edgefield 
county,  S.  C.,  at  Meeting  Street,  and  the  International  Secretaries'  Con- 
ference at  Providence.  I  have  met  with  the  State  Committees  of  North 


31 

Carolina,  South  Carolina  and  Mississippi,  and  had  frequent  conferences 
with  their  State  Secretaries. 

I  co-operated  with  Secretary  Brockman  in  arranging  the  program  for 
the  Student  Summer  School  at  Knoxville,  and  attended  to  much  of  the 
correspondence  and  to  the  distribution  of  printed  matter,  and  as  treasurer 
was  enabled  to  pay  all  expenses  and  have  a  small  balance  in  the  treasury. 
I  also  co-operated  in  planning  the  program  of  the  Southern  Secretarial 
Institute,  and  attended  a  conference  of  southern  State  Secretaries  to  con- 
sider plans  for  future  similar  gatherings. 

I  assisted  in  securing  a  general  secretary  for  the  Asheville  Association, 
«pent  a  week  in  Edgefield  county  aiding  the  county  work,  and  helped 
start  the  subscription  toward  the  payment  of  the  debt  of  the  Charleston 
Association.  Special  effort  was  put  forth  to  increase  the  observance  of 
the  week  of  prayer  in  the  southern  states  with  encouraging  results.  I 
traveled  18,000  miles. 


KEPOET  OF  LOGAN  HERBERT  BOOTS, 

Secretary. 

Nearly  all  of  the  five  months  since  my  engagement  with  the  Committee 
Taegan  has  been  devoted  to  the  college  work.  Fifty-two  institutions  have 
been  visited,  seven  of  them  informally,  in  ten  states  and  one  territory. 
The  first  month  was  spent  among  the  colleges  of  eastern  Tennessee  and 
.a  few  typical  institutions  in  Pennsylvania,  Maryland  and  Ohio.  October 
was  occupied  in  part  by  visitation  and  planning,  but  mainly  by  the  State 
Conventions  of  Tennessee,  Michigan  and  Missouri,  at  each  of  which  I  as- 
sisted in  the  conduct  of  the  special  meetings  for  college  delegates. 

In  November  I  was  for  two  weeks  in  Colorado  and  on  the  way  to  the 
Pacific  coast.  A  day  was  spent  at  Salt  Lake  City  and  two  at  Reno  to 
see  the  Universities  of  Utah  and  Nevada.  These  points  were  not  yet  ripe 
for  organization.  Since  the  last  of  November  I  have  been  in  California, 
traversing  much  of  the  same  ground  covered  for  the  first  time  by 
Secretary  Mott  last  winter. 

The  western  College  Associations  need,  at  present,  internal  development 
rather  than  extension.  I  have,  therefore,  organized  only  three  new  Asso- 
ciations, one  in  Colorado  and  two  in  California.  These,  with  two  others  re- 
cently organized  in  the  latter  state,  a  little  more  than  make  good  the 
year's  loss.  The  most  serious  failure  has  been  in  the  two  preparatory 
schools  of  California,  where  it  seemed  wise,  and  almost  necessary,  to 
abandon  organized  work  altogether  for  the  present.  Four  Associations 
had  to  be  reorganized.  In  the  majority  of  the  Asssociations,  however, 
the  work  of  the  last  year  has  been  very  fair,  although,  as  is  the  case  in 
all  such  new  fields,  the  most  emphasis  had  to  be  laid  on  elementary  prin- 
ciples and  methods.  Following  the  precedent  of  last  year,  conferences 
have  been  arranged  for  the  purpose  of  clinching  the  impressions  of  the 
visits,  and  developing  an  appreciation  of  the  state  and  world-wide  inter- 
collegiate tie.  In  southern  California  a  sort  of  deputation  conference  has 
been  held  for  the  six  institutions  in  and  near  Los  Angeles,  and  a  large 
conference  is  planned  for  the  twelve  Associations  of  northern  California. 
I  spent  a  number  of  days  at  each  of  the  most  important  points  on  the 


82 

coast,  Leland  Stanford,  Jr.  University,  and  the  University  of  California^ 
where  the  Associations  are  making  steady  progress.  On  January  27th  I 
participated  in  the  dedication  of  Stiles  Hall,  at  the  University  of  Cali- 
fornia, the  first  College  Association  building  west  of  the  Kockies,  and 
recently  completed  at  a  cost  of  over  $25,000. 

The  need  of  supervisory  work  in  the  field  is  emphasized  many  fold  by  the 

1 )  that  the  whole  country  is  new,  and  largely  lacking  in  the  conserv- 
ative and  spiritual  traditions  which  are  so  powerful  in  the  east  ;  (2)  that 
comparatively  few  students  have  any  training  in  religious  work  before  they 
enter  college,  and  that  the  transient  nature  of  student  life  renders  the 
training  of  leaders  peculiarly  difficult;  (3)  that  while  the  State  Committees 
are  unable  to  give  adequate  supervision  themselves,  they  have  no  trained 
deputation  men  to  aid  them  ;  (4)  that  college  spirit  is  yet  weak,  and  that 
intercollegiate  relations  are  just  being  established  ;  (5)  that  1,500  to  3,000 

separate  these  institutions  from  the  inspiration  accompanying  the 
great  body  of  the  intercollegiate  movement ;  and  yet  (6)  that,  with  all 
these  disadvantages,  the  future  of  this  vast  and  immensely  rich  country 
depends,  very  largely  upon  the  men  now  being  educated  in  the  colleges. 
Encouraging  facts  are  the  readiness  with  which  the  movement  is  being 
adapted  to  the  needs  of  such  a  variety  of  institutions  in  such  varying  con- 
ditions, and  the  success  which  is  crowning  its  efforts  so  far  as  these  can 
be  carefully  supervised. 


REPORT  OF  GEORGE  B.   HODGE, 

Secretary  of  tlie  Educational  Department. 

.ran  work  October  15,  1892.  The  three  and  a  half  months  have  been 
spent  in  study  and  visitation  of  the  educational  work  of  Associations  and 
some  prominent  industrial  schools.  Twenty  Associations  have  been 
i.  including  New  York,  Brooklyn,  Boston,  Philadelphia,  and  Bridge- 
port and  Hartford,  Conn.  Ten  technical  schools  have  been  visited, 
including  the  Pratt  Institute,  Brooklyn;  the  Drexel  Institute  and  Manual 
Training  schools  of  Philadelphia,  the  New  York  Trade  School,  the  Boston 

:ing  Drawing  schools,  and  the  Newark,  N.  J.,  Technical  School. 

Nearly  one  hundred  men,  secretaries,  teachers,  and  practical  business 

men,  have  been  conferred  with  concerning  the  systematic  and  uniform 

development  of  educational  work  in  our  Associations.     I  visited  the  Train- 

at  Springfield,  giving  a  talk  on  the  educational  work  ;  attended 

the  New  Hampshire  State  Convention,  reading  a  paper  on  "Importance 

of  Educational  Work;"  attended  the  secretaries'  conference  of  New  Jersey, 

ark,  reading  a  paper ;  and  have  given  three  talks  on  Association 

In  my  study  of  the  work  and  field  I  am  surprised  and  gratified  to  find 
tli at  the  growth  for  the  past  four  years  in  educational  facilities,  classes 
and  different  men  enrolled  has  been  three  times  greater  than  in  the  number 
of  Associations  or  membership  ;  that  great  good  is  now  resulting  from 
unorganized  condition ;  that  the  growth  in  fa- 
in   drawing,   physics,    chemistry    and  mathematics— the  funda- 
mental sciences  of  all  industry — have  been  greatly  increased,  especially 
th»-  present  year.     That  there  is  a  wide  field  of  opportunity  is 


33 

seen  from  the  fact  that,  out  of  every  one  thousand  young  men  within 
reach  of  our  Associations  on  this  continent,  less  than  five  are  now  found 
in  our  classes. 

The  $50,000  gift  of  A.  E.  and  Miss  C.  E.  Hilly er  to  the  Hartford  Asso- 
ciation for  its  educational  department  marks  an  era  in  this  work,  and  sets 
an  example  that  may  well  be  followed  in  other  communities. 

An  exhibit  of  class  work  in  free  hand,  architectural  and  mechanical 
drawing,  book-keeping,  penmanship,  mathematics,  electricity,  clay  mod- 
eling, wood  carving,  etc. ,  was  suggested  for  the  State  Conventions  of  New 
York  and  Connecticut,  and  aid  given.  The  results  proved  the  exhibits 
to  be  even  more  successful  than  had  been  anticipated  in  their  stimulating 
and  encouraging  effects  for  the  extension  of  this  work,  ' '  more  than  could 
be  accomplished  by  hours  of  oratory  or  volumes  of  printed  matter." 
Work  is  now  in  progress  for  the  exhibit  at  the  International  Convention 
to  be  held  at  Indianapolis  in  May  and  at  the  Columbian  Exposition  at 
Chicago.  Aid  is  being  given  several  Associations  in  planning  their  edu- 
cational work  for  the  coming  year. 

From  a  blank  sent  to  the  320  North  American  Associations  reported  to 
be  doing  educational  work,  150  replies  have  been  thus  far  received. 
From  these  the  following  points  are  noted : 

1.  Of  the  150  Associations,  50  have  no  working  educational  committee. 

2.  But  70  Associations  have  made  any  special  effort  in  the  line  of  adver- 
tising,  study  of  the  field,   and  personal  visitation  of  employers  or  em- 
ployees, in  order  to  reach  classes  of  men  hitherto  unreached;  but  the  num- 
ber of  men  in  the  classes  of  these  is  four  times  greater  than  in  the  classes 
of  the  other  80  Associations. 

3.  The  conditions  essential  to  success  are :  (a)  study  of  the  local  field  to 
discover  the  needs  of  the  young  men;  (b]  an  adequate  fund;  (c)  meeting 
the  demand  by:   (1)  best  teachers  available;  (2)  room;  (3)  equipment;  (4) 
adaptable  subjects. 

4.  A  deposit  fee  is  charged  for  class  privileges  and  refunded  on  con- 
ditional attendance  by  60  Associations,  and  all  but  eight  of  these  report 
good  results  from  such  practice  in  the  increased  work,   interest   and 
attendance. 

5.  Three  in  every  four  of  the  700  teachers  receive  pay — an  average  of 
$2.20  per  lesson.     About  21,000  different  men  are  enrolled  in  the  classes. 

A  course  in  carpentry,  wood  turning,  chipping  and  filing  and  forge 
work  has  been  successfully  operated  the  past  year  in  the  Springfield, 
Ohio,  Association.  As  far  as  is  known,  this  is  the  first  place  to  carry 
through  the  full  course.  Several  Associations  are  planning  for  similar 
work  the  coming  year. 


EEPOKT  OF  LUTHEE  GULICK,  M.  D. 

My  work  for  the  International  Committee  during  the  year  may  be  con- 
veniently divided  into  three  sections. 

First. — The  advocacy  of  all-round  athletics,  particularly  in  the  form 
of  The  Pentathlon,  adopted  by  the  Committee.  Endeavor  has  been 
made  to  secure  the  co-operation  of  every  State  Committee.  A  number 
of  these  have  already  appointed  physical  department  committees  which 


34 

are  taking  hold  of  their  work  vigorously.  Having  the  International 
Committee  as  a  central  body  to  secure  and  keep  records  and  issue  certifi- 
cates, has  already  afforded  a  definite  basis  for  co-operation  and  unification, 
which  is  new  in  Association  work.  Costly  experience  has  shown  that 
separate  organizations  for  the  purpose  of  handling  Association  athletics 
and  gymnastics  are  detrimental  in  the  long  run. 

Second.—  The  tabulation  of  anthropometric  statistics.  This  work,  which 
I  have  been  doing  for  the  Committee  for  several  years,  has  made  con- 
siderable progress,  and  may  soon  be  completed  and  placed  before  the 
Associations. 

•i I. — General  correspondence.  I  have  corresponded  with  many  As- 
sociations looking  for  physical  directors,  and  have  usually  been  able  to 
suggest  men  for  vacancies.  A  large  number  of  men  have  been  corres- 
ponded with  and  in  many  cases  talked  with  in  regard  to  taking  up  physical 
work.  Similar  intercourse  has  been  held  with  Associations  in  regard  to 
the  fitting  of  gymnasiums,  athletic  work,  field  days,  measurements,  and 
the  like. 

Many  details  connected  with  these  three  branches  of  work  that  have 
been  given  in  former  reports  are  not  repeated  here,  but  every  year  seems 
to  have  some  special  line  of  work  cut  out  for  it.  The  distinctions  between 
the  gymnastics  that  are  most  useful  and  suitable  for  Young  Men's  Chris- 
tian Associations  and  for  schools  were  defined  more  clearly  last  year  than 
before,  and  accordingly  it  has  been  possible  to  develop  more  definitely 
the  peculiar  phases  of  gymnastics  that  are  useful  to  us.  The  chief  de- 
parture has  been  along  the  line  of  recreative  gymnastics.  A  great  advan- 
tage is  gained  if  men  can  secure  needed  exercise  in  a  way  that  is  at  the 
same  time  interesting  for  its  own  sake.  A  good  deal  of  time  has  been 
spent  in  the  study  of  the  situation  and  the  development  of  work  that  shall 
be  as  interesting  as  possible. 


THE  HISTORICAL  LIBRARY   OF  THE  YOUNG  MEN'S   CHRIS- 
TIAN ASSOCIATIONS. 
Annual  Report  of  J.   T.  Bowne,   Custodian. 

Sixty-four  bound  volumes  were  added  during  the  year,  making, 
February  28,  1893,  959  bound  and  1,070  unbound  ;  a  total  of  2,029. 

Nothing  could  better  illustrate  the  world-wide  extent  of  the  Young 
\s  Christian  Associations  than  the  fact  that  their  publications  are 
now  received  by  this  library  in  the  following  nineteen  languages  :  English, 
German,  Dutch,  Swedish,  Danish,  French,  Italian,  Spanish,  Portuguese, 
Wi-ls!i.  Russian,  Bohemian,  Hebrew,  Arabic,  Hungarian,  Finnish, 
Japanese,  Chinese,  and  Dakota  (N.  A.  Indian). 

The  classified  index  of  topics  presented  at  State  and  International  Con- 
ventions has  been  considerably  enlarged,  but  it  will  yet  require  months 
of  continuous  work  before  completion.  The  library  catalogue  and  index 
now  covers  about  16,000  cards.

The  Associations  at  home  and  abroad  have  very  generally  responded  to 

our  requests  for  their   publications.     The  total  number  of  Association 

i  i  >dicals  received  numbers  218,  being  six  less  than  last  jear.     They

may  be  classified  as  follows  :  United  States,  145 ;  Canada,  10 ;  Great

In  many  instances  both  local  and  State  Associations  are  publishing

MISCELLANEOUS  PUBLICATIONS. 

Among  many  kindred  publications  received  during  the  year,  the  fol- 
lowing periodicals  only  are  mentioned :  Six,  for  the  development  of  social 
and  personal  purity  and  temperance;  eleven,  representing  the  work  of  the 
Young  Women's  Christian  Association,  King's  Daughters,  and  Working 
Girls'  Societies;  five,  representing  the  prominent  young  people's  societies; 
three,  representing  the  Boys'  Brigade  movement;  and  six  representing 
the  Salvation  Army,  Missionary  and  Evangelistic  societies. 

Several  lots  of  duplicate  Association  reports  have  been  received,  and 
special  thanks  are  returned  to  Rev.  Frederic  von  Schluembach,  of  Cleve- 
land, for  a  large  lot  gathered  during  the  time  that  he  was  the  German 
Secretary  of  the  International  Committee ;  also  to  the  Montreal  Associa- 
tion, through  the  kindness  of  T.  D.  Patton..  Duplicates  are  always 
valuable  to  us  in  making  up  sets  for  Association  and  public  libraries. 

To  the  large  number  of  the  Associations  that  have  regularly  sent  us 
their  current  publications  we  return  hearty  thanks,  and  hope  that  in  some 
way  we  may  make  the  library  serviceable  to  them. 

We  again  call  the  attention  of  the  pioneers  in  Association  work,  or  the 
families  of  such,  that  may  have  Association  books,  pamphlets,  manu- 
scripts, or  pictures  that  they  are  willing  to  dispose  of,  to  the  importance 
of  sending  them  to  an  international  depository  like  this  library.  Informa- 
tion as  to  the  whereabouts  of  such  papers  will  always  be  gratefully 
received.  Communications  and  parcels  should  be  addressed,  "  The  His- 
torical Library  of  the  American  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations, 
Springfield,  Mass." 


REPORT  OF  J.  TRUMBULL  SWIFT, 

Secretary  for  Japan. 

In  contrast  with  the  two  preceding  years,  1892  was  one  of  comparative 
comfort  and  plenty.  The  floods  from  which  Japan  is  rarely  exempt  were 
of  limited  extent.  The  harvests  were  plentiful,  and  helped  to  efface  the 
lingering  traces  of  want  and  suffering  to  which  the  year  fell  heir.  The 
ohief  disturbances  occurred  in  connection  with  the  February  elections  to 


36 

the  lower  house  of  the  Imperial  Diet.  The  charges  of  official  interference 
brought  against  the  government  by  the  leaders  of  the  opposition  parties 
filled  the  land  with  excitement  that  was  so  intense  in  some  provinces  as 
to  necessitate  military  rule.  As  a  result  of  these  things  Count  Ito,  the 
"  father  of  the  constitution"  and  prince  of  Japanese  statesmen,  was  called 
by  the  Emperor  to  the  premiership.  His  cabinet,  which  the  close  of  the 
year  saw  struggling  with  an  overwhelming  opposition  in  the  lower  house, 
is  the  most  powerful  combination  of  the  leaders  of  the  three  clans, 
Satsuma,  Choshiu  and  Tosa,  which  effected  the  restoration  of  the  Emperor 
to  power  and  established  the  present  regime.  The  aim  of  the  opposition 
is  to  wrest  from  the  "Sat'-Cho"  league  their  long  held  power  and  to 
establish  party  government.  The  opposition  to  Christianity  has  continued 
to  be  severe.  It  has  been  claimed  that  the  teachings  of  Christ  are 
destructive  of  loyalty  and  filial  piety,  the  crowning  virtues  of  Confucian 
morals.  When  it  is  considered  that  the  teachings  of  the  Chinese  sage 
have  furnished  a  light  in  which  for  centuries  much  that  is  beautiful  and 
pure  has  grown  into  the  life  of  the  Japanese  people,  it  is  not  strange  that 
many  of  them  who  know  not  our  Lord  should  hesitate  to  give  up  the 
teachings  of  their  fathers  for  what  is  to  them  an  untried  foreign  system. 
It  is,  however,  startling  to  realize  that  in  the  discussions  of  the  Imperial 
Diet,  which  ended  in  a  postponement  of  the  civil  code,  it  was  urged 
that  these  laws  were  founded  on  Christian  morals,  and  that  Christ  taught, 
"if  any  man  .  .  .  hate  not  his  father  and  mother  ....  he 
cannot  be  my  disciple."*  In  the  face  of  these  things,  however,  the 
spring  conference  of  the  Congregational  churches  met  rejoicing  in  the 
confidence  that  the  period  of  reaction  and  opposition  was  near  its  close. 
The  great  meetings  of  the  Methodists  in  the  summer,  and  of  the  Presby- 
terians in  the  fall,  were  radiant  with  the  same  bright  hope;  and  the  closing 
year  witnessed  the  churches  at  work  more  earnestly  and  unitedly  than 
ever,  and  with  larger  plans  to  meet  the  opportunities  of  the  years  of 
plenty  on  which  they  had  surely  entered.  A  negative  testimony  to  the 
same  effect  is  given  by  the  wailing  of  the  Budhist  papers,  one  of  which 
in  December  headed  its  leading  article,  "A  Christian  Reaction  is 
Coming ! " 

The  condition  and  activities  of  the  Associations  in  Japan  are  presented 
in  detail  in  the  very  complete  report  of  Chief-Justice  Miyoshi,  Corres- 
ponding Member  of  the  International  Committee  (see  page  49) .  It  is  proper, 
however,  that  I  should  add  that  this  work  as  it  stands  is  the  result  of 
earnest,  untiring  effort  on  the  part  of  our  Japanese  brethren.  I 
regret  that  space  forbids  me  to  mention  by  name  the  large  number  who 
are  coming  month  by  month  to  represent  especial  departments  of  the 
work.  It  is  our  privilege  and  joy  to  be  allowed  a  share  in  their  enter- 
prises. Especially  have  the  skillful  and  untiring  efforts  of  Mr.  Niwa, 
the  Tokyo  general  secretary,  been  felt  in  almost  every  part  of  the 
empire.  His  fitness  for  his  office  grows  more  and  more  evident,  and  his 

*  "Just  at  this  time  when  there  is  so  much  need  for  care  on  the  part  of  us  blunt  for- 
"TS  that  we  may  not  unwittingly  offend  any,  I  beg  space  to  urge  that  all  friends  of  th» 
Japanese  Association  and  especially  those  who  write  or  speak  about  it  procure  and  carefully 
study  the  little  book  entitled,  'An  American  Missionary  in  Japan'  (Houghton,  Mifflin  <fc 
Co.)  To  imbibe  its  spirit  is  to  acquire  precious  lessons  otherwise  only  to  be  learned  by  long 
years  of  work  amongst  this  ancient  and  attractive  people." 


37 

zeal  in  it  is  often  in  excess  of  his  strength.  The  frequent  calls  for  trained 
secretaries  which  come  to  us  from  other  cities  make  us  wish  that  another 
such  as  he  might  be  receiving  experimental  training  in  the  office  of  the 
Tokyo  Association.  Only  $250  per  year  is  needed  to  make  this  possible. 

Justice  Miyoshi  in  his  report  mentions  the  Association  boarding  house. 
He  does  not  state  the  fact  that  it  has  attracted  wide  attention  and  is  per- 
haps more  favorably  regarded  than  any  department  of  our  work  thus  far 
developed.  The  rooms  are  small  and  the  house  is  old  and  badly  situated, 
but  a  year's  experience  demonstrates  that  aside  from  the  rent  it  is  self- 
supporting,  and  that  the  boarders  naturally  incline  to  take  active  part  in 
the  work  of  the  Association.  A  suitable  house  can  be  erected  and 
furnished  for  $1,500.  A  few  subscriptions  for  this  purpose  have  already 
been  received  by  W.  D.  Murray,  of  the  International  Committee, 
who  became  interested  in  the  undertaking  during  his  visit  last  summer. 
Others  are  needed  to  complete  the  necessary  amount. 

I  regret  that  I  am  unable  to  report  the  exact  number  of  young  men  led 
to  Christ  during  the  year  by  all  the  Associations*.  One  College  Associa- 
tion reports  sixteen,  another  five,  another  two,  another  six  earnest  en- 
quirers, and  so  on.  Altogether  it  is  probable  that  more  than  fifty  have 
thus  been  brought  into  eternal  life  through  the  prayers  and  efforts  of  our 
young  men. 

My  own  work  has  been  as  follows  :  In  April  I  spent  ten  days  at  Sendai, 
&  college  town  300  miles  north  of  Tokyo,  and  there  conferred  with  the 
officers  and  members  of  one  of  our  leading  College  Associations,  and 
spoke  at  its  annual  meeting.  I  also  did  what  I  could  to  strengthen  the 
city  Association.  With  the  exception  of  that  visit,  however,  the  exigen- 
cies of  the  work  demanded  my  constant  presence  in  Tokyo.  During  the 
first  seven  months  of  the  year  the  plans  for  the  Tokyo  building,  the 
selection  of  a  builder,  the  making  of  the  contracts,  etc.,  made  necessary 
almost  daily  conferences  with  members  of  the  building  committee,  the 
architect,  and  others.  I  also  taught  in  the  Association  evening  school 
and  conducted  a  Bible  class  on  Sundays.  During  the  last  three  months, 
while  continuing  to  pay  special  attention  to  the  work  upon  the  building, 
all  of  my  available  time  was  devoted  to  office  work  which  had  fallen  be- 
hind through  my  ill  health  of  the  previous  winter.  Through  the  entire 
year  I  have  worked  regularly  with  Mr.  Niwa  in  the  various  duties  of  the 
general  secretaryship  of  the  Tokyo  Association,  and  in  the  management 
of  the  monthly  paper.  I  have  received  many  calls  from  gentlemen  rep- 
resenting Associations  in  different  parts  of  the  empire,  and  my  corres- 
pondence continuing  to  be  large  has  demanded  much  time.  The  visita- 
tion of  Associations  outside  of  Tokyo  has  been  carefully  carried  on  by 
Messrs.  Niwa,  Murakami  and  Miller,  as  mentioned  in  Mr.  Miller's  report. 

I  desire  especially  to  acknowledge  our  very  considerable  obligation  to 
Rev.  George  Wm.  Knox,  D.  D.,  and  Eev.  H.  M.  Landis,  of  the  Presby- 
terian Mission  ;  to  Eev.  D.  C.  Green,  D.  D.,  of  the  A.  B.  C.  F.  M.;  to 
J.  McD.  Gardiner,  Esq. ,  of  the  American  Episcopal  Mission ;  to  B.  J. 
Kirby,  Esq.,  to  Rev.  J.  A.  B.  Scherer,  of  the  American  Lutheran  Mission, 
and  to  Dr.  Theodore  Gulick,  of  Kyoto.  All  of  these  gentlemen  have 
given  very  largely  of  their  valuable  time  in  counsel  and  active  effort  in 
support  and  furtherance  of  the  work  of  the  year. 


38 

REPORT  OF  R.  S.  MILLER,  JK. 

Assistant  Secretary  for  Japan. 

My  time  for  the  past  year  has  been  about  equally  divided  between  As- 
sociation work  and  the  study  of  the  language.  After  two  years  of  steady 
application  the  mastery  of  the  language  still  seems  to  be  an  almost  super- 
human task,  and  yet  I  have  made  progress  enough  to  feel  much  en- 
couraged. The  course  of  study  which  I  have  followed  for  the  year  has 
been:  (1),  the  reading  of  moral  addresses,  school  readers,  and  the 
religious  newspapers ;  (2),  writing  of  Chinese  characters,  and  (3),  such 
general  work  as  translation  from  Japanese  to  English,  English  to  Japan- 
ese, preparation  of  short  addresses  in  Japanese,  reading  of  the  Japanese 
Bible,  and  personal  work  in  Japanese.  Rev.  Geo.  Wm.  Knox,  D.D.,  has 
kindly  examined  me  in  these  studies  at  regular  intervals. 

My  more  direct  Association  work  has  been  as  follows : — Teaching  in  the 
evening  classes  of  the  Tokyo  city  Association  from  three  to  five  hours 
each  week,  an  English  Bible  class  once  a  week,  and  personal  work 
among  the  English  speaking  students  following  up  the  Bible  classes  and 
Sunday  meetings.  One  man  is  ready  to  receive  baptism,  two  more  are 
near  the  point  of  decision,  and  others  appear  interested. 

In  the  spring  of  1892  I  visited  with  Mr.  Murakami  the  Associations  of 
Kyoto,  and  again  this  winter  with  Mr.  Niwa,  the  Associations  of  Kyoto, 
Osaka,  Kobe  and  Nagoya,  as  recently  reported  in  the  Era.  After  the  first 
visit  there  was  formed  in  the  Doshisha  a  personal  workers'  band,  which  I 
am  told  resulted  in  the  conversion  of  ten  men.  An  Association  was  also 
formed  at  that  time  in  the  Kyoto  Medical  College,  where  twelve  or  thir- 
teen men  have  recently  received  baptism,  the  result,  I  think,  of  the  work  of 
a  Doshisha  student  as  teacher  of  the  Association  Bible  class.  In  the  sum- 
mer I  attended  the  Summer  School  at  Lake  Hakone,  and  had  some  part 
in  the  meetings  for  the  discussion  of  Association  work.  In  Tokyo  I  have 
visited  the  Associations  at  the  University,  Higher  Middle  College,  the 
Academy,  Technical  School  and  the  Soldiers'  Club  ;  I  have  also  in  turn 
had  members  of  most  of  these  Associations  at  my  home  at  different  times 
for  a  social  evening.  Considerable  time  has  also  been  taken  up  by  con- 
ferences with  Secretaries  Swift  and  Niwa,  calls  upon  officers  of  the  Asso- 
ciation, securing  speakers  and  teachers,  and  a  somewhat  large  corres- 
pondence. 

In  addition  to  the  above  regular  lines  of  work  I  have  tried  to  make  my 
home  attractive  to  students  and  a  center  of  Chistian  influence.  The  presi- 
dent of  the  Higher  Middle  College  Association,  and  one  other  student  are 
living  with  me  ;  we  have  regular  family  worship  each  morning  and  oc- 
casional social  evenings  for  students.  It  has  also  been  necessary  for  me 
to  do  some  reading  on  the  evidences  of  Christianity  ;  and,  finally,  I  have 
lately  taken  a  not  unimportant  step  in  leaving  the  foreign  church  at  the 
Concession,  and  associating  myself  with  a  Japanese  church  for  regular 
worship  and  service. 

REPORT  OF  DAVID  McCONAUGHY,  JR., 

Secretary  for  India. 

Our  third  year  has  been  by  far  the  best  yet  in  the  work  of  the  Madras 
Association,  and  also  throughout  India  generally. 


39 

The  Second  National  Convention,  held  in  Bombay,  April  14-18,  1892y 
marked  a  distinct  advance  in  the  work  of  the  National  Union.  The  con- 
stitution, which  had  been  under  consideration  for  more  than  a  year, 
has  been  finally  approved  by  the  National  Council.  It  provides  that 
every  Association  shall  have  direct  representation  in  the  National 
Convention.  Forms  of  constitution  for  use  in  college  and  town  As- 
sociations have  been  published,  the  latter  in  Tamil  and  Mahratta,  as 
well  as  in  English.  A  topic  book  has  been  published,  giving  subjects  for 
young  men's  meetings  and  a  systematic  course  of  studies  in  the  life  of 
Christ,  for  which  outlines  are  published  monthly  in  ' '  The  Young  Men 
of  India."  Though  the  National  Council  has  directed  its  efforts  to  de- 
veloping existing  Associations,  rather  than  to  extension,  the  number  of 
Associations  on  the  roll  has  nearly  doubled  during  the  past  year.  There 
are  seventy-four  now  reported,  of  which  fifty-seven  are  in  Madras,  nine  in 
Bombay,  one  in  Central  India,  one  in  Central  Provinces,  one  in  Bengal, 
three  in  the  Northwest  Provinces,  and  two  in  the  Punjab. 

The  arrival  of  F.  H.  Wood  early  in  October  to^take  charge  of  the  work 
in  Madras,  enabled  me  to  give  my  whole  attention  to  the  national  work 
during  the  latter  part  of  the  year. 

I  was  able  during  1892  to  make  seven  tours,  visiting  36  of  the  Associa- 
tions, occupying  114  days  and  traveling  8,731  miles,  by  sea  and  land,  by 
bullock  bandy,  boat  and  jinricksha,  as  well  as  by  railway.  The  whole 
field  has  thus  been  covered  from  Cape  Comorin  to  the  Ganges,  and  all 
the  Associations,  except  a  few  in  the  far  North — isolated  hill  stations  in 
the  Himalayas — have  been  brought  into  touch  with  the  National  Union. 
There  has  been  marked  improvement  in  many  of  the  Associations.  Bible 
study  has  become  more  general ;  boys'  work  has  been  undertaken  at  Hy- 
derabad and  Magercoil ;  building  enterprises  have  been  begun  at  Madras, 
Hyderabad,  Bareilly,  Kohlapur  and  Poona,  and  small  inexpensive  build- 
ings have  been  erected  at  Trichoor  and  Nagercoil. 

The  week  of  prayer  for  young  men  was  observed  by  twice  as  many  As- 
sociations in  1892  as  in  the  previous  year.  The  Melkavu  Association — 
the  chief  of  a  group  of  nine  Associations,  situated  on  the  western  slopes 
of  the  Pulney  Hills,  30  miles  back  from  the  Malabar  coast,  composed  of 
illiterate  aborigines,  numbering  250  members — reports  an  average  attend- 
ance of  155  for  five  days  and  increasing  to  250  the  last  two  days  of  the 
week.  "More  than  seventy  of  the  members,"  the  secretary  writes, 
"  publicly  announced  their  willingness  to  work  for  the  Lord  in  and  out  of 
the  church.  Some  of  our  members  who  were  not  very  earnest  about  their 
salvation  showed  signs  of  real  repentance  and  conversion,  and  I  am  glad 
to  observe  them  daily  increasing  in  grace  and  in  the  knowledge  of  our 
Lord  Jesus  Christ."  This  is  a  specimen  of  the  reports  received  from 
more  than  a  score  of  Associations  all  over  the  country. 

I  attended  the  Decennial  Missionary  Conference  in  Bombay,  December 
29,  1892,  and  presented  a  paper  on  "The  Young  Men's  Christian  Asso- 
ciation as  a  Missionary  Agency." 

The  English  National  Council  responded  nobly  to  our  appeal  for  help 
by  sending  out  one  of  the  ablest  and  most  experienced  of  the  British 
secretaries,  Robert  McCann,  formerly  traveling  secretary  for  Ireland, 
whose  services  have  been  placed  wholly  at  the  disposal  of  the  Bombay 


40 

District  Union.     He  is  also  an  officer  of  the  Indian  National  Council, 
although  under  the  immediate  supervision  of  the  Bombay  District  Union. 

A  great  impetus  has  been  given  to  the  work  in  the  Western  Presidency 
since  Mr.  McCann's  arrival  in  October,  1892. 

The  sudden  transfer  of  Mr.  Wood  to  Calcutta,  followed  immediately 
afterward  by  his  departure  from  the  country,  leaves  me  alone  again  to 
carry  on  the  local  work  in  Madras,  giving  to  the  national  work  only  such 
remnant  of  time  as  I  can  save. 

The  Madras  Association  is  making  steady  progress.  The  membership 
had  increased  (from  215  in  1891)  to  268  at  the  end  of  last  year,  and  it  is 
still  larger  now.  An  analysis  shows  that  of  the  associate  members  103  are 
Hindoos  (83  in  1891),  4  Mohammedans  (3  in  1891)  and  4  Parsees  (none 
before).  Probably  no  Parsee  has  ever  joined  the  Young  Men's  Christian 
Association  before.  There  has  been  a  steady  increase  of  Eurasian  mem- 
bers, now  numbering  81,  as  compared  with  60  in  1891  and  43  in  1890.  The 
number  of  undergraduate  students  is  108,  and  of  the  other  members  a 
large  proportion  have  passed  through  college. 

The  branch  started  in  Vepery,  a  few  months  ago,  is  thoroughly  organ- 
ized and  doing  splendid  work.  Citizens  who  have  known  this  section  of 
the  city  for  many  years  have  borne  strong  testimony  to  a  marked  improve- 
ment noticeable  throughout  the  community  since  the  Association  began 
work  on  this  side  of  town. 

The  attendance  in  the  rooms  averaged  186  daily  throughout  the  year. 
Five  meetings  for  young  men  have  been  maintained  weekly — the  Bible 
class  at  Black  Town  averaging  23,  at  Vepery  12;  young  men's  meetings  at 
Black  Town  17,  at  Vepery  17;  gospel  meeting  at  Black  Town  60.  Tamil 
open  air  preaching  is  carried  on  by  native  Christian  members  and  visita- 
tion in  the  hospitals  by  a  committee  of  our  medical  students.  Lectures 
and  socials  are  now  given  regularly  both  in  the  Black  Town  and  Vepery 
rooms.  The  attendance  at  the  members'  quarterly  meeting  averaged  149. 
The  library  has  grown  to  over  800  volumes.  The  restaurant  is  yielding  a 
good  profit.  The  class  in  book-keeping  and  commercial  correspondence 
has  done  very  good  work.  One  of  this  class  who  recently  appeared  for 
the  "Accountant  Test  "  headed  the  list  of  those  who  passed  in  the  presi- 
dency. Two  others  who  appeared  for  the  "book-keeping  test "  were  suc- 
cessful, one  of  them  heading  the  list  of  those  who  passed  in  the  presi- 
dency. The  athletic  grounds  are  more  used  now  than  ever;  a  small 
wooden  house  has  been  erected — the  gift  of  a  Hindoo  gentleman — for 
storing  cricket,  tennis,  base-ball  and  foot-ball  outfit  and  for  changing 
clothes.  Every  Wednesday  afternoon  the  tennis  and  badminton  courts  at 
my  house  are  thrown  open  to  the  members  at  Vepery. 

Our  hearts  have  been  cheered  by  unmistakable  signs  of  spiritual  life 
among  our  members.  Three  of  our  associate  members  have  come  out 
boldly  from  Hindooism  and  have  been  baptized;  not  a  few  are  trying  to  be 
His  disciples,  "but  secretly  for  fear."  Not  a  few  nominal  Christians  also 
give  evidence  of  new  life. 

"Going  forth  with  weeping,  bearing  precious  seed,"  we  expect  to  come 
again  rejoicing  bearing  our  sheaves  with  us  in  God's  own  good  time. 

The  need  of  a  building  of  our  own  for  this  growing  work  is  pressing 
more  and  more.  The  members,  although  most  of  them  quite  poor,  have 


ASSOCIATION  in  II  DI.NC.  WH.KKsisAKKK,  i'.\. 

DKIMC  \in.  |  \M  AKN    i,    i 
7(.x2i5k-rt.  Gust,  597, oc».  Population,  40,000. 


41 

themselves  begun  a  building  fund,  subscribing  over  two  thousand  rupees 
(over  $700) .  The  building  committee  has  issued  an  illustrated  prospectus, 
the  amount  required  being  estimated  at  $30,000.  We  are  praying  that  ere 
long  the  Lord  will  lay  it  upon  the  hearts  of  some  of  His  stewards  to  fur- 
nish the  necessary  funds. 

Whether  the  Christian  young  men  of  the  west  realize  it  or  not,  a  crisis' 
is  upon  us  here  in  India.  Too  late,  it  may  be,  the  American  Associations 
will  awake  to  the  fact  that  the  greatest  opportunity  that  was  ever  pre- 
sented to  them  has  gone  forever.  It  is  simply  impossible  for  one  or  two 
men  to  bear  the  overwhelming  burden  that  has  been  laid  upon  them  on 
this  field.  The  mighty  movement  which  the  International  Committee 
helped  to  set  in  motion  among  the  fifty  millions  of  India's  young  men,  is 
gathering  a  momentum  that  will  not  slow  up  to  suit  the  present  pace  of 
our  little  faith.  More  than  three  years  have  gone  and  Calcutta  is  still 
impatiently  waiting  for  a  secretary,  while  Madras,  Colombo,  Allahabad 
and  Lahore  are  in  no  less  urgent  need  of  men.  It  was  a  mistake  to  think 
that  a  few  trained  leaders  from  the  west  would  suffice  for  India.  For 
years  yet  it  will  be  vain  to  look  for  native  secretaries,  capable  of  taking 
sole  charge  of  the  work  in  the  great  cities.  The  leading  centers  of  the 
Empire  must  be  provided  with  experienced  men,  born  and  trained  in 
Christian  lands.  Dissapointing  as  this  fact  may  be,  it  is  a  fact,  and  the 
sooner  the  fact  is  realized  the  more  hope  there  will  be  for  the  work  in 
India.  "  The  harvest  truly  is  plenteous,  but  the  laborers  are  few;  pray 
ye  therefore  the  Lord  of  the  harvest  that  he  would  send  forth  laborers 
into  his  harvest." 


EEPOET  OF  MYRON  A.  CLAEK, 

Secretary  for  Brazil. 

Your  secretary  for  Brazil  sailed  from  New  York  July  15,  1891,  reach- 
ing the  city  of  Sao  Paulo  on  August  17,  having  touched  at  all  the  port 
cities  and  conversed,  more  or  less  at  length,  with  the  various  missionaries 
at  these  points.  During  September  the  triennial  session  of  the  synod 
of  the  Presbyterian  church  in  Brazil  was  held;  an  opportunity  was 
given  for  the  presentation  of  our  work,  and  a  strong  resolution  of 
sympathy  and  co-operation  was  adopted.  On  September  28,  I  left  for 
Faxina,  a  small  town  some  200  miles  in  the  interior,  where  no  word  of 
English  could  be  heard;  here  five  months  were  spent  with  the  native 
pastor  of  the  Protestant  church  in  diligent  study  of  the  Portuguese  lan- 
guage. Returning  to  Sao  Paulo,  the  month  of  March  was  spent  in  inter- 
views with  the  local  Brazilian  pastor  and  the  missionaries.  A  society  of 
young  men  was  found  already  in  existence  in  the  church,  but  very  poorly 
organized  and  with  no  very  definite  object  in  view.  Of  this  society  I  be- 
came a  member,  hoping  to  direct  its  energies  towards  a  work  for  young 
men  and  ultimately  to  transform  it  into  a  Young  Men's  Christian  Associa- 
tion. These  hopes  have  proven  futile.  April  was  spent  in  extending  ac- 
quaintances and  making  preparations  for  a  public  meeting  in  the  interests 
of  this  society,  at  which  an  address  was  delivered  on  definite  work  for  and 
by  young  men.  During  May  plans  were  laid  for  a  Bible  class  for  young 
men,  with  the  hope  of  stimulating  a  desire  to  do  aggressive  personal  work. 


42 

This  class,  beginning  May  29,  has  been  continued,  with  an  average  at- 
tendance of  some  eight  or  ten,  until  quite  recently.  About  this  time, 
suitable  rooms  were  secured  to  which  to  invite  the  young  men,  and  the 
society  met  weekly  with  me;  later  this  meeting  became  a  social  re-union 
of  young  men  for  conversation  and  games,  thus  showing  the  home  ad- 
vantages of  an  Association.  In  August,  on  invitation  of  friends,  including 
the  missionaries,  I  went  to  Rio  de  Janeiro  to  look  over  the  ground.  At 
this  time  I  also  attended  the  Brazil  Mission  Conference  of  the  Methodist 
church  in  Juiz  de  Fora,  being  warmly  welcomed  both  by  pastors  and 
missionaries,  speaking  on  our  work  and  securing  the  adoption  of  a  resolu- 
tion of  approval  and  co-operation.  After  speaking  on  our  work  in  the 
various  churches  in  Bio  and  meeting  personally  with  interested  parties,  I 
was  convinced  of  the  necessity  of  beginning  as  soon  as  possible  a  definite 
work  in  the  capital.  September  was  spent  in  routine  work  in  Sao  Paulo. 
In  October  I  was  suddenly  called  to  Bio  to  check  a  precipitate  movement 
to  organize  an  Association  in  one  church;  after  several  conferences  we 
succeeded  in  inducing  the  interested  parties  to  postpone  action  until  the 
following  May,  I,  on  my  part,  promising  to  make  every  effort  to  be  in  Bio 
at  that  time.  During  this  month  a  weekly  young  men's  meeting  for 
prayer  and  testimony  had  been  planned  in  Sao  Paulo.  The  first  session 
was  held  October  21,  and  was  quite  encouraging,  and  this  meeting  has 
been  kept  up  with  more  or  less  regularity.  November  13  to  19,  the  week 
of  prayer  for  young  men  was  observed.  Special  sermons  to  young  men 
were  preached  in  the  Presbyterian  and  Methodist  churches,  making  due 
.mention  of  our  work  and  the  story  of  the  celebration  of  the  day.  An  an- 
imated young  men's  meeting  was  held  on  that  day,  as  also  on  Friday  and 
the  following  Sunday.  Thinking  that  the  occasion  might  be  opportune 
for  organization  in  Sao  Paulo,  interviews  were  held  with  the  pastors  and 
various  young  men.  But  the  time  was  thought  to  be  premature,  on  ac- 
count of  financial  reasons  and  certain  unfortunate  questions  in  the 
churches,  and  the  pastors  agreed  that  some  years  later,  under  better  con- 
ditions and  with  perhaps  a  model  Association  in  Bio,  better  results  might 
be  attained.  Since  that  time,  it  has  been  simply  waiting  for  the  yellow 
fever  season  to  pass  in  Bio;  I  look  forward  to  moving  there  in  May.  De- 
cember was  occupied  with  Bible  class  and  young  men's  meeting  work;  I 
also  delivered  an  address  at  the  commencement  exercises  of  the  Methodist 
college  in  Taubate.  In  January  I  attended  the  district  conference  of  the 
Methodist  church  and  gave  a  series  of  Bible  readings. 

During  the  year  various  articles  have  been  written  for  the  Christian 
s,  dealing  with  different  phases  of  our  work,  preparing  the  ground  by 
thus  scattering  general  ideas  of  the  work.  Our  first  humble  publication 
has  been  prepared  and  is  now  in  press,  being  a  pamphlet  on  "The  Classifi- 
cation of  Members  and  the  Active  Membership  Test."  Much  time  has 
been  spent  in  study  of  the  language;  for  fluency  or  even  for  general  satis- 
faction, this  must  be  kept  up  for  a  considerable  time  yet.  Letters  have 
been  exchanged  with  Association  men  in  Argentina  and  Chili,  from 
which  I  learn  that  the  following  Associations  exist :  Argentina,  Buenos 
Ayres,  English-speaking,  William  Barr,  secretary ;  Barracas  branch  of 
same  Association,  Spanish-speaking ;  Monte  Video,  English,  H.  F.  Pratt, 
tary.  The  Associations  in  Chili  have  ceased  to  exist.  There  are 
no  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations  in  Brazil ;  nor  has  any  similar 


43 

work  ever  been  undertaken  here.  The  idea  is  entirely  new  and  the 
work  therefore  must  be  built  up  from  the  very  first  foundation  stones. 
Then  too,  it  must  be  primarily  and  essentially  a  work  for  Brazilian,  Por- 
tuguese-speaking young  men.  Not  that  there  are  no  English-speaking 
young  men,  nor  that  they  do  not  need  equally  such  help,  but  that,  in 
order  to  become  a  national  Brazilian  institution,  the  movement  must 
begin  with  and  among  the  Brazilians.  Later  on,  the  work  may  include 
English-speaking  young  men,  or  a  branch  work  may  be  established  among 
them.  Further,  very  few  Christian  young  men,  desirous  of  working  for 
their  fellows,  have  been  encountered  in  the  churches.  The  time  has 
come  when  the  church  realizes  that  to  evangelize  Brazil  she  must  have  a 
Brazilian  ministry  and  every  nerve  is  strained  now  for  the  maintenance  of 
a  seminary.  Hence  the  thoughts  and  energies  of  the  young  men  of  the 
churches  are  largely  centered  in  this  project.  My  past  year  ought  per- 
haps to  be  regarded  as  a  year  of  preparation  and  of  inquiry  as  to  the  most 
important  and  strategic  point.  So  considered  the 'choice  has  but  just  been 
made  and  the  coming  year's  work  in  the  national  capital  and  metropolis 
is  looked  forward  to  with  hope  of  definite  results.  There  we  will  have 
more  elements  in  three  or  four  churches  ;  we  will  have  some  financial 
backing,  and  the  secretary  will  be  better  prepared  to  cope  with  the  situa- 
tion, being  not  only  more  advanced  in  the  language  but  also  having  a 
better  knowledge  of  the  national  characteristics  of  the  young  men. 

In  no  way  does  the  experience  of  the  past  year  tend  to  show  that  the 
need  of  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  work  here  was  overestimated. 
The  young  men  of  Brazil  are,  as  are  young  men  in  all  lands,  the  hope  of 
the  nation.  They  already  occupy  positions  of  prominence  and  trust,  and 
as  education  is  diffused  their  realm  of  usefulness  and  importance  will 
grow.  They  are,  however,  a  godless  class  of  young  men  and  are  leading 
lives  of  fearful  wickedness  without  any  thought  of  the  future.  As  in 
many  other  countries,  the  old  form  of  religion  has  very  largely  lost  its 
hold  upon  them,  while  materialistic  philosophy — mere  indifferentism — is 
producing  its  natural  fruit  in  their  daily  lives. 


ANNUAL  REPORTS  OF  CORRESPONDING  MEMBERS, 

To  APRIL  1,  1893. 


ATJSTKALASIA. 

The  results  attending  the  year's  work  have  been  varied.  The  seventh 
Intercolonial  Convention,  held  at  Brisbane,  Queensland,  in  May,  was 
regarded  as  the  best  of  the  series,  the  topics  and  discussions  being  practical 
and  interesting.  The  Brisbane  board  has,  however,  felt  obliged  to  dis- 
pense with  its  general  secretary.  Sydney,  New  South  Wales,  has  com- 
pleted an  excellent  year.  A  special  feature  has  been  a  series  of  Sunday 
breakfasts  to  the  unemployed.  The  governor  and  the  church  officials 
have  generously  co-operated  in  the  effort.  New  Castle  is  holding  its  own 
though  still  without  a  secretary.  The  Melbourne,  Victoria,  Association 
has  suffered  through  the  sickness  and  final  retirement  of  its  general  secre- 
tary. Physical  director.  Stock  well,  who  has  been  highly  successful  in  his 
particular  field,  has  kindly  and  ably  assisted  in  the  emergency.  Geelong 
has  recently  opened  a  new  hall  and  is  gradually  extending  its  work.  Ade- 
laide, South  Australia,  has  successfully  formed  several  branches  and  had  a 
year  of  remarkable  success  along  spiritual  lines.  Mainly  through  the  efforts 
of  the  Adelaide  board  a  new  field  has  been  opened  up  in  Western  Australia, 
and  new  Associations  have  been  organized  at  Perth  and  Albany.  Hobart, 
Tasmania,  has  secured  an  excellent  secretary  in  H.  J.  Fairfax,  late  of 
Brisbane.  Lauceston  is  still  without  a  general  secretary.  Auckland  and 
the  other  Associations  of  New  Zealand  are  doing  well,  and  as  the  colony 
has  emerged  from  long  years  of  depression,  decided  improvement  may  be 
expected  in  Association  matters. 

W.  A.  SOUTHWELL,  Cor.  Mem. 


FRANCE. 

An  important  event  of  the  past  year  was  the  National  Conference  held 
at  "Valentigney,  in  the  department  of  the  Doubs,  Sept.  21-25.  Forty 
official  delegates  were  present  from  different  quarters  of  France.  Twenty- 
five  others  followed  attentively  the  work  of  the  conference.  Among  these 
were  Professors  Porret  and  Barde,  and  Ernest  Favre  of  the  International 
Committee.  George  Williams,  W.  H.  Mills  and  Dr.  Kirby,  of  the  English 
it  ions  were  also  present.  Special  attention  had  been  given  to  or- 
tf:uii/ing  a  large  number  of  meetings  for  prayer  during  the  conference, 
and  several  conversions  were  the  result.  Valentigney  is  a  Protestant  vil- 
lage of  3,000  inhabitants,  and  the  immense  value  of  this  fact  in  creating 
u  proper  spiritual  atmosphere  for  the  conference  cannot  be  overestimated, 
important  points  were  the  choice  of  James  Hughes,  of  Lyons, 
as  General  Secretary  of  the  French  National  Committee,  and  the  elabor- 
ation of  a  new  constitution  voted  almost  without  discussion.  Up  to  this 
time  the  National  Committee  has  not  had  the  exclusive  service  of  such 
a  secretary,  and  the  appointment  of  M.  Hughes  will  undoubtedly  be  of 
great  profit  to  the  general  work. 


45 

During  the  past  three  years  there  has  been  an  increase  in  the  number  of 
Associations,  from  63  to  95;  in  membership,  from  1,300  to  2,281;  in  the  num- 
ber of  boys'  branches,  from  139  to  360;  and  in  buildings,  from  1  to  3.  The 
current  expenses  for  1892  aggregated  $68,892.  The  Associations  at  Paris 
and  Lyons  employ  general  secretaries.  The  Paris  Association  expects  to 
enter  its  new  building  at  an  early  date.  It  is  thoroughly  well  equipped 
with  gymnasium,  baths,  lecture  hall,  library,  restaurant,  class  rooms,  etc. , 
and  is  lighted  by  electricity  and  heated  by  steam.  The  Association  num- 
bers in  all  631  members  and  increases  daily  in  its  influence  for  good 
throughout  Paris  and  France.  It  has  corresponding  members  in  the 
principal  countries  of  the  world,  and  during  the  past  year  it  has  widely 
disseminated  its  printed  matter.  IS  Esperance,  the  official  organ,  pub- 
lished under  the  supervision  of  the  National  Committee,  has  been  trans- 
ferred to  Paris,  improved  as  to  its  form  and  subject  matter,  and  will  be 
very  helpful  in  the  development  of  the  work.  The  work  in  Lyons  is 
being  successfully  prosecuted.  The  Association  in  Bordeaux  has  made  an 
effort  to  raise  the  funds  for  an  enlarged  work  and  to  secure  a  general 
secretary,  but  has  not  yet  found  the  right  man.  In  the  death  of  Pastor  J. 
B.  Couve,  of  Bordeaux,  the  Association  has  lost  a  most  valued  friend  and 
helper.  During  the  year  eight  Associations  have  been  founded  in  small 
towns  and  four  Associations  have  moved  into  new  rooms. 

FRANKLIN  GAYLORD,  Cor.  Mem.    • 


GEKMANY. 

Since  my  report  two  years  ago  there  has  been  a  great  activity  in  Asso- 
ciation circles.  One  result  is  shown  in  the  increase  of  Associations  from 
800  to  1,005.  Another  fact  to  be  mentioned  is  the  spiritual  deepening  of 
the  work  and  the  more  fervent  missionary  spirit  now  prevalent. 

The  secretarial  force  is  steadily  increasing.  The  Association  literature, 
especially  as  regards  the  weekly,  fortnightly  and  monthly  bulletins,  has 
grown  more  efficient  and,  what  is  particularly  pleasing,  a  lively  interest 
is  being  taken  in  international  Association  matters. 

The  "white  cross "  movement  has  made  much  progress;  about  4,000 
young  men  have  already  signed  the  pledge.  At  various  places  ' '  soldiers' 
homes "  have  been  opened  in  connection  with  our  Associations,  the 
military  authorities  favoring  the  work. 

Beside  the  already  existing  "sick  fund  for  members,"  which  works 
well,  a  "  savings  bank  "  has  also  been  organized.  The  building  question 
is  still  moving  slowly,  although  some  buildings  have  been  erected,  even 
in  smaller  places. 

Last  January  the  Berlin  Association  held  its  tenth  anniversary,  and  was 
enabled  to  open  at  the  same  time  a  branch  building  in  one  of  the  busiest 
parts  of  the  city  for  special  work  among  waiters,  bakers  and  soldiers. 
Over  8,000  young  men  have  joined  it  as  members,  about  700  of  them 
foreigners.  Fifty  members  have  devoted  themselves  to  mission  work  in 
the  home  and  foreign  fields.  General  collections  have  been  permitted  by 
the  state  in  some  of  the  provinces  in  aid  of  the  Berlin  work. 

For  several  years  past  the  Evangelical  church  council  has  arranged  for 
an  annual  course  of  information  for  young  ministers  respecting  home  mis- 
sion work.  The  visiting  of  some  of  the  leading  Associations,  combined 


46 

with  a  lecture  about  the  work,  has  always  been  a  part  of  the  program. 
The  same  council  has  lately  given  public  testimony  to  the  great  value  the 
Associations  are  to  the  church,  in  supplying  workers  for  the  home 
mission  field ;  the  pastors  have  therefore  been  asked  to  further  the  cause 
as  much  as  they  can.  The  third  National  Conference  of  Germany  will 
be  held  this  year  at  Cassel.  CHRISTIAN  PHTLDTUS,  Cor.  Mem. 


GBEAT  BKITAIN. 

The  work  in  great  Britain  has  during  the  past  year  steadily  forged 
ahead  and  is  rapidly  coming  to  the  front.  This  is  especially  noticeable 
regarding  the  great  attention  that  the  public  press  is  giving  to  the  work 
as  a  whole.  As  a  rule  the  criticisms  are  distinctly  favorable. 

At  the  present  time  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  stands  in  the 
first  place  among  kindred  institutions  as  an  educational  agency,  while 
there  is  nothing  in  the  country  to  compare  with  it  as  a  school  of  physical 
culture. 

Much  attention  is  being  bestowed  at  the  present  time  upon  sectional 
work  in  various  parts  of  the  country,  with  the  happiest  result. 

Building  schemes  are  on  foot  at  Abergavenny,  St.  Austell,  Paignton, 
Hfracombe,  South  Shields,  Sunderland  (extension),  and  Newcastle. 

The  following  abstract  will  explain  the  great  increase  of  work  since  the- 
first  year  of  the  National  Council  in  1883.  These  statistics,  however,  only 
deal  with  England,  Ireland  and  Wales. 

COMPARATIVE  FIGURES  FOR  1892  AND  1883,  THE  LATTER  IN  PARENTHESES.

(£153,637).
