E.  J.  KENNEDY.  Cor.  Mem. 


HAWAII. 

During  the  past  year  the  standing  committees  have  been  better 
organic  •<!  MI  that  the  work  does  not  fall  as  heretofore  almost  entirely 
npon  the  chairmen,  but  is  borne  by  sub-sections  to  whom  definite  duties 
are  a*siirn<-«l. 

The  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Review,  an  illustrated  paper  devoted  to  the  causes 
of  temperance  and  morality  in  Hawaii,  has  been  started.  Much  good 
work  has  been  done  by  the  Association  in  the  daily  press  and  by  personal 
efforts  to  raise  the  tone  of  public  sentiment  against  various  bills  agitated 


47 

in  the  legislature  in  favor  of  opium  and  lottery,  and   "light  wine  and 
beer"  licenses. 

The  number  of  religious  services  held  during  the  week  is  increased  to 
seven  by  a  service  at  the  barracks  for  the  soldiers  of  the  provisional 
government.  Attendance  at  all  the  services  during  the  year  aggregated 
13,000.  A  series  of  evening  meetings  lasting  three  weeks  was  held  at 
Bethel  Hall  at  which  about  25  persons  expressed  a  determination  to  lead 
the  Christian  life.  Many  removals  to  other  countries  have  taken  place 
among  the  members,  but  there  are  accessions  also  which  keep  the  member- 
ship about  as  last  year,  say  225.  It  takes  about  $3,000  for  current  expenses, 
which  is  mainly  raised  by  pledges. 

Mrs.  Andrews  and  Miss  Waterhouse  keep  up  the  interest  in  the  Y.  M. 
C.  A.  Boys,  and  a  Boy's  Brigade  has  been  organized. 

The  general  secretary,  Eev.  H.  W.  Peck,  who  has  been  our  leader  since 
the  resignation  of  S.  D.  Fuller,  two  years  ago,  has  sent  in  his  resignation, 
as  he  enters  the  ministry.  We  are  corresponding  now  with  reference  to 
his  successor. 

All  the  above  refers  to  the  Honolulu  Association,  which  is  composed 
exclusively  of  whites.  The  Chinese  and  Japanese  have  Associations  in 
Honolulu,  and  there  are  about  twenty  among  the  native  Hawaiians, 
distributed  about  the  archipelago.  But  as  these  latter  partake  more  of 
the  character  of  the  Christian  endeavor  societies,  admitting  both 
sexes  to  membership,  they  are  not  reported. 

A.  F.  JUDD,  Cor.  Mem. 


INDIA. 

The  recent  third  anniversary  of  the  Madras  Young  Men's  Christian  As- 
sociation, the  most  progressive  and  active  of  the  multiplying  Associations 
of  this  country,  calls  to  mind  my  relations  to  the  International  Commit- 
tee, and  my  pleasant  annual  duty  of  reporting  the  progress  of  the  Asso- 
ciations in  India. 

Probably  the  most  notable  events  of  the  year  were  the  additions  to  the 
secretarial  staff  of  men  whose  experience  and  training  seemed  especially 
to  qualify  them  for  Association  work,  and  to  give  promise  of  much  efficient 
leadership  in  their  respective  fields  in  India.  The  British  Council  sent 
out  a  representative  to  develop  the  work  more  especially  in  the  Bombay 
Presidency ;  while  the  American  Committee  made  a  vigorous  attempt 
to  supply  Mr.  McConaughy  with  an  assistant  for  Madras  which,  though 
partially  thwarted  by  the  necessary  withdrawal  of  Mr.  Wood,  will,  we 
hope,  be  eventually  successful.  It  is  gratifying  to  know  that  an  appre- 
ciable proportion  of  the  salary  of  this  new  secretary  is  to  be  met  by  Indian 
funds. 

Mr.  McConaughy,  in  his  capacity  as  secretary  to  the  Indian  National 
Committee,  has  spent  several  weeks  in  Calcutta,  organizing,  at  the  earnest 
solicitation  of  the  missionary  conference,  a  Young  Men's  Christian  As- 
sociation in  that  influential  center.  The  importance  of  a  strong  organi- 
zation under  the  efficient  leadership  of  a  thoroughly  equipped  secretary  in 
this  the  capital  of  the  British  government  in  India,  and  the  seat  of  so 
many  colleges,  needs  not  to  be  specially  impressed  upon  those  acquainted 
with  the  delicate  problems  that  confront  the  Associations  of  this  land. 


48 

It  is  sincerely  hoped  that  nothing  will  be  allowed  to  interfere  with  the 
steady  growth  of  this  young  Association  at  this  vital  point.  With  Cal- 
cutta, Bombay  and  Madras  provided  with  model  Associations  under 
trained  secretaries,  no  fears  need  be  entertained  with  regard  to  the  de- 
velopment of  this  branch  of  Christian  effort  in  India. 

WM.  I.  CHAMBERLAIN,  Cor.  Mem. 


JAPAN. 

In  this  empire  the  enterprises  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Associa- 
tion naturally  center  in  the  imperial  city.  We  may  therefore  consider 
them  most  intelligently  perhaps  by  treating  their  collective  works  in 
three  divisions,  viz. : 

1.  The  Tokyo  city  Association. — S.  Kimura  has  been  made  second  vice- 
president.  Mr.  Onuma  has  also  been  secured  as  assistant  secretary  and 
is  proving  an  efficient  helper.  The  new  buildings,  the  commencement  of 
which  had  been  prevented  in  1891  by  the  great  earthquake,  were  des- 
tined to  meet  with  a  further  delay  on  account  of  a  vast  conflagration 
which  swept  over  the  city  early  in  1892,  and  made  it  clear  that  certain 
changes  in  the  plans  were  necessary  in  order  to  render  the  structures  as 
far  as  possible  fire-proof.  The  contract,  however,  was  finally  signed  in 
July.  The  plans  provide  for  two  brick  buildings,  of  which  the  rear  one 
is  a  hall  60x60  feet,  and  is,  with  its  gallery,  capable  of  seating  one  thou- 
sand persons.  This  communicates  by  a  passageway  with  the  front  build- 
ing (also  60x60  feet),  the  basement  of  which  will  contain  one  long  room 
suitable  for  a  gymnasium,  and  other  rooms  needed  for  heating  and  caring 
for  the  building.  The  first  floor  will  be  divided  into  two  parlors,  a 
library  and  reading  room,  a  central  social  hall  and  office  room,  and  the 
general  secretary's  office.  The  second  floor  will  have  five  class-rooms, 
and  the  top  of  the  tower  will  contain  a  quiet  room  or  study.  It  is  ex- 
pected that  the  buildings  will  be  completed  in  April,  1894. 

The  work  done  in  1892  was  as  follows  :  The  rooms  were  opened  daily. 
The  attendance  averaged  1,053  per  month,  the  principal  attractions  being 
the  reading  room  and  night  school.  Occasional  social  meetings  and  in- 
formal lectures  have  also  been  held.  The  religious  work  has  been  quite 
successful.  Bible  classes  conducted  each  week  have  been  attended  by 
members  of  the  evening  classes.  Small  evangelistic  meetings  for  young 
men  have  been  held  every  Sunday  afternoon,  and  since  September  they 
have  been  under  the  charge  of  K.  Matsumura,  an  evangelist  whose  popu- 
larity amongst  young  men  has  often  more  than  crowded  the  whole  upper 
floor  of  our  little  house.  Under  Mr.  Matsumura  a  committee  of  personal 
workers  has  been  formed  for  increasing  the  definiteness  of  the  evangelistic 
work.  The  week  of  prayer  in  November  was  observed  by  the  Tokyo  city 
and  College  Associations,  and  to  some  extent  by  those  in  other  cities. 

The  members  of  the  Tokyo  Association  number  100,  of  whom  65  are 
.     These  figures  do  not  include  the  students  of  the  night  school ; 
and  the  present  rooms  are  so  small  that  few  other  privileges  can  be  offered, 
and  no  regular  canvass  for  members  has  yet  been  made. 

-y  interesting  work  has  been  begun  in  the  establishment  of  an  Asso- 
ciation boarding-house.  Tokyo  contains  a  vast  multitude  of  young  men 
from  the  provinces,  who  as  strangers  in  a  large  city  are  exposed  to  all  the 


49 

fierce  temptations  of  their  class.  In  the  boarding-house  the  Association 
provides  for  a  few  of  them  a  Christian  home.  The  building  now  rented 
for  the  purpose  has  rooms  for  15  men,  but  usually  20  have  crowded  into 
it.  It  is  under  the  charge  of  a  Christian  family,  and  evening  prayers  and 
Bible  study  are  held  for  an  half  hour  each  night.  Since  its  establishment 
32  different  young  men  have  lodged  in  it,  the  average  length  of  stay  being 
six  months.  Though  there  has  been  no  rule  on  the  point  it  has  happened 
that  none  of  the  boarders  have  been  residents  of  the  vicinity,  but  represent 
20  different  provinces,  all  of  them  distant  from  Tokyo.  A  number  of  these 
young  men  have  been  unbelievers,  but  all  have  gratefully  acknowledged 
the  spiritual  help  derived  from  a  daily  life  with  pure  surroundings.  It  is 
our  opinion  that  the  boarding-house,  if  continued,  will  prove  one  of  the 
most  fruitful  agencies  of  the  work. 

The  "railway  employees'  branch,"  reported  last  year,  was  abandoned  on 
account  of  certain  complications  which  made  it  appear  wise  to  postpone 
undertakings  in  that  direction.  In  its  place,  however,  the  "  soldiers' 
branch  "  was  organized  in  May,  and  is  having  'a  most  successful  career. 
"Under  the  care  of  sergeants  Ikeda  and  Higuchi  its  membership  has  grown 
to  46.  At  the  autumn  maneuvers  a  meeting  was  held  of  the  Christian 
soldiers,  gathered  from  all  parts  of  the  empire. 

Tokyo  has  maintained  through  its  secretaries  a  constant  correspondence 
with  the  other  Associations  throughout  the  empire.  In  order  to  develop 
this  department  of  the  work  the  publication  of  a  monthly  magazine  was 
begun  in  October.  It  is  used  as  the  official  organ  of  intercommunication 
by  all  the  Associations,  and  so  forms  an  important  bond  of  union  between 
them.  Most  of  our  Associations  are  engaged  in  efforts  for  the  abolition 
of  public  and  private  immorality.  The  Tokyo  Association  has  published 
translations  of  tracts  upon  personal  purity,  and  it  is  a  matter  of  con- 
gratulation that  the  demand  for  them  exceeds  the  expectation.  They  fur- 
nish the  first  direct  teaching  on  the  subject  that  has  ever  been  given  to 
our  young  men,  and  we  trust  that  the  publications  of  the  year  may  be 
followed  by  others  from  the  pens  of  our  physicians  and  teachers. 

II.  Other  Local  Associations. — Of  these  we  have  the  following  informa- 
tion :  Osaka,  organized  1870,  owns  a  large  brick  hall  and  a  reading  room. 
Has  held  once  a  month  during  the  year  a  prayer  meeting  and  a  lecture 
meeting.  The  members  number  122.  The  Kobe  city  Association,  organ- 
ized 1888,  has  36  active,  50  associate,  and  11  honorary  members ;  rents  a 
building,  has  a  library  of  130  volumes,  a  night  school  with  an  attendance 
of  about  45  ;  holds  weekly  prayer  and  evangelistic  meetings,  and  monthly 
social  meetings.  General  secretary  S.  Inouye  gives  all  his  time  to  the 
work.  The  Nagoya  Association,  organized  1889,  rents  a  building  centrally 
located,  has  a  library  of  150  volumes,  a  reading  room,  and  holds  weekly 
social  gatherings  and  meetings  for  Bible  study.  Its  members  number 
active,  34;  associate,  8;  honorary,  38.  During  the  year  it  received  the 
formal  thanks  of  the  police  department  of  the  city  for  having  stopped 
the  corruption  of  the  children  and  the  local  newspapers.  Besides  these 
there  are  the  Associations  in  Hiroshima,  Kumamoto,  Oita,  Shinoi,  Jomo, 
Miyagi,  Hakodate,  Chiba,  Koshiu  and  Shinshiu.  From  these  we  have  as 
yet  no  definite  statistics,  but  feel  that  they  are  all  of  such  character  as 
entitles  them  to  be  named  in  this  report. 


50 

HI.  The  College  Associations.— The  colleges  and  schools  in  which  there 
are  Associations  in  correspondence  with  one  another  are  as  follows :  The 
Sapporo  Agricultural  College,  50  members;  the  Imperial  University;  the 
Imperial  University  Agricultural  School;  the  First  Preparatory  College; 
the  Higher  Commercial  College;  the  Tokyo  High  School;  the  Semmom 
Gakko;  the  Aoyama  Ei-wa  Gakko  (M.  E.  Mission);  the  Azabu  Ei-wa 
Gakko  (Canadian  Methodist  Mission) ;  the  Kikkyo  Gakko  (P.  E.  Mission) ; 
all  of  Tokyo.  These  Associations  have  a  total  membership  of  349,  whilst 
the  total  number  of  students  enrolled  in  the  institutions  named  is  about 
4,700.  The  Second  Preparatory  College  at  Sendai,  has  47  members 
among  600  students ;  the  Third  Preparatory  College ;  the  Commercial 
School,  and  the  Medical  School,  at  Kyoto,  have  1,200  students  and  50 
members;  the  Osaka  Middle  School,  400  students,  12  members.  These 
Associations  without  exception  report  Bible  classes  and  other  religious 
meetings.  Their  letters  breathe  deep  devotion,  and  express  on  the  part 
of  most  of  them  a  lively  sense  of  their  responsibility  as  messengers  of  the 
gospel  to  their  fellow  students.  Their  organizations  and  their  rooms  are 
every  year  becoming  more  useful  as  a  means  of  bringing  the  city  pastors 
into  contact  with  unbelieving  students. 

The  chief  features  in  the  work  of  the  College  Associations  were  the 
summer  schools,  which  were  held  one  at  Hakone  Lake  in  July,  and  the 
other  at  a  mountain  resort  in  Kiushiu  in  August.  The  Hakone  school, 
under  the  presidency  of  Rev.  Y.  Honda,  president  of  the  Aoyama  Ei-wa 
Gakko,  was  arranged  by  a  committee  of  delegates  representing  the  various 
College  Associations  in  the  central  and  nothem  parts  of  the  country.  It 
was  attended  by  208  students  representing  twenty  schools  and  colleges. 
Its  sessions  lasted  twelve  days.  Among  many  speakers  was  the  Rev. 
Professor  Ladd,  of  Yale  University,  who  came  from  America  to  lecture 
at  the  school.  His  visit  was  productive  of  great  good.  As  a  whole  the 
school  was  characterized  by  the  presence  of  a  considerable  number  of 
unbelieving  students,  by  the  time  allotted  to  the  discussion  of  Association 
matters,  and  by  the  spiritual  hunger  with  which  all  came  and  which 
brought  the  blessing  promised  by  the  Savior.  The  school  in  Kiushiu,  the 
southern  island,  was  held  August  3-12,  under  the  presidency  of  K.  Kura- 
hara,  principal  of  the  Kumamoto  English  school.  It  was  attended  by 
120  students  representing  eight  provinces  and  six  schools  and  colleges. 

IV.  In  General- — Our  Associations  enjoy,  we  think,  the  confidence  and 
sympathy  of  the  churches  and  the  clergy;  their  work  makes  yearly  pro- 
gress and  every  one  hopes  for  their  success.  The  officers  of  the  different 
societies,  so  far  as  known  to  us,  are  men  of  repute  and  actively  engaged 
in  their  work.  We  feel  that  a  solid  foundation  has  been  laid.  For  this 
we  have  nothing  but  deep  thanksgiving  to  our  Lord,  in  whose  name  all 
has  been  done.  In  the  building  of  the  superstructure,  the  work  of  the 
future  which  is  of  so  great  importance  to  the  young  men  of  our  rising 
generation,  we  earnestly  hope  to  have  your  continued  sympathy  and 
prayers.  TAIZO  Mrrosm,  Cor.  Mem. 


BRITISH  COLUMBIA. 

(See  Oregon.} 


51 

MANITOBA. 

The  year's  work  has  been  one  of  prosperity  all  over  the  country,  and 
the  convention  just  closed  had  an  attendance  of  121  delegates.  Calgary 
and  Brandon  have  now  paid  secretaries. 

The  building  for  the  Winnipeg  Association  will  not  be  planned  at 
present,  as  we  wish  to  put  up  a  large  building,  but  not  to  commence  until 
the  whole  amount  has  been  subscribed.  The  Provincial  Committee 
closed  the  year  with  a  debt  of  $350,  but  expects  to  do  better  this  year. 

EOBEBT  D.  RICHARDSON,  Cor.  Mem. 

NEW  BEUNSWICK. 

We  are  pleased  to  note  many  encouraging  features  in  the  province.  In 
St.  John  the  boys'  branch  is  an  established  fact,  its  membership  con- 
stantly increasing  and  much  good  work  being  done.  As  a  whole  the  As- 
sociation is  in  a  healthy  condition  and  rapidly  outgrowing  its  present  ac- 
commodations, a  new  building  being  much  needed.  Moncton  is  in  a 
nourishing  condition  and  has  completed  its  elegant  and  commodious  new 
building,  one  of  the  finest  in  Canada.  St.  Stephen,  although  the  youngest 
Association  in  the  province,  has  an  increasing  membership  and  employs  a 
general  secretary.  The  smaller  Associations  still  have  an  existence,  but 
work  in  small  villages  is  not  encouraging. 

From  Fredericton  and  Mt.  Allison  reports  are  most  encouraging,  and 
these  College  Associations  have  proved  a  great  blessing  to  the  students. 

The  Provincial  Secretary,  E.  W.  Gorton,  has  been  actively  engaged 
throughout  the  provinces  in  promoting  the  extension  of  the  work,  and 
the  Association  at  St.  Stephen  is  the  direct  result  of  his  personal  efforts. 
His  work  has  been  fully  appreciated  and  has  been  a  wonderful  blessing 
to  very  many,  and  we  regret  his  withdrawal  from  the  field. 

The  Maritime  Convention,  held  in  Yarmouth,  N.  S. ,  in  August,  was 
largely  attended.  We  are  deeply  indebted  to  the  International  Com- 
mittee for  the  efficient  services  rendered  by  Secretary  S.  A.  Taggart. 

W.  S.  MORRISON,  Cor.  Mem. 

NOVA   SCOTIA. 

Good  progress  has  marked  the  past  year,  not  in  numbers,  but  in  im- 
proved facilities  and  better  work.  Spring  Hill  has  moved  into  new  rooms 
and  employs  a  general  secretary.  Yarmouth  has  taken  possession  of  its 
splendid  new  quarters,  and  added  a  physical  director  to  its  force.  Boys' 
branches  have  been  organized  at  Halifax  and  Yarmouth.  Windsor  has 
secured  a  fine  lot,  and  New  Glasgow  has  materially  increased  its  building 
fund.  Increased  attendance  and  interest  at  religious  meetings  is  reported, 
with  many  conversions — some  seventy  at  Yarmouth  alone. 

The  annual  convention  for  the  Maritime  Provinces  was  a  most  suc- 
cessful gathering.  A  conference  of  college  students  was  also  held  at 
Mt.  Allison  University,  Sackville,  N.  B.,  October  16,  at  which  all  but  one 
of  our  provincial  College  Associations  were  represented.  F.  A.  Keller, 
of  Yale  University,  sent  us  through  the  International  Committee,  did  much 
to  assure  the  success  of  the  meeting.  Pictou  county  held  a  convention  at 
River  John,  November  19,  which  was  well  attended,  and  all  the  sessions 
were  interesting  and  helpful. 

W.  B.  McNuTT,  Cor.  Mem. 


52 

ONTARIO. 

There  has  been  real  progress  in  connection  with  the  work  in  this 
province  during  the  past  year,  although  the  number  of  Associations  is 
no  larger.  Several  have  been  supplied  with  secretaries  where  none  were 
formerly  employed. 

Bible  and  training  class  work  has  received  special  attention,  and  at  a 
number  of  important  points  there  has  been  unusual  spiritual  activity,  and 
the  work  considerably  developed  on  right  lines. 

JOHN  J.  GARTSHORE,  Cor.  Mem. 

PRINCE  EDWARD  ISLAND. 

No  change  in  the  number  of  Associations  during  the  year.  The  Sum- 
merside  Association  continues  to  do  good  work  and  enjoys  the  confidence 
of  the  Christian  public.  The  Charlottetown  Association  has  been  much 
improved  during  the  year.  General  secretary  Mafit  resigned  in  October 
and  J.  S.  Raymond,  formerly  secretary  at  Yarmouth,  N.  S. ,  has  been  en- 
gaged. The  gymnasium  is  well  patronized,  additional  interest  is  taken  in 
educational  work,  and  best  of  all  the  religious  services  are  being  better 
attended  than  ever,  and  the  interest  in  the  work  deepens. 

J.  D.  SEAMAN,  Cor.  Mem. 

QUEBEC. 

The  Associations  in  Sherbrooke  and  Quebec  have  each  received  the 
impetus  incident  to  the  engagement  of  new  secretaries,  R.  J.  Farrell 
in  the  former  and  H.  H.  Distin  in  the  latter  field,  and  good  work  is  being 
done  by  each. 

The  Quebec  building  was  partially  destroyed  by  fire  last  fall,  but  being 
fully  covered  by  insurance  the  Association  was  enabled  to  make  some  very 
desirable  alterations. 

The  all-round  work  of  the  Montreal  Association  has  been  its  chief 
characteristic.  A  movement  to  improve  the  Association  library  has  re- 
ceived responses  to  the  extent  of  nearly  two  thousand  dollars. 

The  Association  enjoyed  the  privilege  of  entertaining  a  successful  and 
blessed  interprovincial  convention  in  January  last,  when  Secretary  J.  R. 
Mott,  of  the  International  Committee,  rendered  invaluable  service. 

CHARLES  GUSHING,  Cor.  Mem. 

MEXICO. 

All  plans  for  improvements  in  the  rooms  of  the  Association  in  the 

city  of  Mexico,  as  outlined  at  the  beginning  of    the  year,  were  duly 

executed  under  the  efficient  supervision  of  general  secretary  George  N.

HENRY  P.  WEBB,  Cor.  Mem. 


53 

ALABAMA. 

The  headquarters  of  the  State  Committee  have  been  removed  from 
Selma  to  Birmingham.  Following  the  instructions  of  the  last  convention 
the  state  has  been  divided  into  five  districts,  in  two  of  which,  Uniontown 
and  Huntsville,  conferences  have  been  held.  These  proved  valuable  in 
educating  the  young  men  and  enthusing  the  people  generally,  besides 
rendering  financial  assistance  to  the  State  Committee.  The  results  were 
so  satisfactory  that  conferences  will  probably  be  held  in  most  if  not  all  the 
districts  another  year.  There  are  twenty  Associations  in  the  state — five 
college  and  sixteen  city  and  town— besides  six  young  men's  prayer  meet- 
ings which  it  is  hoped  may  develop  into  Associations.  Two  secretarial 
points  have  been  added,  namely,  Huntsville  and  the  Decaturs,  mainly 
by  the  personal  supervision  the  State  Secretary  was  able  to  give  by  making 
these  places  in  turn  his  temporary  residence.  We  feel  hopeful  over  the 
marked  improvement  in  almost  every  department,  and  believe  it  to  be 
largely  owing  to  the  fact  of  our  having  a  State  Secretary  in  the  field 
during  the  entire  year.  We  have  been  encouraged  by  the  valuable  aid 
given  us  by  representatives  of  the  International  Committee,  especially 
Mr.  Andersen.  We  wish  to  express  our  continued  allegiance  to  the  Com- 
mittee and  hope  to  increase  our  contributions  to  the  support  of  its  work 
the  coming  year.  HARKY  HAWKINS,  Cor.  Mem. 

ARKANSAS. 

Arkansas  has  passed  through  one  of  the  severest  financial  strains  in 
its  history!  It  has  been  next  to  impossible  to  hold  some  of  the  organiza- 
tions together,  yet  the  year  closed  with  the  same  number  of  Associations 
in  the  state  as  last  reported.  One  College  Association  disbanded  and  one 
new  one  was  organized,  at  Batesville  college. 

The  state  was  represented  by  ten  delegates  at  the  Southern  Student 
Summer  School,  at  Knoxville,  Tenn. ;  two  College  Associations  sent  eight 
delegates,  and  two  city  Associations  one  each. 

A  State  Secretary  has  been  employed  for  the  entire  year.  Six  secre- 
taries are  employed  by  four  city  Associations. 

H.  P.  EDMONSON,  Cor.  Meni. 

CALIFORNIA. 

All  things  considered,  the  work  has  made  good  progress  during  the  year. 
The  twelfth  annual  convention,  at  Pasadena,  in  October,  was  the  largest 
yet  held,  and  very  helpful  to  our  work  throughout  the  state.  There  were 
present  201  delegates  and  38  corresponding  members. 

A  most  encouraging  feature  of  our  work  at  present  is  the  college  de- 
partment, and  we  have  had  valuable  aid  from  Secretaries  Mott  and  Boots. 
A  fine  College  Association  building,  erected  in  connection  with  the  state 
university  at  Berkeley,  and  costing,  with  the  ground,  some  $32,000,  was 
the  sole  gift  of  Mrs.  A.  J.  Stiles.  It  is  a  handsome  and  well  adapted 
structure,  and  already  its  influence  is  being  realized  in  the  moulding  of 
religious  sentiment  in  this  great  university. 

Wm.  H.  Mead,  for  three  years  State  Secretary,  resigned  November  1, 
and  we  have  not  been  able  thus  far  to  secure  his  successor.  Harry  Hillard 
was  retained  as  college  secretary,  giving  a  part  of  his  'time  to  the  local 


54 

work  at  Berkeley.  We  are  in  hopes  that  a  building  movement  will  soon 
be  inaugurated  at  Stanford  University,  and  are  looking  forward  to  a  most 
prosperous  year  in  our  college  work.  The  local  Associations  for  the  most 
part  are  in  good  shape,  and  a  commendable  work  is  being  accomplished 
at  nearly  all  the  important  points  ;  and  when  the  right  man  can  be  se- 
cured for  State  Secretary  we  shall  hope  to  see  an  increased  efficiency. 

H.  J.  McCoy,   Cor.  Mem. 

COLOEADO. 

The  year  1892  witnessed  great  advance  in  nearly  every  field.  Three 
new  organizations  were  effected — Trinidad,  Canon  City  and  the  State 
Agricultural  College  at  Fort  Collins.  There  are  at  present  twelve  Asso- 
ciations in  the  state,  and  sufficient  money  has  been  raised  for  a  successful 
organization  at  Durango.  Fifteen  men  are  employed  as  secretaries  or 
assistants. 

The  work  at  Denver  has  been  materially  strengthened  by  the  securing 
of  some  of  the  most  substantial  business  men  of  the  city  for  the  directorate. 
New  rooms,  equipped  at  an  expense  of  nearly  $7,000,  were  entered  in 
August,  and  since  that  time  the  advance  along  all  lines  has  been  marked. 
In  October  five  and  a  half  lots  on  an  ideal  corner  were  purchased,  at  an 
expense  of  $27,000,  and  the  time  for  the  erection  of  a  building  seems  not 
far  distant.  Leadville,  Aspen  and  Pueblo,  are  also  in  new  rooms  and 
are  doing  effective  work. 

A  special  need  is  a  man  to  devote  his  time  to  laboring  among  the  miners 
in  the  smaller  mountain  towns.  Many  of  these  settlements  of  a  thousand 
men  or  more  are  without  effective  Christian  effort.  The  condition  of  some 
of  these  towns  is  lamentable.  Black  Hawk,  with  a  population  of  1,100, 
reports  no  active  Christian  young  men;  Breckenridge,  with  a  population 
of  1,350,  reports  but  seven  communicants  among  the  young  men.  These 
are  but  samples.  It  is  a  gratifying  fact  that  in  every  town  having  an 
Association  the  true  principles  of  the  work  are  carried  out. 

W.  L.  GRAHAM,  Cor.  Mem. 

CONNECTICUT. 

We  have  24  Associations,  employing  44  salaried  officers,  and  with  a 
membership  of  8,010.  Eighteen  Associations  have  gymnasiums,, patronized 
by  2,183,  or  more  than  25$  of  our  entire  membership;  13  physical  directors 
are  employed. 

Ten  Associations  own  completed  buildings  valued  at  $411,000.  Seven 
others  own  real  estate  valued  at  $74,700,  six  of  which  have  building  funds 
and  subscriptions  amounting  to  nearly  $210,000.  Two  buildings  are  in 
process  of  erection;  one  in  Hartford,  a  splendid  structure,  to  cost,  together 
with  lot,  $183,000,  and  one  in  Waterbury,  to  cost  $65,000,  while  three 
other  Associations  have  purchased  lots  and  are  soon  to  build. 

We  have  four  College  Associations  that  are  doing  grand  work.  Wesleyan 
Association,  with  the  hearty  commendation  of  the  faculty,  is  securing 
funds  for  the  erection  of  a  $30,000  building  on  grounds  owned  by  the 
university. 

Great  attention  is  being  paid  to  the  educational  department  of  our 
Association  work.  Eighty -four  classes  have  an  enrollment  of  1,137  who,

Tinder  efficient  instructors,  are  taught  mechanical,  architectural  and 
free-hand  drawing,  modeling,  wood  carving,  chemistry,  bookkeeping, 
penmanship,  stenography,  typewriting,  commercial  forms,  English  litera- 
ture, history,  physiology  and  German.  An  interesting  feature  at  our 
State  Convention  was  an  exhibit  from  eleven  different  Associations  of  com- 
mendable specimens  of  their  work.  Hartford  Association  has  received 
the  generous  gift  of  $50,000  from  Appleton  E.  and  Miss  Clara  E. 
Hillyer  for  the  endowment  of  the  educational  department  and  the  begin- 
ning of  manual  training  work. 

Norwich  Association  is  the  recipient  of  $20,000  from  the  estate  of  W.  W. 
Backus,  the  income  of  which  is  to  be  used  for  current  expenses,  and  one 
thousand  dollars  from  the  estate  of  Mrs.  Julia  F.  Walker  for  the  building 
fund,  while  New  Britain  Association  receives  one  thousand  dollars  from 
the  estate  of  Mrs.  Helen  S.  North  to  apply  on  the  debt  of  the  building. 
Very  few  secretarial  changes  have  occurred,  which  has  given  greater 
stability  and  consequent  better  results  to  our  work. 

The  religious  work  has  been  emphasized  and,  as  a  result,  our  Bible 
classes,  workers'  training  classes,  and  young  men's  meetings  have  been 
more  than  doubled,  and  380  young  men  have  professed  conversion.  The 
State  Committee  conducted  an  Association  at  the  annual  encampment  of 
our  state  militia  in  August,  unique  in  its  provisions  to  meet  the  wants  of 
the  soldiers,  and  eminently  successful  in  exerting  a  healthful  influence. 
There  was  an  estimated  daily  attendance  of  1,600,  and  the  work  received 
the  hearty  commendation  of  Brigadier  General  Haven,  commanding. 
District  work,  covering  the  entire  state,  is  already  inaugurated  with 
promise  of  entire  success  and  will  be  a  feature  in  our  progressive  work 
during  the  present  year. 

On  the  whole  the  Association  work  of  our  state  has  never  been  in  a 
more  healthy  and  hopeful  condition  than  at  the  present  time.  This  is 
owing,  in  no  small  degree,  to  the  fidelity,  zeal  and  wise  management  of 
State  Secretary  J.  W.  Cook,  who  came  to  us  May  ,15.  He  has  the  con- 
fidence and  support  of  the  entire  committee  and  of  the  Associations 
throughout  the  state. 

k-  Our  recent  State  Convention,  held  at  New  Britain,  was  well  attended, 
full  of  enthusiasm  and  signally  practical  and  helpful.  J.  B.  Mott, 
College  Secretary  of  the  International  Committee,  rendered  most  efficient 
and  valuable  service  at  the  convention. 

W.  E.  BURNHAM,  Cor.  Mem. 

DELAWAEE. 

(See  Maryland. } 


DISTEICT  OF  COLUMBIA. 

(See  Maryland. ) 

FLOEIDA. 

No  improvement  has  taken  place  the  past  year  in  this  state.  The  Or- 
lando Association  suspended  work  last  September,  leaving  but  one  Asso- 
ciation in  the  State,  at  Pensacola.  I  trust  that  there  may  some  time  be 
a  revival  of  this  work  among  the  young  men  in  Florida. 

F.  A.  CURTIS,  Cor.  Mem, 


56 

GEOKGIA. 

Decided  progress  has  been  made  in  the  character  of  the  work  in  Georgia, 
During  the  greater  part  of  the  year  H.  P.  Andersen,  of  the  International 
Committee,  has  been  acting  State  Secretary,  and  a  regularity  and  effi- 
ciency of  organization  has  been  attained  far  in  advance  of  anything  we 
have  heretofore  had.  Better  work  has  been  done  for  young  men,  and  the 
Association  has  a  stronger  hold  upon  the  confidence  of  the  people  than 
ever  before.  We  have  now  twenty  Associations,  with  a  total  membership 
of  2,991 — 12  city  and  town,  1  railroad,  and  7  college.  The  College  As- 
sociations have  an  aggregate  membership  of  291 ;  and  the  railroad  branch 
at  Atlanta  has  a  membership  of  262. 

W.  M.  Lewis,  of  Waco,  Texas,  has  been  appointed  State  Secretary  of 
Georgia,  and  began  work  March  1.  From  the  excellent  reputation  he 
brings  with  him,  the  friends  here  believe  that  he  will  be  able  to  build 
well  upon  the  foundations  laid  by  Mr.  Andersen  during  the  past  year. 

The  relations  between  the  State  Committee  and  the  local  Associations 
are  most  cordial ;  and  both  are  very  grateful  for  the  valuable  counsel  and 
assistance  they  receive  from  the  International  Committee 

HENKY  HZLLYEK,   Cor.  Mem. 

IDAHO. 

(See  Oregon.) 

ILLINOIS. 

The  year  has  been  one  of  great  strengthening  of  the  work  along  all  lines. 
The  growth  has  been  normal,  and  for  this  reason  we  count  confidently 
on  retaining  the  ground  now  occupied. 

The  number  led  through  Association  agencies  to  an  acceptance  of  Christ 
has  exceeded  by  over  200  that  in  any  previous  year.  There  has  been  a 
gratifying  improvement  in  Bible  study,  particularly  in  College  Associa- 
tions. The  effect  of  the  Lake  Geneva  Summer  School  has  been  marked. 
The  college  delegation  from  this  state  was  larger  than  ever  before  and 
promises  to  be  almost  doubled  this  year.  There  are  now  thirty-one  Col- 
lege Associations  in  the  state,  including  a  strong  Association  organized 
during  the  past  year  in  the  University  of  Chicago.  The  students  there, 
having  decided  upon  the  organization,  invited  the  counsel  and  assistance 
of  International  Secretary  Mott  and  assistant  state  secretary  Burt. 

The  twentieth  annual  State  Convention  was  held  at  Bloomington 
with  a  total  attendance  of  439.  International  Secretaries  Wishard,  Mott 
and  Hicks  gave  valuable  assistance.  The  district  conferences,  particu- 
larly those  in  the  nothern  part  of  the  state,  have  been  specially  large  and 
helpful.  They  are  most  valuable  additions  to  the  State  Conventions  as 
they  afford  opportunity  for  work  and  discussion  with  greater  reference 
to  local  questions  and  necessities. 

We  still  rejoice  in  the  splendid  body  of  men  serving  as  secretaries  and 
other  Association  officers  throughout  the  state.  The  changes  have  been 
few  and  almost  no  vacancies  of  disastrous  length  have  occurred.  The 
state  force  remains  unchanged  under  the  leadership  of  I.  E.  Brown.  The 
average  term  of  service  of  its  seven  men  is  now  over  five  years.  The  sys- 
tem of  corresponding  membership  has  been  greatly  increased  and 
there  are  now  about  350  in  the  state. 


ASSOCIATION   BUILDING,    EVANSV1LLE,    INI). 

DEDICATED  SEPTEMBER  23,  1891. 
Dimensions.  75x100  feet.  Cost,  $67,900.  Population,  50,600. 


57 

The  financial  condition  of  the  state  executive  committee  seems  to  be 
"better  than  ever  before.  Good  pledges  have  been  made  which  cover 
all  expenses  to  date  together  with  the  debt  which  had  rested  upon  the 
committee  for  several  years.  A  successful  effort  has  been  made  to  ex- 
tend the  number  of  subscribers.  This  wider  distribution  of  the  finan- 
cial constituency  tends  to  interest  a  larger  number  and  to  lessen  the  calls 
upon  our  ever  generous  and  faithful  friends. 

There  is  a  steady  and  satisfactory  advance  in  building  moyments  and 
the  necessary  funds.  The  Chicago  Association  has  been  unhappily  de- 
layed in  the  construction  of  its  magnificent  new  building  by  reason  of  the 
complicated  nature  of  the  steel  frame  work;  but  the  work  is  now  pro- 
gressing rapidly,  and  it  is  hoped  to  entertain  Association  visitors  during 
the  World's  Fair  year  in  a  portion  of  the  building,  although  it  will  still 
be  under  construction.  Elgin  has  received  gifts  of  fine  lots  for  a  build- 
ing and  other  property  to  the  amount  of  $25,000.  Pana's  fund  seems  to 
warrant  the  expectation  of  entering  a  new  building  this  fall.  The  West 
Side  department  in  Chicago  is  now  engaged  in  a"  canvass  and  is  encour- 
aged by  a  conditional  gift  of  about  $16,000.  A  building  for  the  Associa- 
tion at  the  University  of  Illinois  is  practically  assured. 

In  Chicago  the  intercollegiate  department  is  established  in  five  of  the 
medical  colleges  in  the  city.  The  other  departments  have  had  a  well  sus- 
tained work  The  Madison  Street  department  is  laboring  under  difficulties 
arising  from  its  limited  quarters  by  reason  of  the  destruction  of  a  part 
of  the  old  building  to  make  room  for  the  new  one. 

AKTHUB  D.  WHEELEK,  Cor.  Mem. 


INDIANA. 

During  the  year  we  have  gained  one  city,  one  railroad  and  two  college 
Associations;  also  1,030  members;  336  active  members,  and  198  more  men 
serving  on  committees.  Current  expenses  are  now  nearly  $40,000  an- 
nually, and  valuation  of  buildings  and  other  real  estate  is  $328,900,  with 
two  new  building  projects  in  hand.  The  fine  new  building  at  New 
Albany  will  be  occupied  in  March. 

There  is  an  increase  in  the  number  of  Bible  classes,  and  the  total 
average  attendance  at  young  men's  gospel  meetings  has  increased  from 
699  to  992.  The  professed  conversions  among  young  men  only  number 
255,  and,  including  general  evangelistic  efforts  in  connection  with  some 
of  the  Associations  and  prayer  bands,  the  number  is  increased  to  nearly 
1,000. 

The  progress  in  the  college  department  is  quite  gratifying.  Over  one- 
half  of  the  5,000  young  men  in  our  higher  educational  institutions  are  re- 
ported as  Christians,  and  1,100  of  them  are  Association  members,  while 
the  year  previous  there  were  but  860. 

The  year  was  also  the  best  financially  since  the  beginning  of  the  work 
in  Indiana.  More  money  has  been  raised  and  expended  for  the  general 
work  than  ever  before,  an  indication  that  the  cause  is  more  fully  appre- 
ciated . 

From  the  International  Committee  we  have  received  occasional  valua- 
ble co-operation.  By  arrangement  of  our  State  Committee,  Secretary 
Hague  aided  the  Richmond  Association  in  connection  with  its  build- 


58 

ing  project.  Bailroad  Secretary  Hicks  has  worked  in  conjunction  with 
our  State  Secretary  in  railroad  fields;  his  assistant,  Mr.  Moorman,  render- 
ing continued  service  at  Indianapolis  and  Frankfort.  College  Secretary 
Boots  visited  two  College  Associations  and  with  good  results.  Secretaries 
Wishard,  Hicks  and  Moorman  also  rendered  valuable  assistance  at  our 

last  convention. 

WALTER  C.  NUNEMACHER,  Cor.  Mem* 

IOWA. 

The  past  year  has  been  a  very  successful  one  in  work  for  the  young  men 
of  Iowa.  There  are  52  Associations  in  the  state — 22  college,  1  railroad,  and 
28  city  and  town.  Thirty -nine  men  are  giving  their  whole  time  to  the 
work  as  general  secretaries,  assistants  and  physical  directors,  and  three 
are  employed  on  the  state  force. 

Our  finances  are  in  a  good  condition.  The  committee  expended 
$4,944  and  closed  the  year  with  all  bills  paid.  The  district  work  has 
made  an  advance.  Conventions  were  held  in  all  but  one  of  the  seven  dis- 
tricts, and  have  never  had  their  equal  in  attendance,  interest,  or  spiritual 
power. 

A  decided  advance  has  been  made  in  the  college  work.  More  men  were 
present  at  the  summer  school  at  Lake  Geneva  than  ever  before.  A 
marked  increase  in  Bible  study  and  spiritual  work  has  been  the  result. 
Three  of  the  College  Associations  have  added  bath-rooms  to  their  equip- 
ment. The  railroad  deputation  has  held  meetings  for  railroad  men  at  12, 
division  points.  Over  200  have  professed  conversion  at  these  meetings. 

Additional  subscriptions  aggregating  $25,000  have  been  secured  toward 
the  debt  on  the  Des  Moines  building.  Through  the  generosity  of  Mr.  and 
Mrs.  C.  B.  Soutter,  the  Cedar  Bapids  Association  has  received  the  finest 
equipment  of  baths  in  the  country,  costing  $12,000.  The  new  Associa- 
tion at  Dubuque  has  received  a  bequest  of  an  interest  in  a  brick  block, 
worth  $10,000,  expected  to  be  available  in  a  few  years.  We  are  glad  to 
record  that  men  who  have  given  largely  toward  the  buildings  are  more 
than  satisfied  with  their  investments.  One  of  them  testified  to  a  com- 
pany of  business  men  recently,  that  after  watching  the  work  carried  on 
for  less  than  two  years,  in  a  building  he  had  given  the  Association,  he 
would  not  undo  what  he  had  done  for  a  title  to  the  state  of  Iowa.  It  is 
gratifying  that  the  eight  buildings  and  better  equipments  which  have 
been  secured  during  the  past  few  years,  have  greatly  increased  the 
efficiency  of  the  Associations.  No  one  year  has  seen  so  many  young  men 
benefited  physically,  socially,  and  mentally,  nor  has  any  one  been  so 
rich  in  spiritual  results.  The  counsel  and  assistance  of  the  International 
Committee  has  been  greatly  appreciated. 

M.  H.  SMITH,  Cor.  Mem. 

KANSAS. 

If  we  count  figures  only,  this  report  from  Kansas  will  not  appear  as 
flattering  as  in  former  years.  Many  of  the  Associations  in  the  smaller 
towns  have  disbanded,  leaving  us  a  less  number  to  report.  However,  we 
are  confident  that  the  Association  pulse  was  never  in  a  more  healthy  con- 
dition than  at  the  present  time,  and  the  Associations  in  the  cities  have 
taken  on  a  new  impetus  and  healthy  growth,  laying  deep  and  well  the 


59 

foundations  for  a  true,  aggressive  Young  Men's  Christian  Association 
work.  Our  Associations  have  been  wonderfully  blessed  of  God,  and  are 
much  encouraged;  a  brighter  day  is  dawning. 

We  have  to  report  now  in  active  operation  24  city  and  18  College  Asso- 
ciations. There  are  14  general  secretaries,  3  physical  directors,  and  9  other 
paid  employees,  aside  from  the  three  men  who  serve  as  secretaries  of  the 
State  Committee.  Our  State  Convention  was  held  at  Lawrence,  in  October, 
having  an  attendance  of  385,  and  was  a  great  spiritual  feast.  The  annual 
Bible  school  was  held  in  connection  with  the  Winfield  Chautauqua,  and  was 
a  source  of  instruction  enjoyed  by  a  large  number;  Kev.  Geo.  C.  Needham 
was  in  charge.  Two  district  conferences  and  one  county  convention 
were  held.  The  State  Committee  reported  an  expenditure  of  $3,162  and 
all  debts  paid. 

FEED.  W.  PAKKOTT,  Cor.  Mem*. 

KENTUCKY. 

The  past  year  has  been  marked  by  the  development  and  strengthening 
of  the  work  ;  the  improvement  of  facilities  and  methods  rather  than  by 
numerical  growth.  The  total  number  of  Associations  in  the  state  is  22;  ten 
local,  nine  in  educational  institutions,  two  doing  work  for  railroad  men, 
and  one  among  colored  men.  The  secretarial  force  of  the  state  numbers 
twelve. 

There  has  been  a  marked  growth  of  efficiency  in  the  work  of  the  Col- 
lege Associations.  The  two  railroad  departments  have  had  general  en- 
couragement and  prosperity.  The  district  work  has  been  inaugurated 
during  the  year  with  most  satisfactory  results. 

The  twelfth  annual  State  Convention  met  at  Winchester,  Feb.  23-26, 
and  was  in  all  respects  the  best  ever  held  in  Kentucky.  There  were  238 
delegates  in  attendance.  The  outlook  for  1893  is  full  of  promise.  After 
three  years  of  careful  consolidation,  the  State  Committee  is  in  a  better 
position  than  ever  before  to  develop  the  work  in  the  unorganized  cities  of 
the  state.  JOHN  G.  CECIL,  Cor.  Mem. 

LOUISIANA. 

I  regret  to  report  that  there  has  been  but  little  progress  during  the  past 
year.  No  state  work  has  been  carried  on,  but  helpful  visits  by  Messrs. 
Ober,  Cree  and  Brockman,  of  the  International  Committee,  have  been  ap- 
preciated. The  New  Orleans  Association  is  doing  good  work  and  is  con- 
tinuing its  efforts  to  secure  a  building.  The  Baton  Eouge  Association  is 
in  good  financial  condition  and  a  new  organization  has  recently  been 
effected  at  the  A.  and  M.  College  in  the  same  city.  At  a  few  other  points 
the  work  has  been  continued  with  varying  interest  and  success. 

CHAKLES  H.  SHUTE,  Cor.  Mem. 


MAINE. 

We  have  made  a  slight  progress  during  the  year,  an  Association  having 
been  formed  at  Thomaston. 

Our  work  suffers  from  the  constant  secretarial  changes.  Of  eight  Asso- 
ciations employing  secretaries,  five  have  changed  during  the  year.  Some 
Associations  are  doing  a  good  work,  while  others  are  barely  kept  alive. 


60 

Our  State  Secretary  E.  H.  Shelton,  has  labored  efficiently  during  the 
year,  and  his  work  must  tell  in  the  near  future. 

The  Portland  and  Bath  Associations  expect  soon  to  commence  building 
operations. 

The  College  Associations  are  doing  excellent  work.  The  State  Conven- 
tion was  held  at  Augusta,  in  October,  and  was  well  attended. 

W.  S.  COREY,   Cor.  Mem. 

MAEYLAND,  DELAWAEE,  DISTEICT  OF  COLUMBIA,  AND 
WEST  VIEGINIA. 

The  twenty-first  annual  State  Convention  was  held  at  Wilmington,  Del., 
Jan.  19-21,  1893.  A  conference  of  the  secretaries  and  physical  directors 
preceded  the  convention.  Eighteen  of  the  thirty-six  Associations  in  our 
territory  sent  133  delegates  and  corresponding  members.  The  Interna- 
tional Committee  was  represented  by  H.  Thane  Miller,  Cephas  Brainerd, 
L.  D.  Wishard,  C.  J.  Hicks,  and  G.  L.  Leonard,  who  did  us  excellent  ser- 
vice. J.  C.  Sims,  who  has  served  us  as  State  Secretary  since  November, 
1891,  resigned  at  the  convention  and  his  place  has  not  yet  been  filled. 

New  Associations  have  been  organized  at  Sparrows  Point  and  New 
Cumberland  in  Maryland,  and  Westernport,  W.  Va.  The  number  of 
general  secretaries  and  physical  directors  is  27. 

The  Cumberland  Association  building  project  has  materialized;  a  lot 
on  the  best  street  of  the  city  has  been  secured,  $15,000  of  the  amount 
needed  pledged  and  paid  in,  and  the  building  will  probably  be  erected 
this  year.  A  building  for  the  Association  at  Sparrows  Point  has  also  been 
erected  during  the  year  and  will  be  ready  for  occupancy  in  the  autumn. 
The  Baltimore  Association,  through  the  co-operation  of  the  trustees  of  an 
estate,  has  secured  a  new  and  fully-equipped  building  for  its  West  branch, 
to  cost  not  less  than  $32,000.  It  will  be  ready  for  use  before  January 
next. 

The  week  of  prayer  was  observed  by  nearly  all  the  Associations  in  our 
district.  Special  services  every  night  for  young  men  were  held  at  Wash- 
ington, Baltimore,  Wheeling,  and  Wilmington.  The  reports  show  that 
over  500  young  men  have  indicated  their  purpose  to  lead  Christian  lives 
through  the  direct  influence  of  the  Associations. 

The  college,  railroad  and  German  work  have  been  carried  on  vigorously, 
and  a  system  of  deputation  work  conducted  by  the  college  students  has 
had  the  effect  of  stimulating  the  work  in  the  educational  institutions. 
We  are  indebted  to  the  International  Committee  for  valuable  service 
rendered  by  their  secretaries. 

W.  H.  H.  SMITH,  Cor.  Mem. 

MASSACHUSETTS  AND  EHODE  ISLAND. 

The  year  just  closing  has  been  the  most  successful  one,  spiritually  and 
financially,  and  in  general  progress,  that  these  states  have  ever  had.  This 
is  due  very  largely  to  the  indefatigable  labor  of  our  State  Secretary,  E. 
M.  Armstrong,  supported  by  a  State  Committee  intensely  interested  in  all 
that  pertains  to  the  work. 

We  have  at  present  eighty  Associations,  with  a  total  membership  of 
25,309.  The  new  Associations  are  Beverly,  Whitman,  Millbury,  Gardner, 


ASSOCIATION    BUILDING,   NEW   BEDFORD,   MASS. 

DEDICATED  DECEMBER  12,  1891. 
1  Miiu-iisions,  70x80  feet.  Cost,  $62,000.  Population,  44,000. 


61 

and  Flint  Village  branch  of  Fall  Eiver.     The  Associations  at  the  first 
three  places  employ  general  secretaries. 

The  buildings  at  Holyoke  and  Southbridge  are  nearing  completion. 
The  former  will  cost  $125,000,  and  the  latter,  $105,000.  A  building  fund 
of  $134,000  has  been  secured  for  the  Springfield  Association. 

The  district  conferences  and  "Association  days  "  have  been  most  help- 
ful and  resulted  in  a  large  number  of  professed  conversions  and  requests 
for  prayer.  During  the  year  941  men  professed  to  find  Christ  through  the 
efforts  of  the  Association. 

One  of  the  most  pleasing  and  profitable  gatherings  of  the  year  was  an 
all  day  conference  of  general  secretaries,  physical  directors,  and  mem- 
bers of  the  State  Committee.  The  gathering  was  held  at  the  building  of 
the  Cambridge  Association. 

The  State  Convention  was  held  at  Pittsfield,  October  20-23,  at  which 
there  were  315  delegates.  The  pentathlon  contest  and  state  athletic  meet 
was  held  at  Pittsfield  in  connection  with  the  convention. 

Special  attention  has  been  given  to  junior 'department  work.  The 
third  annual  conference  was  held  at  Worcester,  at  which  there  were  292 
delegates.  The  conference  was  held  over  the  Sabbath,  and  there  were  47 
professed  conversions.  Boys'  summer  camps  were  held  in  various  parts 
of  the  two  states  with  good  results. 

There  are  now  fifty  women's  auxiliaries,  with  a  total  membership  of 
over  7,000.  Several  new  auxiliaries  have  been  organized.  The  annual 
women's  auxiliary  conference  was  held  at  Chelsea,  at  which  there  were 
350  delegates. 

The  state  organization  is  favored  by  being  allowed  from  three  to  four 
columns  space  in  the  Boston  Daily  Traveller  once  each  month  for  the 
publication  of  Association  news. 

While  no  systematic  canvass  has  yet  been  made  for  funds  for  the  new 
State  Committee  building,  twenty-eight  subscriptions  of  $1,000  each  have 
been  secured,  and  among  these  was  one  from  the  women's  auxiliary  of 
the  Cambridge  Association.  The  total  amount  pledged  is  in  the  vicinity 
of  $30,000,  and  every  indication  points  to  a  successful  carrying  out  of  the 
enterprise. 

O.  H.  DUKKELL,  Cor.  Mem. 


MICHIGAN. 

The  year  has  witnessed  the  organization  of  new  Associations  at  Ad- 
rian and  at  Hancock,  also  the  East  Side  branch  at  Detroit.  Movements 
are  in  progress  that  will  undoubtedly  result  in  Associations  at  Ann 
Arbor,  Calumet  and  Grand  Haven.  Two  new  buildings  have  been 
dedicated,  at  Grand  Eapids,  costing  $80,000,  and  at  Kalamazoo,  costing 
$50,000,  each  figure  including  lot.  Hancock  purchased  and  remodeled  a 
building,  and  the  East  Side  branch  at  Detroit  occupies  its  own  building, 
which  was  owned  by  the  city  Association  and  formerly  used  as  an  athletic 
club  house.  The  railroad  branch  at  Detroit  has  increased  its  building  fund. 
The  East  Side  department  at  Saginaw  has  started  a  canvass  for  a  building 
to  cost  $60,000.  Owosso  Association  has  secured  a  small  amount  toward 
the  purchase  of  a  lot. 

Increase  of  power  and  efficiency  along  spiritual  lines  is  noted  with 


62 

gratitude,  and  nearly  four  hundred  professed  conversions  have  been 
reported  during  the  year.  College  Associations  report  larger  enrollment 
in  Bible  classes  and  in  general  more  efficient  work.  Our  intercollegiate 
deputation  has  visited  nearly  all  the  College  Associations  with  excellent 
results.  The  Association  tent  at  the  annual  military  encampment  was  a 
center  of  attraction  and  had  an  influence  for  good.  Sixty  corresponding 
members  represent  the  Association  in  unorganized  fields.  Our  State 
Convention  was  held  at  Lansing  with  408  in  attendance,  being  160  more 
than  last  year  and  the  largest  ever  held  in  the  state.  It  was  a  meeting  of 
great  practical  efficiency,  spiritual  power  and  far  reaching  influence. 
The  International  Committee  was  ably  represented  by  Logan  Herbert 
Boots.  Five  district  conferences  have  been  held  during  the  year  and 
another  series  is  now  in  progress. 

J.  E.  DUTTON,  Cor.  Mem. 

MINNESOTA. 

The  annual  reports  of  the  work  are  full  of  good  results.  Bible  training 
classes  number  40  with  300  members,  19  classes  being  at  points  without 
secretaries.  Membership  at  points  occupying  new  buildings  shows  an 
unusual  increase.  Winona  has  a  building  fund  of  $11,200  which  has 
been  recently  secured. 

The  State  Convention,  held  at  Winona,  February  16-19,  was  one  of 
great  value,  attended  by  151  persons,  32  of  them  students.  L.  D.  Wishard, 
for  the  International  Committee,  rendered  valuable  aid  in  the  conven- 
tion. 

New  College  Associations  have  been  formed  at  Wasioja  Seminary  and 
Windom  Institute,  and  a  county  Association  in  Olmsted  county,  making 
a  total  of  29  Associations  in  the  state. 

Woodsmen's  work  has  been  of  unusual  value.  Two  secretaries,  John 
T.  McKay  and  Henry  Chester,  have  sung  and  preached  the  gospel  to 
thousands  of  woodsmen,  sold  hundreds  of  Testaments,  and  report  eleven 
conversions  in  a  single  month.  This  work  is  sustained  wholly  by  the 
lumbering  companies. 

The  college  work  gives  the  greatest  reason  for  thanksgiving.  Seventy 
students  were  engaged  in  the  student  vacation  work,  visiting  14  towns 
and  holding  evangelistic  meetings  during  the  Christmas  holidays,  and  in 
every  case  God  used  their  testimony  in  the  salvation  of  souls,  largely 
young  men.  Professed  conversions  are  reported  to  the  number  of  270  and 
thousands  received  great  and  lasting  spiritual  benefit.  The  result  in  the 
colleges  represented  has  .been  a  strong  spiritual  work  during  the  college 
year  and  an  increased  number  of  students  giving  their  lives  to  the  Lord's 
work. 

Secretaries  and  physical  directors  to  the  number  of  22  are  employed 
in  the  state  and  two  fields  are  vacant.  The  resignation  of  State  Secre- 
tary Hildreth  in  September  was  a  severe  loss  to  the  work.  William 
Francis  has  been  acting  secretary  since  that  time. 

JOHN  H.  ELLIOTT,  Cor.  Mem. 

MISSISSIPPI. 
Tin*  work  in  Mississippi  has  been  nearly  at  a  stand  still  the  past  year. 


63 

We  have  had  three  meetings  of  the  State  Committee  but  have  been 
unable  to  put  a  secretary  in  the  field.  With  the  consent  of  the  Alabama 
committee  we  hope  to  secure  its  secretary  for  a  few  months  the  present 
year.  Natchez  still  maintains  and  enlarges  her  work,  but  is  the  only 
thriving  Association  in  the  state.  Secretary  H.  P.  Andersen  was  with  us 
at  a  meeting  in  December  and  has  done  everything  he  could  for  us  in 
justice  to  his  already  heavy  work.  The  college  work  has  improved. 
Looking  to  the  Master  for  help  we  hope  yet  to  do  something. 

J.  B.  DOBYNS,  Cor.  Mem. 

MISSOUEI. 

Immediately  following  the  State  Convention,  the  matter  of  district 
work  was  taken  up  and  vigorously  prosecuted.  Changes  were  made  in 
the  boundaries,  committees  appointed,  meetings  of  the  same  held,  their 
work  outlined,  and  conferences  arranged  for.  Four  of  these  were  held, 
with  an  aggregate  attendance  of  160,  and  collections  for  state  work 
amounted  to  $327.  A  beginning  was  also  made  in  the  holding  of  local 
conferences,  and  we  believe  they  demonstrated  the  great  power  for  good 
that  lies  in  this  channel. 

We  employed  J.  S.  Langhorne  and  S.  A.  Kincaide  as  assistant  secre- 
taries and  assigned  them  to  work  in  Sedalia  and  Hannibal,  their  expenses 
being  borne  by  the  Associations  enjoying  their  services,  and  with  the 
result  that  they  were  finally  called  by  the  respective  Associations  to 
become  their  general  secretaries. 

The  college  work  is  in  a  healthier  and  better  condition  than  ever  before. 
This,  in  a  large  measure,  is  to  be  attributed  to  the  "intercollegiate 
letter,"  the  visits  of  the  deputation  men,  the  conference  of  presidents, 
and  the  summer  school,  in  conjunction  with  the  intelligent  and  valuable 
oversight  given  by  the  State  Secretary. 

No  special  features  of  local  work  require  particular  mention,  the  Asso- 
ciations, with  but  few  exceptions,  being  in  a  healthy  condition.  The  St. 
Louis  Association  has  disposed  of  the  old  quarters,  llth  and  Locust 
streets,  for  $128,000  (the  price  paid  for  this  property  by  the  Association 
12  years  ago  was  $37,500).  All  the  secretarial  points  are  well  manned, 
and  we  have  not,  as  a  year  ago,  to  report  vacant  fields. 

The  number  of  Associations  in  the  state  is  40 — city  and  town.  18;  col- 
lege, 15;  railroad,  4;  German,  2;  colored,  1.  Of  these  39  report  a  mem- 
bership of  7,916;  36  expended  $85,007  for  current  expenses;  10  own  build- 
ings and  real  estate  valued  at  $474,500;  21  report  an  average  daily  attend- 
ance at  rooms  of  1,870;  38  report  an  average  weekly  attendance  at  gospel 
meetings  of  1,854;  24  report  an  average  weekly  attendance  at  Bible  classes 
of  275;  22  report  558  young  men  seeking  religious  counsel,  and  277  addi- 
tions to  the  churches.  The  secretarial  force  of  the  state  numbers  35. 

A  very  successful  State  Convention  was  held  at  Carthage  in  October, 
with  163  delegates.  Secretaries  Taggart  and  Boots,  of  the  International 
-Committee,  rendered  invaluable  service  by  their  presence  and  efforts. 

E.  P.  V.  BITTER,  Cor.  Mem. 

NEBBASKA. 

Nebraska,  with  a  population  of  a  little  over  one  million,  has  a  member- 


64 

ship  of  3,330,  an  increase  in  one  year  of  30  per  cent.  There  are  now  36 
Associations;  24  general  (5  new  ones),  10  college,  2  railroad.  Omaha 
Association  is  the  largest  and  has  a  membership  of  1,056;  its  property  is 
valued  at  $200,000,  and  while  there  is  a  mortgage  indebtedness  of  $75,000, 
there  is  a  rental  income  of  89,000  per  year  to  offset  it.  Lincoln  Associa- 
tion has  moved  into  its  new  building,  one  of  the  best  equipped  in  the 
country.  The  plant  is  valued  at  $100,000,  but  is  considerably  incum- 
bered. 

The  State  Convention  was  held  at  Hastings,  in  November,  with  an 
attendance  of  400.  A  large  number  of  those  present  were  college 
students,  and  were  greatly  helped  by  J.  R.  Mott,  of  the  Inter- 
national Committee.  The  summer  conference  for  Bible  study  and 
Association  training  was  held  in  August,  at  Beatrice,  with  an  attendance 
of  200.  Eleven  students  attended  the  Lake  Geneva  conference,  and  one 
that  at  Northfield.  A  college  band  of  four  gave  their  vacation  to  work 
for  young  men,  and  as  a  result  30  young  men  expressed  a  desire  to  lead  a 
Christian  life.  Two  hundred  and  ninety -five  young  men  have  expressed  a 
desire  to  become  Christians,  through  Association  work.  There  are  seven 
boys'  Associations  with  a  membership  of  261.  Three  district  conventions 
were  held.  The  county  work  in  Gage  county  has  been  discontinued, 
because  no  suitable  secretary  could  be  secured  to  take  the  place  of  Mr. 
Montgomery,  who  resigned. 

Thirty-nine  hundred  dollars  have  been  expended  in  the  state  work. 
The  indebtedness  of  the  committee  at  the  convention  was  $524;  $1,500 
was  there  subscribed  to  cover  this  and  to  apply  on  the  coming  year's 
work.  Mr.  Nash,  who  has  been  State  Secretary  since  June,  1888,  has 
resigned  to  go  into  foreign  mission  work.  His  successor  has  not  yet  been 
chosen. 

The  veteran  International  Secretary,  Robert  Weidensall,  whose  home  is- 
in  this  state,  has  given  much  assistance  by  his  counsel  and  timely  advice. 
Acknowledgement  should  also  be  made  of  the  services  of  Secretaries 
Wishard  and  Mott,  of  the  International  Committee. 

C.  R  HARRISON,  Cor.  Mem. 


NEW  HAMPSHIRE. 

The  work  was  never  before  on  so  good  footing  in  this  state  ;  there  is  a 
larger  membership  and  more  money  is  being  expended  for  young  men. 
The  Keene  Association  expects  to  break  ground  about  May  1  for  a  three- 
story  brick  building,  to  cost,  with  lot,  $30,000.  The  Concord  Associa- 
tion has  received  a  fine  lot  for  its  proposed  building.  Nashua  has  re- 
ceived a  legacy  of  between  $40,000  and  $50,000,  which  means  a  building  in 
the  near  future. 

The  twenty -fifth  annual  convention,  held  at  Concord,  December  8-11, 
was  well  attended  and  very  helpful.  The  International  Committee  was 
represented  by  H.  M.  Moore,  of  Boston,  and  Secretary  John  R.  Hague. 
The  Maine,  Vermont  and  New  Hampshire  State  Committees  have  ar- 
ranged for  a  joint  employment  of  R.  H.  Shelton  for  the  ensuing  year. 
The  International  Committee  has  always  responded  promptly  to  any  call 
from  our  state,  and  many  thanks  are  due  for  valuable  assistance  rendered, 

H.  E.  FAY,  Cor.  Mem.

NEW  JEESEY. 

The  Associations  in  this  state  are  in  a  generally  healthful  and  progress- 
ive condition.  An  increase  is  noted  in  the  number  of  Associations  and 
their  membership,  in  attendance  at  young  men's  meetings,  in  current  ex- 
penses and  value  of  buildings.  The  building  feature  is  especially  mani- 
fest. The  Trenton  and  Paterson  Associations  occupy  their  new  buildings, 
the  former  valued  at  $130,000,  the  latter  $65,000.  The  new  organization  at 
Long  Branch  began  life  in  a  $10,000  home.  Summit  is  building  at  a  cost 
of  $20,000.  The  $40,000  building  at  Plainfield  will  be  erected  at  once. 

The  spiritual  tone  of  the  work  is  excellent,  more  conversions  than  ever 
being  reported.  This  feature  is  especially  marked  in  the  college  depart- 
ment. At  Princeton  at  least  one  hundred  have  professed  conversion.  In 
the  eight  institutions  having  Associations  65  per  cent,  of  the  students  are 
professing  Christians. 

The  railroad  work  is  in  a  promising  condition.  Kooms  have  been 
opened  at  Trenton  under  a  general  secretary,  and  full  organization  is  in 
progress  at  Camden  and  Jersey  City.  The  International  Committee, 
through  its  railroad  secretary,  Mr.  Hicks,  rendered  a  very  important 
service  in  connection  with  the  inauguration  of  the  work  at  these  points. 

District  conventions  have  been  held  in  the  six  districts,  with  strong 
programs  and  followed  by  definite  results  including  conversions  in  each 
case.  The  recent  state  meeting  at  Camden  was  the  best  ever  held,  both 
in  the  character  of  the  program  presented  and  the  quality  of  the  delegates. 
Its  local  influences  were  very  helpful,  including  the  beginning  of  a  gen- 
erous building  fund.  The  state  work  is  well  organized,  with  D.  F.  More 
as  State  Secretary. 

EDWABD  P.  HOI/DEN,  Cor.  Mem. 


NEW  YOBK. 

There  are  150  Associations  with  a  membership  of  40,000.  Six  new  As- 
sociations have  been  organized.  Ten  new  points  have  been  opened  for 
general  secretaries.  The  number  of  paid  officers  is  214.  Greater  perma- 
nency is  to  be  noted  in  the  secretarial  office.  This  satisfactory  result  is 
due  largely  to  the  efficient  work  of  our  State  Secretary  and  his  assistants. 
The  return  of  Mr.  Hall  to  the  work,  after  his  long  illness,  is  a  cause  of 
thankfulness  to  Association  men  throughout  the  state. 

The  number  of  buildings  is  45— valued  at  $3,004,250.  Building  lots  and 
other  real  estate  are  owned  amounting  to  $119,400,  and  endowment  and 
library  funds  of  $303,495,  making  a  total  of  $3,427,145.  New  buildings 
have  been  secured  at  Canarsie,  Corning,  Glens  Falls  and  Port  Jervis.  The 
Binghamton  railroad  branch  has  secured  a  lot.  At  Elmira,  the  New  York, 
Lake  Erie  &  Western  branch,  has  paid  for  its  building.  Harlem  has 
$50,000  pledged  toward  its  indebtedness.  As  a  result  of  the  last  State 
Convention,  Auburn  has  secured  $20,000  to  clear  off  a  long-carried  burden 
of  debt.  Elrnira  has  raised  $40,000  to  make  good  the  gift  of  Mrs.  J.  Dor- 
man  Steele  of  $10,000  for  a  building,  and  $25,000  for  a  library.  Buffalo 
German  department  has  $17,000  pledged  towards  a  building.  The  West 
Troy  Association  has  its  new  home  inclosed.  A  $60,000  building  is  ex- 
pected to  be  ready  at  Tonawanda  in  April.  Geneva  has  30,000  pledged 
toward  its  building,  now  being  erected.  New  York  city  German  branch 


66 

has  paid  its  $20,000  debt.  Newburgh  has  received  $5,000  from  the  late  T. 
S.  Quackenbush.  It  is  expected  the  Syracuse  University  Association  will 
receive  $5,000  from  the  estate  of  D.  Edgar  Grouse.  By  the  will  of  the  late 
David  Ingalls  property  valued  at  $100,000  is  bequeathed  to  the  Buffalo 
Association,  subject  to  a  life  annuity. 

Ten  district  conventions  were  held  (one  being  a  conference  of  presi- 
dents and  secretaries  only)  with  an  aggregate  attendance  of  799  as  against 
596  last  year.  Collections  taken  secured  money  enough  to  pay  all  ex- 
penses and  a  balance  over  of  $149  towards  state  work.  These  conven- 
tions, by  their  discussion  of  practical,  every-day  Association  work,  are 
stimulating  every  delegate  to  more  intelligent  service. 

Boys'  branches  are  conducted  in  58  places,  and  have  a  membership  of 
4,279.  Mr.  Dudley  is  more  devoted  than  ever  to  this  department,  but  is 
able  to  give  only  a  portion  of  his  time  to  the  work.  Boys'  conferences 
were  held  in  three  sections  with  increased  attendance.  The  boys' camp 
was  attended  by  72  boys  from  8  Associations.  During  one  quarter  of  the 
year  there  were  47  professed  conversions  among  the  boys. 

Gilbert  A.  Beaver,  college  secretary  of  Pennsylvania,  assisted  in  our 
state  work  for  one  month,  during  which  time  he  visited  all  but  one  or  two 
of  the  College  Associations,  with  satisfactory  results.  We  should  have 
sufficient  help  to  visit  all  the  colleges  twice  a  year.  By  efforts  among  the 
fitting  schools  we  secured  the  names  of  300  young  men,  and  introduced 
each  to  the  Association  in  the  college  that  he  expected  to  enter. 
About  50  college  men  from  New  York  attended  the  Northfield  Conference. 

The  27  Railroad  Associations,  with  8,625  members,  employing  27  gen- 
eral secretaries,  and  occupying  13  buildings,  expressly  erected  for  or  as- 
signed to  their  use,  are  doing  thoroughly  practical  work,  and  each  of 
them  reports  fully  every  quarter.  C.  L.  Gates,  of  the  International  Com- 
mittee, visited  most  of  our  Railroad  Associations,  and  was  able  to  ac- 
complish much  in  infusing  new  energy  and  system  into  the  work  of  this 
department. 

There  are  76  gymnasiums,  with  39  physical  directors  and  assistants.  A 
state  field  day  of  all-round  games  was  held  on  the  New  York  grounds  in 
September.  Twelve  Associations  were  represented  and  sixteen  medals 
awarded. 

Our  educational  work  is  advancing,  many  classes  along  industrial  lines 
being  successfully  conducted.  An  interesting  exhibit  in  these  lines  was 
made  at  our  annual  State  Convention. 

Bible  study  has  been  encouraged,  courses  outlined  and  thorough 
organization  urged.  The  spiritual  results  of  the  steady  work  of  the  year 
are  the  most  encouraging  features  of  the  work.  From  correspondence 
and  the  visits  of  the  secretaries  increased  attention  to  the  spiritual  wel- 
fare of  young  men  is  noticeable. 

The  work  at  the  state  military  camp  is  increasing  in  appreciation  on  the 
part  of  the  militia.  There  was  a  daily  attendance  of  over  400,  a  large 
increase  over  previous  years,  and  a  daily  correspondence  of  over  200 
letters.  The  services  were  well  attended  and  fruitful  in  results.  Fifty- 
five  new  memberships  were  secured. 

There  are  four  non-English  speaking  Associations.  One  has  been 
securing  money  for  a  building,  another  to  clear  away  its  debt. 

The  annual  convention  was  held  at  Saratoga,  February  23-26.     Despite
