a,  severe  storm  and  snow  blockade  between  five  and  six  hundred  delegates 
were  present.  The  convention  was  a  success,  especially  in  the  spiritual 
results;  a  strong  religious  interest  was  manifest  and  many  conversions 
were  reported  at  the  meetings.  The  secretaries  conference  was  held  in 
Albany  preceding  the  convention  with  an  attendance  of  142.  State 
Secretary  Hall's  presence  at  both  gatherings,  after  his  absence  of  last  year, 
was  a  source  of  pleasure  to  all. 

WM.  H.  MIGRAINES,  Cor.  Mem. 

NORTH  CAROLINA. 

The  Association  year  in  this  state  has  not  developed  quite  the  vigor  that 
was  foreshadowed  at  the  Greensboro  convention  in  March  last;  the 
distractions  incident  to  the  political  canvass  of  1892  and  the  continued 
financial  difficulties  of  this  section  have  made  the  year  one  of  arduous 
work,  though  there  is  abundant  evidence  that  the  organization  is  taking 
deeper  root  and  winning  greater  respect  and  confidence. 

Our  two  secretaries  have  followed  the  plan  previously  outlined — to 
foster  the  work  chiefly  in  the  larger  towns,  while  establishing  it  in  smaller 
places  whenever  an  opportunity  occurs.  Raleigh  has  been  re-opened  as 
£i  secretarial  point  and  a  fine  work  has  been  done  there. 

The  only  "departure"  during  the  year  has  been  the  establishment  of 
a  county  work,  under  E.  L.  Harris,  in  Robeson  county;  it  has  com- 
menced under  auspicious  circumstances,  and  good  work  has  already  been 
done. 

The  district  conventions  this  year,  which  almost  necessarily  occur  in 
the  fall,  were  only  moderately  attended,  owing  to  the  intense  interest 
.aroused  by  the  political  campaign,  but  the  work  done  was  of  great  value. 

GEO.  B.  HAKNA,  Cor.  Mem. 

NORTH  DAKOTA. 

The  work  in  this  state  has,  notwithstanding  the  depression  in  business 
circles,  made  a  decided  advance.  The  city  work  at  Grand  Forks  has 
been  organized  on  Association  principles,  with  M.  B.  Yan  Vranken  as  gen- 
eral secretary,  and  is  prospering  under  his  leadership.  In  the  city  and 
railroad  work  at  Fargo  good  has  also  been  accomplished ;  the  member- 
ship has  increased  about  33  1-3  per  cent.,  while  the  work  among  the  rail- 
road employees  has  made  steady  progress.  Messrs.  Brown,  of  the  inter- 
national force,  and  Chase,  of  the  local  Association,  have  also  organized 
the  work  in  Fargo  College.  In  the  State  Normal  School,  at  Mayville,  the 
work  has  also  been  organized.  We  plan  also  to  come  into  closer  relations 
with  the  Indian  Associations  the  coming  year.  We  now  have  one  town, 
one  railroad  and  city,  four  Indian,  and  three  college  Associations,  making 
nine  in  all,  and  with  the  prospect  of  soon  adding  another  College  Associa- 
tion at  the  State  Agricultural  College  at  Fargo.  Secretary  H.  E.  Brown, 
of  the  International  Committee,  has  rendered  the  work  most  valuable 
assistance.  WM.  H.  WHITE,  Cor.  Mem. 

OHIO. 

The  promise  of  a  year  ago  has  been  happily  fulfilled.  The  College 
Associations  have  continued  their  activitv,  with  better  methods  and  with 


68 

the  benefit  of  a  wider  experience.  Perhaps  no  one  agency  was  more  pro- 
ductive of  good  than  the  conference  of  presidents  of  College  Associations, 
held  in  April,  at  Otterbein  University.  There  were  present  36  students, 
representing  29  colleges,  and  of  these  23  were  presidents  of  Associations 
for  the  next  college  year.  This  was  the  first  gathering  of  the  kind 
known  in  the  country.  Its  great  success  will  probably  lead  to  the  organ- 
ization of  similar  conferences  in  other  states,  which  will  surely  give  a 
decided  impetus  to  the  work  in  educational  institutions.  Nor  has  the  effort 
been  relaxed  in  the  local  work  among  the  students  in  the  large  cities  and 
other  educational  centers. 

Gratifying  progress  has  been  made  in  the  Railroad  Associations.  A 
new  branch  of  the  Cincinnati  Association  was  opened  March  11,  and  the 
finely  arranged  and  handsomely  furnished  rooms  are  freely  used  by  the 
railroad  men.  T?His  branch  alone  has  a  membership  of  320. 

Constant  effort  has  been  made  to  increase  the  efficiency  of  the  Associa- 
tions generally.  The  reports  of  the  State  Convention  show  a  great  interest 
in  Bible  study  and  in  the  strictly  religious  work.  At  the  same  time,  the 
number  of  men  devoting  their  entire  time  to  the  Associations  has  increased 
from  75  to  86,  of  whom  43  are  general  secretaries.  There  are  also  14 
educated  physical  directors — a  larger  number  than  ever  before.  The 
State  Committee  has  kept  three  men  in  the  field  and  has  expended  nearly 
$7,000  in  its  supervisory  work.  The  State  Convention  was  held  at  Lima, 
in  February,  and  was  largely  attended.  It  was  one  of  the  best  conven- 
tions held  in  the  state,  and  left  upon  the  community  a  most  gratifying 
influence.  The  outlook  for  the  coming  year  is  exceedingly  bright.  The 
International  Committee  and  its  agents  have  rendered  helpful  service. 

H.  P.  LLOYD,  Cor,  Mem. 

OREGON,  WASHINGTON,  BRITISH  COLUMBIA,  AND  IDAHO. 

The  year  has  been  a  trying  one,  the  depression  in  business  making  the 
financial  problem  very  serious  to  both  general  and  local  fields.  But  still 
a  vigorous  work  has  been  carried  on.  Our  territory  is  an  immense  one, 
containing  588,000  square  miles,  with  a  population  of  over  950,000,  of 
whom  150,000  are  young  men  under  thirty.  The  agencies  at  work  for  the 
destruction  of  young  manhood  are  legion.  Never  had  sin  and  Satan  so 
fair  a  field  as  in  the  Pacific  Northwest.  A  prominent  clergyman  address- 
ing our  last  convention  said:  " Tradition,  conventionalism,  custom, are 
restraints  in  other  lands,  but  in  this  Pacific  Northwest  we  lightly  over- 
leap them  and  laugh  them  to  scorn."  There  are  at  present  thirty-five 
Associations  in  our  territory;  twenty  local,  fourteen  college,  one  railroad. 
The  executive  committee  consists  of  twenty-one  business  men,  represent- 
ing the  leading  cities.  James  A.  Dummett  is  the  traveling  secretary,  now 
in  his  third  year,  and  is  doing  excellent  work.  The  ninth  annual  conven- 
tion, held  at  Tacoma,  was  a  successful  one.  There  were  present  161  dele- 
gates, representing  19  local  Associations,  with  a  total  membership  of 
3,367.  Eighteen  Associations  expended  $37,760  for  current  expenses. 

District  work  is  better  organized  and  three  interesting  conferences  were 
held  during  the  year.  The  work  of  securing  corresponding  members  is 
being  pushed  with  vigor.  College  work  is  a  most  encouraging  feature. 
A  splendid  conference  was  held  at  the  State  Agricultural  College,  Cor- 


69 

vallis,  Oregon,  February  24-26.  Twelve  institutions  were  represented  by 
145  delegates.  The  reports  presented  show  that  112  young  men  were 
converted  in  the  College  Associations  during  the  year. 

Building  matters  have  been  at  a  standstill,  owing  to  the  financial 
stringency.  Portland,  Seattle  and  Tacoma  are  working  toward  this  end. 
Albany,  Oregon,  has  erected  a  small  building  to  be  dedicated  in  April. 

Valuable  aid  has  been  rendered  by  the  International  Committee 
through  correspondence  and  by  the  visits  of  its  secretaries,  C.  L.  Gates 
and  Logan  H.  Roots. 

J.  THOBBUBN  Ross,  Cor.  Mem. 

PENNSYLVANIA. 

We  have  143  Associations  in  the  state,  a  gain  of  13,  with  116  paid 
officers,  including  general  secretaries,  assistants,  physical  directors, 
librarians  and  State  Secretaries,  a  net  gain  of  7  for  the  year.  The  total 
membership  as  per  report  at  the  Germantown  cenvention  is  21,673  ;  104 
Associations  report  3,597  members  serving  on  committees  ;  23  own  build- 
ings valued  at  $1,469,403  ;  78  report  total  value  of  property,  funds,  etc., 
above  indebtedness,  $1,812,375. 

The  interest  along  all  lines  of  work  during  the  last  year  has  been  per- 
haps greater  than  in  any  previous  year  in  our  history. 

The  International  Committee  has  rendered  valuable  aid  through 
Secretaries  Morse  and  Taggart,  and  the  work  of  Secretary  Mott,  in  our 
conference  of  College  Association  presidents  was  especially  helpful. 

C.  H.  ZEHNDEB,  Cor.  Mem. 


RHODE  ISLAND. 

(See  Massachusetts. ) 

SOUTH  CAROLINA. 

Various  causes  have  worked  against  any  marked  or  aggressive  progress 
in  South  Carolina,  especially  the  failure  of  the  cotton  crop  and  the  con- 
sequent exceeding  stringency  in  financial  matters.  We  were  also  several 
months  without  a  State  Secretary. 

The  Edgefield  county  organization  has  been  very  successful.  The 
work  in  Columbia  has  been  reorganized,  is  now  on  a  much  firmer  basis, 
and  the  outlook  is  full  of  encouragement.  The  Charleston  Association  is 
at  present  engaged  in  what  appears  to  be  a  successful  effort  to  raise  the 
debt  on  its  building.  Aiken,  Walterboro  and  several  other  places  are 
doing  good  work.  Several  Associations  have  disbanded  including  Green- 
ville and  Orangeburg. 

I  am  not  able  to  give  the  exact  number  of  Associations  in  the  state  at 
the  present  time.  There  are  eight  College  Associations,  including  every 
important  institution,  and  in  nearly  every  case  a  fairly  excellent  work  is 
maintained.  Particular  attention  has  been  devoted  to  Bible  study  and 
Bible  teaching.  We  would  place  on  record,  with  gratitude  to  God,  the 
timely  help  of  the  International  Committee,  without  whose  wise  counsel 
and  substantial  assistance  it  is  doubtful  if  our  state  work  could  have  been 
maintained. 


70 

The  State  Committee  is  composed  of  an  earnest-hearted  set  of  men,  and 
they  are  standing  firmly  by  the  work  at  this  critical  period,  and  there  is 
good  reason  to  believe  that  our  state  work  will  before  many  months  be  in 
a  very  much  more  encouraging  condition. 

ATHA  T.  JAMISON,  Cor.  Mem. 

SOUTH  DAKOTA. 

We  have  very  little  to  report  for  the  past  year.  Outside  the  grand 
work  done  in  Sioux  Falls,  under  the  efficient  leadership  of  Secretary 
Wight,  but  little  has  been  done  in  the  state.  A  germ  work  has  been  or- 
ganized at  Huron,  and  the  college  work  at  Vermillion,  Yankton  andRed- 
field  helped.  We  have  been  aided  and  blessed  by  the  visits  of  Secretaries 
Hague  and  Brown  of  the  International  Committee.  We  are  in  hopes  of 
more  aggressive  work  in  our  state  the  coming  year. 

C.  S.  PALMEB,  Cor.  Mem. 

TENNESSEE. 

While  we  report  a  decrease  in  the  number  of  Associations,  this  loss  is  more 
than  compensated  for  by  the  increase  both  in  the  number  and  efficiency 
of  the  membership.  There  are  to-day  39  Associations  with  a  membership 
of  4,164;  number  of  members  serving  on  committees  710;  total  average 
attendance  at  young  men's  meetings  1,314.  Nine  Associations  report 
special  work  for  boys. 

The  work  for  young  men  in  our  institutions  of  learning  is  steadily  in- 
creasing in  efficiency,  the  most  marked  improvement  being  shown  in  the 
organized  effort  to  reach  new  students  and  in  the  increase  in  the  number 
of  Bible  classes  and  those  attending  them.  Our  College  Associations  have 
been  greatly  helped  by  the  visits  of  Secretaries  Brockman  and  Roots. 
The  southern  deputation  conference  as  well  as  the  southern  student 
summer  school  were  held  for  the  first  time  on  the  grounds  of  the  Univer- 
sity of  Tennessee  at  Knoxville.  Both  of  these  gatherings  have  been  of 
great  value  to  the  college  work  of  our  state. 

Three  district  conferences  have  been  held.  The  State  Convention 
at  Clarksville,  in  October,  had  a  limited  attendance,  the  place  not 
being  accessible  to  the  largest  number  of  our  Associations.  Secretaries 
Ober  and  Roots  represented  the  International  Committee,  and  their 
presence  added  much  to  the  interest  of  the  different  sessions.  By  vote  of 
the  convention  the  headquarters  of  the  State  Committee  were  removed  to 
Nashville. 

The  Memphis  Association  has  recently  fitted  up  and  moved  into  hand- 
some quarters  in  the  center  of  the  business  portion  of  the  city  and  has 
enlarged  its  work  in  all  departments.  The  Clarksville  Association  is  now 
in  the  midst  of  a  successful  building  canvass.  The  Nashville  and  Knox- 
ville Associations  show  a  steady  growth  during  the  year,  the  latter  having 
a  membership  of  640,  the  largest  it  has  ever  known. 

JAMES  H.  COWAN,  Cor.  Mem. 

TEXAS. 

No  special  effort  has  been  made  the  past  year  to  increase  the  number  of 
Associations,  the  work  being  mainly  that  of  strengthening  existing  organ- 


RAILROAD  ASSOCIATION   BUILDING,  HINTON,  VV.  VA. 

DEDICATED  NOVEMBER  u,  1891. 
Dimensions,  35x56  feet.  Cost,  $5,500. 


71 

izations.  We  now  have  33  Associations  in  the  state;  22  general  and  11 
college.  There  are  14  secretarial  points  and  19  persons  give  their  time  to 
the  work.  There  has  been  a  change  of  secretaries  in  six  fields  during  the 
year. 

Four  successful  district  conferences  have  been  held,  the  first  attempt 
at  this  kind  of  work.  The  beginning  was  very  gratifying,  considering 
the  long  distances  between  Associations,  in  some  instances  nearly  1,000 
miles,  and  the  consequent  large  traveling  expenses. 

Two  important  Associations  have  moved  into  new  quarters,  giving  them 
better  facilities  and  increasing  their  opportunities  for  usefulness.  The 
work  throughout  the  state  is  in  better  condition  to-day  than  ever  before, 
and  the  prospect  for  an  unusually  good  year's  work  is  very  flattering. 

The  International  Committee  rendered  us  valuable  assistance  at  our 
last  convention  through  their  representatives,  Messrs.  C.  L.  Gates  and 
F.  S.  Brockman.  Mr.  Brockman  also  gave  the  month  of  November  to  a 
tour  of  visitation  of  the  colleges  of  the  state. 

JUDSON  B.  PALMER,  Cor.  Mem. 


VEEMONT. 

Our  work  is  in  a  very  satisfactory  condition  as  compared  with  the  past. 
A  new  Association  has  been  organized  at  Johnson,  with  a  prospect  of 
accomplishing  effective  work.  The  convention  at  Brattleboro  was  pro- 
nounced by  old  Association  workers  the  best  ever  held  in  the  state.  A 
successful  college  conference  has  been  held  and  the  deputation  work 
appears  to  be  increasing  in  interest  and  results.  Four  Associations  have 
secured  new  secretaries  during  the  year :  Bennington,  C.  J.  Hoyt ; 
Brattleboro,  N.  M.  Simmons;  Eutland,  W.  H.  Fuller  (formerly  of  Brat- 
tleboro); and  St.  Johnsbury,  R.  E.  Lewis,  who  for  the  past  two  years 
has  been  at  the  head  of  the  deputation  work  of  the  state. 

The  State  Committee  secured  a  tent  as  Association  headquarters  at  the 
annual  encampment  of  the  National  Guard  and  the  work  amply  paid. 

Vermont  has  been  for  the  past  two  years  without  a  state  secretary,  but 
arrangements  have  been  made  whereby  R.  H.  Shelton,  State  Secretary  of 
Maine  and  New  Hampshire,  will  devote  one-fourth  of  his  time  to  the  work 
in  this  state,  and  the  committee  is  confident  that  his  services  will  be  a 
great  help. 

Valuable  assistance  has  been  rendered  by  the  International  Committee 
in  the  way  of  correspondence,  counsel,  etc. 

G.  F.  NORTH,  Cor.  Mem. 


VIRGINIA. 

There  has  been  a  noticeable  growth  in  every  department  of  Association 
work.  Five  Associations  have  been  organized,  and  general  secretaries 
employed  in  three  new  fields.  Several  Associations  that  existed  in  name 
only  have  been  dropped  from  our  list,  leaving  58 — 29  local,  19  college, 
9  railroad  and  1  army.  Five  district  conferences  have  been  held  and  one 
conference  of  Railroad  Associations.  In  September  the  independent  Rail- 
road Association  at  Roanoke,  by  vote  of  the  membership,  became  a 
department  of  the  Roanoke  city  Association,  and  is  now  thoroughly 


72 

officered  and  working  along  this  line.  Three  college  deputation  students 
have  given  considerable  time  to  visitation  of  the  several  College  Asso- 
ciations. 

Noticeable  progress  has  been  made  in  the  matter  of  buildings.  The 
Boanoke  Association  owns  and  occupies  a  temporary  building,  costing 
$4,000;  the  Crewe  Kailroad  Association  has  just  completed  a  $4,000  build- 
ing; the  Petersburg  Association  has  now  under  roof  a  building  which, 
when  completed  and  furnished,  will  cost  $55,000.  A  fund  has  been 
secured  for  the  purpose  of  erecting  a  building  for  railroad  men  at  Clifton 
Forge,  amounting  to  $10,500,  and  a  building  has  been  promised  for  rail- 
road men  at  Gladstone,  to  cost  $4,000. 

Fifty -two  Associations  report  a  membership  of  6,256;  8  report  buildings 
valued  at  $149,500;  40  report  day  and  week  of  prayer  observed  last 
November;  27  report  495  professed  conversions. 

The  seventeenth  annual  convention  was  held  at  Norfolk,  Feb.  15-19, 
with  379  delegates.  The  International  Committee  was  represented  by  C. 
K.  Ober  and  H.  P.  Andersen.  About  $4,000  were  pledged  for  state  work 
and  the  amount  will  be  increased  to  $6,000  during  the  year. 

H.  O.  Williams  has  continued  his  services  as  State  Secretary,  being 
ably  assisted  by  W.  B.  Haight,  in  charge  of  the  office  and  detail  work. 
Efficient  service  has  been  rendered  on  frequent  occasions  during  the  year 
by  Secretaries  Hicks,  Ober,  Hunton,  Brockman  and  Andersen  of  the 

International  Committee. 

THOS.  A.  JOHNSON,  Cor.  Mem. 

WASHINGTON. 

(See  Oregon.) 


WEST  VIBGINIA. 

(See  Maryland. ) 

WISCONSIN. 

There  are  38  Associations  (including  departments)  now  in  active  opera- 
tion, with  a  force  of  31  secretaries,  assistants  and  physical  directors.  The 
current  expenses  of  these  Associations  during  the  year  amounted  to  $48,935, 
and  all  are  doing  good  work.  The  net  value  of  the  property  now  held  is 
$236,319— a  gain  of  $34,814  over  a  year  ago.  The  State  Committee 
expended  $6,113,  and  a  small  debt  was  carried  over.  The  eighteenth 
annual  convention,  held  at  Appleton,  was  a  good  meeting,  with  a  fair 
attendance.  International  Secretaries  Wishard  and  Hicks  rendered  valu- 
able assistance.  The  lumbermen's  work  has  been  conducted  now  for 
eleven  years  and  is  growing  in  value  and  results  each  season.  Forty -nine 
district  conventions  and  local  conferences  have  been  held  with  excellent 
results  in  conversions  and  financial  aid.  Bible  study  has  been  specially 
emphasized,  and  the  entire  state  work  put  on  a  more  solid  basis  than 
ever  before.  C.  B.  WZLLIS,  Cor.  Mem.

TABLE  IV.— COLLEGE  DEPARTMENT. 


orf 


428  College  Associations  are  in  existence. 

42  have  been  organized  this  year. 
374  have  reported  statistics  of  their  work. 
366  Report  a  total  Membership  of  25,207. 
364       "       an  Active  Membership  of  18,548. 
331       "       6,504  Members  serving  on  Committees. 
210       "      $40,225  paid  out  last  year  for  current  Expenses. 
121       "       Rooms  devoted  exclusively  to  their  use. 

30       "       Libraries  containing  8,440  volumes. 
112       "       300  Lectures  or  Entertainments. 
199       "       520  Sociables.

Eighteen  Departments  own  and  occupy  buildings  valued  at  $128,000;  nine  Departments  have 
building  funds  paid  in  amounting  to  $14,311,  and  five  Departments  own  other  real  estate  valued  at 
$16,800.

railroad  companies  or  officials.

THIS  SCHOOL  STANDS 


for  the  best  possible  training  for  leu 
in  the  definite  organized  and  aggressive 
work   of    the    Young   Men's    Christian 
Association  for  young  men  throughout 
the  world. 


The   International 

Young  Men's  Christian  Association 
Training  School, 

SPRINGFIELD.  MASS. 


ORIGIN  : 

Established,   1885  ;    incorporated  under  present  name,   1890. 

OBJECT  : 

To  train  Christian  young  men  for  the  General  Secretary-ship  and  Physical 
Director-ship  of  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations. 

DEMAND 

For  trained  leaders  continues  several  times  greater  than  the  supply. 

RESULTS : 

The  School  has  helped  train  more  than  one  out  of  every  ten  Secretaries 
employed  to-day  by  the  Associations  in  this  country;  four  out  of  every  ten  of  the 
Physical  Directors;  besides  four  Secretaries  and  one  Physical  Director  in 
foreign  lands. 


}.    T.     BOWNE,    Su.pt.   Secretarial  Department. 
LUTHER     GULICK,     M.  D.,    Supt.   Physical  Department. 


DROP  A  POSTAL  FOR 

STH  CATALOGUE  TO 

INSTRUCTION  BY  MAIL  r\      p 

FOR  THOSE  WHO  CAN'T 

GET  TO   THE   SCHOOL.  Corresponding  Secretary. 


Xll 

EbUOlTlONdL   WORK 

IN  THE  WEST,  CONSISTING  OF 

I.  The  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  Training 

School, 

CHICAGO, 


Established  and  Incorporated  in  June,  1890,  endorsed  as  an  INTERNATIONAL 
TRAINING  SCHOOL  by  the  International  Convention,  at 
their  meeting  in  Kansas  City,  May,  1891. 

OBJECT. 

To  train  young  men  for  the  duties  of  General  Secretaries,  Physical  Directors  and  other 
officers  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian  Associations. 

COURSE    OF    STUDY. 

The  complete  course  covers  two  years,  and  comprises  in  its  Secretarial  and  Physical  De- 

partments: First,  a  thorough  and  systematic  course  of  theoretical  studies,  covering  every 

phase  of  Association  work;  Second,  a  practical  training,  each  student  being  assigned  to 

regular  duties  in  one  of  the  nine  departments  of  the  City  As- 

sociation; Third,  a  comprehensive  study  of  the  Bible,  and  bow 

to  use  and  teach  it;  Fourth,  training  in  the  conduct  of  tbe 

BIBLE   TRAINING  CLASS,  and  how  to  do   PERSONAL  WORK; 

Fifth,  daily  instructions  in  gymnastics. 

NEW    EQUIPMENT. 

The  bright,  cheerful  and  spacious  class  rooms  of  tbe  School 
in  the  new  Association  Building,  which  will  be  ready  for  oc- 
cupancy this  fall,  arid  the  magnificent  advantages  offVred  by 
the  new  Gymnasium  which  will  be  the  fluent  and  mo.*t  thor- 
oughly equipped  Association  Gymnasium  on  th;s  Continent. 
will  greatly  add  to  the  efficiency  of  the  School  for  the  coming 
year. 

CALENDAR.  -FOURTH  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

FALL    TERM.  —  Begins    Wednesday  morning,    September 

1'Uh.  Ie9:<. 
WINTER    TERM.—  Begins  Wednesday  morning,  January 

3d.  1894. 
SPRING  TERM.—  Begins  Monday  morning,  April  2d,  1894. 

ESTIMATED  COST  FOR  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

Tuition,  $50;  Living  Expenses  for  the  School  Tear,  includ- 
ing Board,  Room,  Association  Membership.  Gymnasium  Suit, 
Laundry,  Text  Books  and  attendance  upon  Convention, 
estimated  at  $-225  to  $300.

XIX 


CAST-STEEL  WORKS 


OF 


FRIED.  KRUPP, 


ES3EJT,  GERMANY. 


AMERICAN    OFFICE: 

1 5  GOLD  ST.,  NEW  YORK. 


».  o, 


Represented  by  THOMAS  PROSSER  &  SON. 


These  Works  cover  an  area  of  1,200  acres,  employ  about  18,000  men, 
have  the  most  improved  plant,  and  stand  unique,  from  the  fact  that  they 
have  their  own  Ore  and  Coal  Mines,  Blast  Furnaces,  etc. ,  and  that  every 
stage  of  manufacture  is  under  their  own  supervision,  and  are  not  (like 
others)  dependent  on  the  open  market  for  a  miscellaneous  assortment  of 
crude  material,  which,  in  connection  with  75  years'  experience,  enables 
them  to  turn  out  a  product  of  a  very  superior  quality,  second  to  none,  and 
at  the  same  time  the  different  grades  of  Steel  are  always  of  the  same 
uniform  quality. 

Locomotive  Tires,  Steel  Tired  Wheels, 

Axles,  Crank  Pins,  Shafts  and 

Steel  Forgings  up  to  70  Tons. 

Steel  of  every  description,  Forged,  Rolled,  etc.,  into 
any  form  or  article  desired. 


After  a  test  of  over  35  years,  the  "  Krupp  Tire  "  has  proved  itself  to  be 
the  best  in  the  market,  and  parties  intending  ordering  Locomotives  would 
do  well  to  insert  in  their  specifications  that  "Krupp  Tires"  be  used  on 
drivers,  and  thereby  obtain  an  article  which  will  give  satisfaction.

THE  GRIFFIN  CAR  WHEEL  CO., 


MANUFACTUEEES  OF 

Car  Wheels  and  Car  Castings, 

Annual  Capacity  75,000  Car  Wheels,

Cor.  Foundry  Street  and  M.  C.  R.R., 
DETROIT,  MICH. 

"  SPECIAL"  "  MACHINED"  CAR  WHEELS. 

We  make  these  wheels  in  the  following  diameters  and  weights: 

42  inches,  -     1,200  pounds. 

40       "  1,000       " 

36       "  750       "               Double  Plate  or 

33       "  600       "                  Open  Spoke. 

30       "  550       " 

28       "  500       " 

They  are  offered  especially  for  passenger  and  locomotive  service 
and  are  made  under  our  System  of  Comparative  Tests,  each  wheel 
having  individual  tests  to  establish  quality. 

These  tests  prove  in  each  case  the  particular  conditions  in  each 
wheel,  and  for  "  Special "  wheels  the  basis  of  strength  is  50  per 
cent,  higher  than  for  standard  wheels  on  any  known  test  for 
strength — "  Pennsylvania,"  etc. 

Our  36-inch,  40-inch  and  42-inch  wheels  are  in  use  on  some  of  the 
leading  railroads,  replacing  steel-tired  wheels.  They  are  bored, 
ground  absolutely  true,  and  balanced  before  shipment.  Further 
information  furnished  upon  application  by 

New  York  Car  Wheel  Works,  Buffalo,  N.  Y.
